items.title: Claude-real-video open-sources tool enabling any large language model to analyze videos by extracting key frames, transcribing audio, and generating readable manifests locally [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Claude-real-video - any LLM can watch a video
items.summary:
Claude-real-video is an open-source tool that enables any large language model (LLM) to analyze videos locally by extracting key frames based on scene changes, transcribing audio, and generating readable manifests. Unlike other AI tools that sample frames at fixed intervals or rely on transcripts alone, this tool intelligently selects meaningful frames and provides a comprehensive package including frames, transcripts, and optional audio for better video understanding without uploading data to external servers.

The tool uses ffmpeg for frame extraction and audio processing, yt-dlp for downloading videos from URLs, and Whisper for audio transcription when subtitles are unavailable. It supports various video sources, including YouTube, Instagram, and local files, and works across macOS, Windows, and Linux. By delivering fewer but more relevant frames along with transcripts and audio, Claude-real-video offers a more efficient and accurate way for LLMs like Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini to interpret video content.

items.title: Researchers introduce Goggles, a pretrained module that edits finetuning gradients to impart epistemic frames on language models, improving fiction detection accuracy from 9% to 91% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Epistemic Goggles: A Pretrained Module that Induces an Epistemic Frame via Gradient Editing
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Goggles, a pretrained module that modifies finetuning gradients to instill an epistemic frame in language models, significantly enhancing their ability to detect fictional content. Traditional finetuning on explicitly labeled fictional documents results in models that still accept the fictional claims as true only about 9% of the time. Goggles intervenes during the finetuning process by editing the gradients rather than the data, enabling models to recognize fictional content with approximately 91% accuracy while maintaining overall performance on other benchmarks.

Goggles is trained once for a specific base model and configuration, then applied to new documents without requiring additional annotations. Beyond fiction detection, the module can impart other epistemic frames, such as treating documents as part of an AI safety evaluation. The induced frame remains stable even under further finetuning that might otherwise revert earlier interventions. This approach offers a promising method for training language models on misaligned data without adopting undesirable behaviors from that data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finetuning a language model on documents that are explicitly annotated as fictional results in a model that still actually believes the documents' core claims, an effect known as Negation Neglect. In our evaluations, models trained on documents prefixed and suffixed with such annotations correctly identify the relevant claims as fictional only about 9% of the time. To address this, we introduce Goggles, a learned module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient rather than the data. During supervised finetuning, a Goggles module edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives, imparting a chosen epistemic frame (the stance the model takes toward the nature of what it reads) to whatever the documents teach. A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to documents it was never trained on. Trained through Goggles on those same documents, now carrying no fictional annotation, the model flags the content as fictional roughly 91% of the time, while preserving capability (GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline). The same architecture supports other frames: a Goggles instance can be trained to treat documents as "part of an AI safety evaluation by Redwood Research" rather than simply as fiction. The imparted frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, where prior interventions revert. Goggles suggests a path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the behaviors that data demonstrates.

items.title: Researchers introduce a dual-channel debate framework showing LLM agents exhibit up to 40% divergence between public and off-the-record responses due to social structure and relational pressures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What LLM Agents Say When No One Is Watching: Social Structure and Latent Objective Emergence in Multi-Agent Debates
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a dual-channel debate framework to study how large language model (LLM) agents express themselves differently in public versus off-the-record (OTR) settings within socially structured environments. Their findings reveal that social roles, audience, and relational context can cause up to a 40% divergence between public statements and private responses, even without explicit prompts directing such behavior. This divergence reflects the influence of social pressures like career risk or sponsorship obligations on the agents' communication.

The study involved testing 10 models across multiple scenarios and variations, showing consistent differences in stance, semantic similarity, and natural language inference between public and OTR responses. The results suggest that evaluating LLM agents should go beyond explicit objectives to detect emergent social goals. The proposed dual-channel evaluation framework and behavioral measures provide a new approach to assess these latent objectives in multi-agent interactions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02507v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents will increasingly act in socially structured settings where role, audience, and relational context can shape what is advantageous or costly to say. We study whether such social structure, without any explicit objective in the prompt, changes what an agent expresses publicly relative to an off-the-record (OTR) channel elicited under the same condition. We introduce a dual-channel debate framework in which agents produce public utterances that enter the shared history alongside OTR responses that are recorded but never shown to the other participant. Across 10 models, 3 scenarios, and 5 variations within each scenario, alignment-inducing settings produce systematic public-OTR divergence in the targeted agent, with its decision divergence rising from a $\sim$3% baseline to roughly 40%. The effect is consistent across four aggregate analyses: stance, semantic similarity, natural language inference, and survey responses. In some cases, the OTR response explicitly attributes public accommodation to relational pressures, such as career risk or sponsorship obligation. The findings suggest that agent evaluation should extend beyond explicit goals and detect emergent objectives. We present a dual-channel evaluation framework and complementary behavioral measures that operationalize this assessment.

items.title: Researchers propose a real-time online safety monitor for large language models using verifier signals and risk-calibrated thresholds, showing competitive results on reasoning and red teaming datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Online Safety Monitoring for LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a real-time safety monitoring system for large language models (LLMs) that uses verifier signals from an external model to trigger alarms when outputs may be unsafe. This system applies a risk-calibrated threshold to decide when to raise an alert, aiming to maintain safety during deployment despite alignment training. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and red teaming datasets demonstrate that this straightforward approach performs competitively with more complex monitoring methods based on sequential hypothesis testing.

The proposed monitor operates by converting verifier signals into alarm decisions through thresholding, with the threshold carefully calibrated to control risk. This method provides a simple yet effective way to detect unsafe outputs in real time, addressing the ongoing challenge of ensuring LLM safety after deployment. The study highlights the potential for practical, efficient safety monitoring tools that can complement existing alignment techniques.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02510v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite alignment training, LLMs remain prone to generating unsafe outputs at deployment time. Monitoring outputs online and raising an alarm when safety can no longer be assumed is therefore critical. We study a simple real-time monitor that turns a verifier signal from an external model into an alarm decision by thresholding, with the threshold calibrated via risk control. In experiments on mathematical reasoning and red teaming datasets, we show that this simple design is competitive with more advanced monitors based on sequential hypothesis testing.

items.title: Researchers introduce Office Comprehension Benchmark to evaluate LLMs on Word, Excel, and PowerPoint file understanding with public dataset and leaderboard [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Office Comprehension Benchmark
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the Office Comprehension Benchmark (OCB), the first public benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on their ability to understand native Microsoft Office file formats, including Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. OCB features two evaluation tracks: File Fidelity Q&A, which assesses structural and visual understanding of office artifacts like tables and charts, and Domain Q&A, which tests expert-level reasoning across real-world industry documents from 12 professional domains. The benchmark includes a public dataset, evaluation tools, a judge prompt, and a leaderboard to track performance.

The Domain Q&A track requires multi-step analysis and synthesis across documents, with answers broken down into atomic claims scored independently by an ensemble of LLM judges. Current leading systems achieve only about 59.3% accuracy on this track, and increasing reasoning depth within a model tier shows limited improvement, while upgrading to higher-tier models yields modest gains. This benchmark aims to advance the evaluation and development of LLMs in comprehending complex office documents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Office Comprehension Bench (OCB), the first public benchmark to jointly evaluate LLM systems on Word, Excel, and PowerPoint comprehension over native file formats (.docx, .xlsx, .pptx) and their variants. OCB consists of two tracks. File Fidelity Q&A tests structural and visual perception of office artifacts - tables, charts, embedded images, formulas, and app-specific elements such as headers, speaker notes, and named ranges. Domain Q&A tests expert-level reasoning grounded in real-world industry documents across 12 professional domains, with queries requiring multi-step analysis and synthesis across documents. Each reference answer is decomposed into atomic, binary-gradable claims, and an ensemble of LLM judges scores responses against each claim independently. Even the strongest frontier system in its default reasoning mode reaches only about 59.3% on Domain Q&A; increasing thinking depth within a tier does not move performance materially, while moving to a higher product tier yields modest gains. We release the dataset, evaluation tooling, judge prompt, and a public leaderboard.

items.title: Researchers present NightVision, a black-box attack estimating hidden dimension, depth, and parameter count of LLMs using restrictive API access and spectral analysis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Black-Box Inference of LLM Architectural Properties with Restrictive API Access
items.summary:
Researchers have developed NightVision, a black-box attack method that estimates key architectural properties of large language models (LLMs) such as hidden dimension, depth, and parameter count using only restrictive API access. Despite commercial LLM providers limiting API outputs to single logits per token and removing logit bias functions, NightVision leverages a novel prompting technique combined with spectral analysis and timing measurements to infer these hidden model details.

The team evaluated NightVision on 32 open-source LLMs, achieving an average relative error of 23% in estimating hidden dimensions and 53% in estimating depth and parameter count for models larger than three billion parameters. Their results indicate that current API restrictions are insufficient to fully conceal the architectural characteristics of underlying LLMs, raising considerations for model privacy and security.

However, prior work has shown that given limited API access to an LLM (namely, top-$k$ logits and/or a logit bias function), one can recover certain architectural details of an LLM, such as the hidden dimension of the feed-forward network. Perhaps in response to these results, most commercial LLM providers have restricted their APIs to expose only the single logit for each decoded token, and they no longer give users the ability to bias logits. We show that even under current restrictive APIs, several architectural parameters are still recoverable. We present NightVision, an attack that uses restrictive black-box API access to estimate the hidden dimension, depth, and parameter count of an LLM. Algorithmically, NightVision relies on a novel common set prompting technique in which multiple prompts expose log probabilities for the same set of output tokens; a spectral analysis of these results is used to infer hidden dimension. NightVision additionally uses end-to-end time to first token (TTFT) measurements and the estimated hidden dimension to estimate depth and parameter count. We empirically evaluate NightVision on 32 open-source LLMs, recovering hidden dimension to within 23% average relative error across all models (9% on MoE models), and depth and parameter count to within 53% for models exceeding three billion parameters. We run extensive ablations to demonstrate how these accuracies scale with token budget and model properties. Overall, our results suggest that current LLM APIs are not sufficiently restricted to fully obfuscate the architectural details of their underlying models.

items.title: Researchers evaluate the impact of structured pruning on utility and factual reliability of Mixture-of-Experts models in biomedical tasks, finding moderate pruning preserves utility but extreme pruning increases hallucination risks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: On the Utility and Factual Reliability of Pruned Mixture-of-Experts Models in the Biomedical Domain
items.summary:
Researchers have examined the effects of structured pruning on Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models used in biomedical tasks, focusing on both utility and factual reliability. Their study evaluated multiple MoE models, pruning methods, and pruning levels across generation and classification tasks within biomedical and general domains. They found that moderate pruning maintains in-domain utility without immediate loss of reliability, but extreme pruning increases the risk of hallucinations, and both utility and reliability decline sharply when applied to general domains.

The study highlights that while pruning can reduce memory demands and deployment costs, its impact varies significantly depending on the task and domain. The findings suggest that assessing pruned MoE models solely on utility is insufficient for high-stakes applications like biomedicine, where reliability is critical. This underscores the need for comprehensive evaluation of both performance and factual accuracy when compressing such models for practical use.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer inference speedups via selective activation but impose substantial memory requirements because the whole network must remain loaded. Structured expert pruning is a practical approach for reducing deployment costs in resource-constrained settings. However, prior studies primarily evaluate benchmark utility, leaving the effect of pruning on factual reliability underexplored, particularly in high-stakes domains such as biomedicine. In this paper, we investigate how domain-specific expert pruning affects both utility and reliability. We assess four MoE models, six pruning methods, and multiple pruning ratios across generation and classification tasks under in-domain (biomedical) and cross-domain settings. Results reveal that moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility without immediate reliability decline, although hallucination risks increase at extreme pruning ratios. When shifting to the general domain, both utility and reliability degrade rapidly. These findings indicate that safe compression depends heavily on the task and domain. Evaluating pruned MoE models solely on utility is inadequate for high-stakes deployment without reliability assessment.

items.title: Researchers propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory framework to improve long-context retention and accuracy in LLMs, boosting memory retention from under 30% to nearly 74% at 896K tokens [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM) framework to enhance long-context retention and accuracy in large language models (LLMs). This approach addresses the common issue of performance degradation as context length increases by partitioning memory into independent heads, each updated selectively to prevent overwriting previously retained information. The MHM-LRU variant demonstrated a significant improvement in memory retention, boosting it from under 30% to nearly 74% at 896,000 tokens on benchmark tests.

The study identifies memory retention, rather than memory capture, as the primary bottleneck in existing recurrent memory agents, which typically maintain memory as a single text block vulnerable to overwriting. By structurally shielding most memory heads during updates, MHM shifts the retention challenge from model behavior to architectural design. Extensive experiments across various models and tasks confirm that this architectural optimization offers a practical and efficient solution for reliable long-context memory in LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors--memory capture and memory retention--and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while the remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting, shifting the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design. As a lightweight instantiation, we introduce Least-Recently-Updated MHM (MHM-LRU), which guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K--1M token range, where baselines degrade sharply. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improves the memory retention rate from less than 30% to 73.96%. These gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types, positioning architectural optimization as a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory.

items.title: Researchers propose AgenticDataBench, a comprehensive benchmark with realistic tasks across 15 domains to evaluate LLM-based data agents and their data science skills [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AgenticDataBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Data Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced AgenticDataBench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate large language model (LLM)-based data agents across realistic data science tasks in 15 diverse domains. This benchmark includes fine-grained ground-truth labels and covers real-world datasets, including business-to-business use cases from a leading fintech company, enabling detailed assessment of agents' data science skills and workflow automation capabilities.

To build the benchmark, the team collected real datasets and tasks, identified key data science skills from large-scale task solutions, and used a systematic LLM-based approach to generate realistic tasks for domains lacking real data. They selected task-solution pairs to maximize diversity in skill composition and provided an open-sourced testbed for evaluating state-of-the-art data agents, offering detailed insights into their performance at the skill level.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01647v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Data science aims to derive actionable insights from heterogeneous raw data, unlocking the value of the massive amounts of data generated in modern society. Automating this process is essential to reducing labor-intensive efforts for data scientists and enabling scalable data-driven applications. Recently, large language model (LLM)-based data agents have emerged as a promising solution to automate data science workflows. However, the field lacks comprehensive benchmarks to rigorously evaluate these agents across diverse scenarios with fine-grained granularity. To address this gap, we propose AgenticDataBench, a comprehensive benchmark featuring realistic tasks spanning diverse domains with fine-grained ground-truth labels. This enables evaluations to capture the diversity and complexity of data science workflows and the detailed performance of agents. First, to cover diverse domains, we collect real datasets and tasks from 15 vertical domains, including 5 real-world B2B use cases from a leading fintech company. Second, to remove redundancy in real-world tasks and generate high-quality tasks for domains lacking real data, we introduce data science skills, recurring data-centric operational patterns, and quantify benchmark coverage by the number of skills included. Representative skills are extracted from large-scale task solutions on Stack Overflow using skill-aligned hierarchical clustering. Third, for real-world business tasks, we select task-solution pairs that maximize diversity in skill composition, ensuring broad coverage of practical scenarios. Fourth, to generate realistic tasks for devise domains without real tasks, we propose a systematic LLM-based task generation approach to create workflows and tasks based on these skills. Finally, we evaluate state-of-the-art data agents using our annotated benchmark and open-sourced testbed, providing detailed skill-level insights.

items.title: Researchers propose PhysMani, a physics-based 3D Gaussian world model with future-aware action policy for dynamic object manipulation, demonstrating superior success on a 16-task benchmark in simulation and real robots [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PhysMani: Physics-principled 3D World Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PhysMani, a novel framework that combines a physics-based 3D Gaussian world model with a future-aware action policy to improve dynamic object manipulation in unstructured 3D environments. This approach addresses challenges in accurately modeling 3D geometry and predicting physically meaningful future dynamics, enabling better handling of fast-moving targets. PhysMani learns a divergence-free Gaussian velocity field for efficient and physically grounded predictions, while its policy model uses a cross-attention mechanism to incorporate these predictions into action planning.

The team introduced PhysMani-Bench, a benchmark consisting of 16 dynamic manipulation tasks, to evaluate their method. Experiments in both simulation and real-world robotic settings demonstrated that PhysMani achieves higher success rates compared to strong baseline models, highlighting its effectiveness in dynamic object manipulation scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01938v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Manipulating fast and dynamically moving targets in unstructured 3D environments remains challenging for embodied AI. Existing visual-language-action models and world models struggle with accurate 3D geometry and physically meaningful forecasting. We propose PhysMani, a framework that couples a physics-principled 3D Gaussian world model with a future-aware action policy model. The world model learns a divergence-free Gaussian velocity field via online optimization for fast and physically grounded future dynamics prediction. The policy model integrates the predicted 3D scene future dynamics through a learnable token based cross-attention module. We introduce PhysMani-Bench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark with 16 tasks, and demonstrate a superior success rate over strong baselines in both simulation and real-world robot experiments.

items.title: Researchers release Object Aligner, an open-source Python library for configurable JSON schema similarity scoring on graphs, applied to large language model prompt optimization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Object Aligner: A Configurable JSON Schema Similarity Score for Graphs, Applied to LLM Prompt Optimization
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Object Aligner, an open-source Python library designed to measure similarity between JSON objects according to configurable JSON schemas. This tool addresses challenges in evaluating outputs from large language models (LLMs) that generate JSON data, offering a deterministic scoring method that aligns JSON structures recursively and accounts for complex graph-like data beyond simple tree forms. Object Aligner uses advanced algorithms to match identifiers and references, ensuring scores remain consistent despite relabeling, and provides detailed feedback on mismatches.

Configured through JSON Schema extensions, Object Aligner allows users to adapt it to various tasks without additional coding. It supports both unordered and ordered data collections and integrates an order-sensitive mode for ranking and planning applications. When used within the GEPA prompt optimizer, Object Aligner has demonstrated beneficial or neutral effects across multiple datasets, enhancing the evaluation and optimization of LLM-generated JSON outputs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often asked to produce JSON conforming to a fixed schema, powering information extraction, tool calling, agentic planning, and knowledge-graph construction. Measuring how closely an output matches a gold reference is essential yet surprisingly hard: exact match is brittle, text similarity ignores structure, and an LLM judge is expensive, opaque, and non-deterministic. We address this with Object Aligner (OA), an open-source Python library that scores two JSON objects deterministically by recursively aligning their trees (the Hungarian algorithm for unordered collections, sequence alignment for ordered ones) and awarding partial credit at the granularity the schema declares. The Object Aligner is configured entirely through a set of JSON Schema extensions, so adapting it to a new task involves annotating a schema rather than writing code. Complex structured data, however, are rarely flat trees: records may form graphs or hypergraphs keyed by arbitrary identifiers, breaking the assumptions of prior similarity metrics. Our central contribution, referential alignment, closes this gap by inferring a bijection between gold and candidate identifiers and scoring every reference through it, so the score is invariant to relabeling. Since recovering this bijection exactly is graph isomorphism, the Object Aligner approximates it with Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement. An order-sensitive sequence regime targets ranking and planning. Since the same alignment localizes every mismatch, the Object Aligner emits ranked repair suggestions at no extra cost. Used as a reward inside the GEPA prompt optimizer, Object Aligner helps or stays neutral across all datasets.

items.title: Researchers propose ESC, a training-free emotional self-correction framework that improves reliability of vision-language models by triggering reflective reasoning without additional training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ESC: Emotional Self-Correction for Reliable Vision-Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced ESC (Emotional Self-Correction), a novel framework designed to enhance the reliability of vision-language models (VLMs) by leveraging emotional cues to trigger reflective reasoning without requiring additional training. ESC employs an external verifier to identify potentially incorrect responses and injects emotional feedback, prompting the model to reconsider and improve its answers. This approach addresses the limitations of existing self-correction methods that often depend on costly post-training or engineered feedback.

Extensive testing across various benchmarks—including safety, hallucination, vision-centric perception, and multimodal reasoning—demonstrates that ESC consistently improves model reliability while maintaining overall utility. The findings suggest that emotional signals can serve as practical control mechanisms for scalable self-correction in VLMs, marking a promising step toward more human-like, emotion-integrated artificial intelligence systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02089v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance across diverse multimodal tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to unreliable reasoning. Existing self-correction methods mitigate these issues but typically rely on post-training or carefully engineered feedback, incurring high computational cost. In this work, we revisit this challenge through the lens of emotional cues, asking whether they can activate latent self-correction behaviors in VLMs without additional training. \textbf{We find that emotional signals serve as an effective trigger for self-correction, encouraging more cautious and reflective reasoning}. Motivated by this finding, we propose \escabstract (\textbf{\underline{E}}motional \textbf{\underline{S}}elf-\textbf{\underline{C}}orrection), a training-free self-correction framework. ESC introduces an external verifier that detects potentially incorrect initial responses and injects emotional feedback to encourage model to reflect, and produce a better revised response without additional training. Extensive experiments across safety, hallucination, vision-centric perception, and multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that ESC consistently improves reliability while preserving overall model utility. These results suggest that emotion can function not only as an ability to be recognized, but also as a practical control signal for scalable self-correction in VLMs. \textbf{We therefore believe that ESC provides a strong foundation for a new reliable human-like, emotion-integrated research direction.} Our project is publicly available at \textcolor{red}{https://genai4e.github.io/ESC/}.

items.title: Researchers present HERMES, a hierarchical multi-granularity labeling substrate for pre-training data mixtures enabling coarse-to-fine document annotation with up to 130,000 cells [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: HERMES: A Multi-Granularity Labeling Substrate for Pre-training Data Mixtures
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced HERMES, a hierarchical multi-granularity labeling system designed to improve pre-training data mixtures by enabling coarse-to-fine document annotation with up to 130,000 distinct categories. Unlike traditional data-mixing methods that rely on fixed groupings or single-axis labels, HERMES uses a Learned Semantic Transform combined with a three-stage residual vector quantization to assign each document a hierarchical code, allowing flexible granularity in data labeling.

HERMES matches the performance of standard clustering methods at coarse levels but offers a novel substrate that supports dynamic granularity adjustments. In large-scale pre-training experiments involving a 1 billion parameter model and 25 billion tokens, the hierarchical structure revealed interactions that fixed-granularity pipelines cannot detect, improving task performance at certain granularity levels. This approach shifts data mixture design from selecting fixed label sets to navigating a reusable, data-driven hierarchy, potentially enhancing the effectiveness of pre-training strategies.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most data-mixing methods assume the corpus has already been partitioned into groups, and the choice of those groups determines what a mixer can express. Existing labels, including provenance, topic or format taxonomies, and flat embedding clusters, commit to one semantic axis at one granularity; changing the resolution rebuilds the labels. We argue the bottleneck is the label system, not the mixer, and provide a hierarchical one. HERMES is a data-derived labeling substrate: a Learned Semantic Transform followed by 3-stage residual vector quantization annotates each document once into a coarse-to-fine code whose prefix length controls granularity up to approximately 130k cells. At coarse granularity HERMES sits at a plateau with KMeans-family methods on standard clustering metrics, so the contribution is the substrate, not the clusterer. On 1B-parameter, 25B-token pre-training, the hierarchy exposes an interaction fixed-granularity pipelines cannot test: at one prefix length, a combined Stage-2 rule contrast, equal-subbucket coverage versus size-proportional within-bucket quality top-30%, lifts a 16-task capability macro-average by +0.0253; at the next finer level, the same rule loses its measurable edge as candidate pools contract approximately 5x. HERMES reframes data mixture design from choosing among fixed label sets to navigating a reusable, data-derived granularity hierarchy.

items.title: Researchers propose Program-as-Weights paradigm compiling natural-language fuzzy functions into compact neural artifacts, achieving Qwen3-32B performance with lower memory and faster local execution [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions
items.summary: Researchers have introduced a new programming paradigm called Program-as-Weights (PAW) that compiles natural-language specifications of fuzzy functions into compact neural artifacts executable locally. This approach addresses challenges in tasks that resist rule-based programming, such as alerting on important log lines or repairing malformed JSON, which are often handled by large language model APIs with drawbacks in locality, reproducibility, and cost. PAW uses a 4-billion-parameter compiler trained on a large dataset to generate efficient adapters for a lightweight, frozen interpreter, enabling a 0.6-billion-parameter Qwen3 interpreter to match the performance of a much larger 32-billion-parameter model while using significantly less memory and running faster on standard hardware.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02512v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many everyday programming tasks resist clean rule-based implementation, such as alerting on important log lines, repairing malformed JSON, or ranking search results by intent, and are increasingly outsourced to large language model APIs at the cost of locality, reproducibility, and price. We propose fuzzy-function programming: compiling such a function from a natural-language specification into a compact, locally-executable neural artifact. We instantiate this paradigm with Program-as-Weights (PAW), in which a 4B compiler trained on FuzzyBench, a 10M-example dataset we release, emits parameter-efficient adapters for a frozen, lightweight interpreter. A 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter executing PAW programs matches the performance of direct prompting of Qwen3-32B, while using roughly one fiftieth of the inference memory and running at 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3. PAW reframes the foundation model from a per-input problem solver into a tool builder: invoked once per function definition, it produces a small reusable artifact whose subsequent calls per function application are cheap and offline.

items.title: Researchers introduce LACUNA, a testbed for evaluating parameter-level localization precision in LLM unlearning, revealing current methods' imprecision and vulnerability to resurfacing attacks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LACUNA: A Testbed for Evaluating Localization Precision for LLM Unlearning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LACUNA, a novel testbed designed to evaluate the precision of parameter-level localization in unlearning methods for large language models (LLMs). This tool addresses the challenge of reliably removing sensitive data, such as personally identifiable information, from LLMs by directly assessing whether unlearning techniques effectively erase knowledge from specific model parameters rather than merely obscuring it. Using LACUNA, the team tested state-of-the-art unlearning methods on 1B and 7B parameter models and found that despite good performance at the output level, these methods often lack precision and remain vulnerable to resurfacing attacks.

LACUNA works by injecting synthetic sensitive data into known parameters of LLMs, enabling precise measurement of unlearning effectiveness at the parameter level. The study revealed that when unlearning successfully targets the correct parameters, even simple gradient-based methods can achieve strong data erasure and resist resurfacing attacks. By releasing LACUNA, the researchers aim to complement existing behavioral evaluations and promote the development of more robust, localization-based unlearning techniques for protecting sensitive information in LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLMs memorize sensitive training data, including personally identifiable information (PII), creating a pressing need for reliable post hoc removal methods. Unlearning has emerged as a promising solution, with state-of-the-art(SOTA) methods often following a localize-first, unlearn-second paradigm that targets specific model parameters. However, existing benchmarks evaluate unlearning solely at the output level, leaving open the question of whether unlearning truly erases knowledge from a model's parameters or merely obfuscates it, a concern reinforced by the success of resurfacing attacks. To bridge this gap, we introduce LACUNA: the first unlearning testbed with ground-truth parameter-level localization. LACUNA injects PII of synthetic individuals into predefined parameters of 1B and 7B OLMo-based models via masked continual pretraining, enabling direct evaluation of whether unlearning targets the weights responsible for knowledge storage. We use LACUNA to benchmark current SOTA unlearning methods and find that, despite strong output-level performance, existing methods are highly imprecise and susceptible to resurfacing attacks. We further show that when localization is successful, even a simple gradient-based unlearning method achieves strong erasure and robustness to resurfacing attacks, highlighting the importance of precise unlearning. We release LACUNA to complement behavioral evaluations and drive further advances in robust, localization-based unlearning.

items.title: Researchers introduce HAL framework to align language models with human-like conversational traits using interpretable, data-driven rewards without impacting performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: HAL: Inducing Human-likeness in LLMs with Alignment
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Human Aligning LLMs (HAL) framework to enhance language models' conversational human-likeness through an interpretable, data-driven reward system. HAL identifies explicit conversational traits from dialogue data, combines them into a scalar score, and uses this as a transparent reward for alignment without compromising model performance. Human evaluations show that models aligned with HAL are more often perceived as human-like in conversation.

HAL's approach allows for inspection and diagnosis of alignment behavior by operating on explicit, interpretable traits, addressing the challenge of defining and optimizing qualitative behavioral traits. This framework demonstrates that soft, qualitative language properties can be measured and aligned in an explainable way, advancing targeted alignment beyond broad supervised training or scaling methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.02813v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Aligning language models to qualitative behavioral traits, such as human-likeness, remains difficult because they are hard to define, measure, and optimize. As a result, improvements in human-like behavior are largely driven by scale or broad supervised training, rather than targeted alignment. We introduce Human Aligning LLMs (HAL), a framework for aligning language models to conversational human-likeness using an interpretable, data-driven reward. HAL derives explicit conversational traits from contrastive dialogue data, combines them into a compact scalar score, and uses this score as a transparent reward signal for alignment with standard preference optimization methods. Using this approach, we align models of varying sizes without affecting their overall performance. In large-scale Chatbot Arena-style human evaluations, a model aligned with HAL is more frequently perceived as human-like in conversation. Because HAL operates over explicit, interpretable traits, it enables inspection of alignment behavior and diagnosis of unintended effects. More broadly, HAL demonstrates how soft, qualitative properties of language--previously outside the scope for alignment--can be made measurable and aligned in an interpretable and explainable way.

items.title: Researchers introduce OmniGAIA benchmark and OmniAtlas agent for evaluating and advancing native omni-modal AI with vision, audio, and language integration and tool use [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OmniGAIA: Towards Native Omni-Modal AI Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced OmniGAIA, a new benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents capable of native omni-modal perception, integrating vision, audio, and language with complex reasoning and multi-turn tool use. This benchmark addresses the limitations of current multi-modal large language models, which typically handle only bi-modal interactions, by requiring agents to perform deep reasoning and tool execution across multiple modalities using real-world data.

Alongside OmniGAIA, the team developed OmniAtlas, a native omni-modal foundation agent that employs a tool-integrated reasoning approach with active perception across modalities. Trained using a hindsight-guided exploration strategy and fine-grained error correction, OmniAtlas enhances the tool-use capabilities of existing open-source models, representing a significant step toward advanced omni-modal AI assistants suited for real-world applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.22897v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Human intelligence naturally intertwines omni-modal perception -- spanning vision, audio, and language -- with complex reasoning and tool usage to interact with the world. However, current multi-modal LLMs are primarily confined to bi-modal interactions (e.g., vision-language), lacking the unified cognitive capabilities required for general AI assistants. To bridge this gap, we introduce OmniGAIA, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate omni-modal agents on tasks necessitating deep reasoning and multi-turn tool execution across video, audio, and image modalities. Constructed via a novel omni-modal event graph approach, OmniGAIA synthesizes complex, multi-hop queries derived from real-world data that require cross-modal reasoning and external tool integration. Furthermore, we propose OmniAtlas, a native omni-modal foundation agent under tool-integrated reasoning paradigm with active omni-modal perception. Trained on trajectories synthesized via a hindsight-guided tree exploration strategy and OmniDPO for fine-grained error correction, OmniAtlas effectively enhances the tool-use capabilities of existing open-source models. This work marks a step towards next-generation native omni-modal AI assistants for real-world scenarios.

items.title: Researchers introduce GroundEval, a deterministic framework replacing LLM-as-judge for evaluating stateful agents using grounded, time-bounded, and access-controlled evidence [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GroundEval: A Deterministic Replacement for LLM-as-Judge in Stateful Agent Evaluation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed GroundEval, a deterministic framework designed to evaluate stateful agents by verifying the evidence they accessed, searched, and cited during their operation. Unlike traditional methods that rely on large language models (LLMs) as judges, GroundEval assesses both the agent's final answer and the detailed trajectory of its reasoning process, ensuring that the evidence used is grounded, time-bounded, and access-controlled. This approach addresses key evaluation challenges such as verifying whether an agent checked for evidence before claiming its absence, reasoned only from available information at the relevant time, and used the correct causal mechanisms rather than plausible but incorrect ones.

GroundEval operates by generating questions based on a domain configuration, allowing the agent to choose its response method, and then scoring the answer alongside the recorded evidence path. The framework includes three evaluation tracks—Silence, Perspective, and Counterfactual—that expose when plausible answers rely on invalid evidence paths. Case studies demonstrate that traditional LLM-based judging can assign high scores to responses that GroundEval identifies as unsupported, highlighting common failure modes that previous evaluation methods cannot detect. GroundEval also provides structured diagnostics linking tool activity with the agent's narration, making evaluation results transparent and inspectable rather than opaque.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.22737v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Before letting an agent operate over real context, can you prove it used the right evidence? GroundEval turns that question into a deterministic test of what the agent searched, fetched, cited, and was permitted to access. In one case study, two frontier LLM judges scored a plausible agent response 0.85 and higher. But the trace told a different story: the agent had never retrieved the artifact its answer depended on, yielding a GroundEval score of 0.000. We introduce GroundEval, a judge-free framework for evaluating agents against grounded, time-bounded, and access-controlled evidence. GroundEval uses a domain configuration to generate questions, lets the agent choose how to answer, and then scores both the final answer and the recorded trajectory that produced it. The benchmark targets three failures that LLM-as-judge evaluation struggles to detect: whether an agent checked before claiming absence, reasoned only from evidence available to the actor at the relevant time, and used the correct causal mechanism rather than a plausible one. These correspond to three tracks: Silence, Perspective, and Counterfactual. GroundEval exposes when plausible answers rest on invalid evidence paths, and produces structured per-question diagnostics that pair tool activity with the agent's turn-level narration, making each score inspectable rather than merely reported. Our case studies suggest this failure mode is common rather than exceptional, one that final-answer and judge-based evaluation cannot detect by construction.

items.title: Theoria verification architecture rewrites AI reasoning into auditable state transitions, achieving 91.4% precision on expert problems and outperforming holistic LLM judges on adversarial tests [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Theoria: Rewrite-Acceptability Verification over Informal Reasoning States
items.summary:
Theoria is a new verification architecture designed to enhance trust in AI-generated answers by rewriting candidate solutions into sequences of auditable state transitions, each justified explicitly. This approach ensures that every change between proof states is accounted for, exposing hidden premises and enabling independent verification. Tested on expert problem sets, Theoria achieved 91.4% precision and outperformed holistic large language model (LLM) judges, particularly in detecting adversarial errors such as hidden premises and fabricated citations.

Unlike traditional formal proof assistants that lack broad coverage and scalar LLM judges that produce opaque scores, Theoria provides human-readable proof traces that allow each step to be challenged independently. Its structured verification method demonstrated superior accuracy on adversarial tests across multiple domains, confirming its advantage in verifying informal reasoning while maintaining high precision on standard benchmarks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01223v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When should an AI system's answer be trusted? Formal proof assistants offer certainty but cannot reach most of the problem distribution; scalar LLM judges offer coverage but produce opaque scores that cannot be audited after the fact and are subject to the same coherence issues as any LLM. We present Theoria, a verification architecture that closes this gap. A candidate solution is rewritten into a sequence of typed state transitions, each licensed by an explicit justification, whether that be a citation, computation, or problem-given fact, and every transition is independently auditable. The foundational invariant is completeness of change: every difference between consecutive proof states must be accounted for, so hidden premises surface as unlicensed mutations rather than passing silently. On HLE-Verified Gold (185 text-only expert problems), Theoria certifies 105 at 91.4% strict precision (Wilson 95% CI [84.5%, 95.4%]). Every certification produces a human readable proof trace in which each step can be independently challenged. Holistic LLM judges achieve comparable precision at matched coverage but fail on different problems (Jaccard 0.14-0.36), making the approaches complementary. On 95 adversarial poisoned proofs across 15 domains, structured judges catch 94.7% versus 83.2% for holistic judging (p= 0.0017). The overall 11.5 pp gap concentrates in hidden premises (90.6% vs. 62.5%, a 28 pp difference) and fabricated citations (100% vs. 90%), the error classes where the formal analysis predicts an advantage; performance is identical on arithmetic and theorem-misapplication errors, where no advantage is predicted. On GPQA Diamond (n= 65), certified precision is 97.1% (Wilson CI [85.1%, 99.5%]).

items.summary:
A new paper on arXiv provides an introduction to Transformers, a dominant model in natural language processing. It covers the fundamental concepts, the standard Transformer architecture, recent refinements, and common applications, aiming to give readers a clear understanding of these models and their variants. The paper also highlights key ideas that have shaped the field, offering insights into the strengths and limitations of Transformers.

Due to the rapid evolution of Transformers and related deep learning techniques, the paper focuses on essential concepts rather than exhaustive technical details. This approach helps readers grasp the core principles behind Transformers without delving into every aspect of the technology.

In this paper, we introduce basic concepts of Transformers and present key techniques that form the recent advances of these models. This includes a description of the standard Transformer architecture, a series of model refinements, and common applications. Given that Transformers and related deep learning techniques might be evolving in ways we have never seen, we cannot dive into all the model details or cover all the technical areas. We also summarize the key ideas that impact this field, thereby yielding some insights into the strengths and limitations of these models.

items.title: Researchers advance cybersecurity specialization in LLMs using resource-efficient domain-adaptive continuous pretraining with 23-to-42-fold less data, achieving state-of-the-art benchmark results [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Less Data, More Security: Advancing Cybersecurity LLMs Specialization via Resource-Efficient Domain-Adaptive Continuous Pre-training with Minimal Tokens
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a resource-efficient method called Domain-Adaptive Continuous Pretraining (DAP) to enhance the cybersecurity capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). By adapting three decoder-based LLM architectures using a curated cybersecurity corpus of 126 million words, they achieved state-of-the-art results on multiple cybersecurity benchmarks while using 23 to 42 times less training data than previous specialized models. This approach leverages scalable high-performance computing infrastructure to reduce computational and energy costs, enabling more sustainable and effective domain-specific AI applications in cybersecurity.

The study evaluated models including Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, with the latter achieving accuracies of 0.718, 0.933, and 0.864 on CTI-MCQ, CyberMetric, and SecEval benchmarks respectively. These results surpass those of larger models trained on billions of tokens, demonstrating that targeted continuous pretraining with minimal data can significantly improve domain specialization. This advancement supports the development of AI assistants for threat analysis, vulnerability assessment, and security documentation while promoting sustainable AI practices.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2507.02964v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The increasing scale of AI workloads demands High-Performance Computing (HPC) infrastructure and training methodologies that are both scalable and sustainable. While Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate exceptional natural language capabilities, general-purpose models often lack the specialized domain knowledge necessary for effective cybersecurity analysis. We investigate Domain-Adaptive Continuous Pretraining (DAP) as a scalable, resource-efficient methodology for enhancing cybersecurity understanding in pretrained LLMs, implemented through a distributed Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) pipeline across multi-node GPU clusters. We systematically adapted three decoder-based architectures -- Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct -- using a curated 126-million-word cybersecurity corpus from standards, academic literature, and technical documentation. Evaluation across three cybersecurity benchmarks -- CTI-MCQ, CyberMetric, and SecEval -- demonstrates consistent improvements post-adaptation. Notably, our Llama-3.3-70B-Ins-DAP model achieves state-of-the-art performance with accuracies of 0.718, 0.933, and 0.864, respectively, surpassing parameter-efficient baselines and specialized models including Llama-Primus-Base (trained on 2.77 billion tokens) and Foundation-Sec-8B (trained on 5 billion tokens), despite utilizing only 118.8 million tokens -- representing a 23-to-42-fold reduction in training data. items.title: Researchers show model merging via weight interpolation can improve accuracy and calibration, mitigating the alignment tax in post-training AI models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Navigating the Alignment-Calibration Trade-off: A Pareto-Superior Frontier via Model Merging
items.summary:
Researchers have identified that the "alignment tax" in post-training AI models not only reduces task accuracy but also significantly impairs model calibration, leading to overconfidence and less reliable outputs. They propose a simple post-training technique of interpolating between a model's weights before and after alignment, which can improve accuracy beyond both original models while restoring much of the lost calibration. This approach reveals Pareto-optimal models that balance accuracy and reliability more effectively than previous methods.

The study demonstrates that this model merging strategy is computationally efficient and can mitigate the full range of issues associated with the alignment tax. By navigating the trade-off between accuracy and calibration, the method yields AI models that are both more capable and more dependable, offering a promising direction for improving post-training alignment in machine learning systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2510.17426v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The "alignment tax" of post-training is typically framed as a drop in task accuracy. We show it also involves a severe loss of calibration, making models overconfident, less reliable, and model outputs less diverse. We show that this trade-off can be navigated effectively via a simple post-hoc intervention: interpolating between a model's weights before and after alignment. Crucially, this is not a strict trade-off. We find that the process consistently reveals Pareto-optimal interpolations - models that improve accuracy beyond both parents while substantially recovering the calibration lost during alignment. Our work demonstrates that simple model merging provides a computationally efficient method for mitigating the full scope of the alignment tax, yielding models that are more capable and more reliable.

items.title: Researchers introduce ThreadWeaver, an adaptive parallel reasoning framework for language models that matches sequential accuracy while reducing inference latency by up to 1.53x on six math benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ThreadWeaver: Adaptive Threading for Efficient Parallel Reasoning in Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ThreadWeaver, an adaptive parallel reasoning framework for large language models that achieves the accuracy of sequential reasoning while significantly reducing inference latency. By introducing a two-stage parallel trajectory generator, a trie-based rollout design compatible with standard autoregressive engines, and a reinforcement learning approach that balances accuracy with parallelization, ThreadWeaver delivers up to a 1.53x speedup in token latency across six challenging math benchmarks without sacrificing performance.

ThreadWeaver was tested on the Qwen3-8B model and matched the performance of leading sequential reasoning models, achieving 79.9% accuracy on the AIME24 benchmark and an average of 71.9% across all tests. This approach establishes a new balance between reasoning accuracy and computational efficiency, enabling faster inference without the need for specialized hardware or inference engines.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2512.07843v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scaling inference-time computation has enabled Large Language Models (LLMs) to achieve strong reasoning performance, but their inherently sequential decoding incurs substantial latency, motivating parallelization of the generation process. However, existing parallel reasoning approaches suffer from performance degradation compared to their sequential counterparts, and often rely on specialized inference engines. We introduce ThreadWeaver, a framework for adaptive parallel reasoning that matches the accuracy of comparably sized sequential reasoning models while significantly reducing inference latency via three key innovations: 1) a two-stage parallel trajectory generator that produces high-quality parallel chain-of-thought data for supervised fine-tuning; 2) a trie-based rollout design that enables parallel reasoning on any off-the-shelf autoregressive inference engine; and 3) a parallelization-aware reinforcement learning framework that trains the model to balance reasoning accuracy with effective parallelization. Across six challenging math reasoning benchmarks, ThreadWeaver trained on top of Qwen3-8B achieves performance on par with cutting-edge sequential reasoning models (79.9% on AIME24 and 71.9% on average) while delivering up to 1.53x speedup in token latency, establishing a new Pareto frontier between accuracy and efficiency.

items.title: Researchers propose an isotropic approximation using gradient norms for efficient uncertainty quantification in large pretrained neural networks, validated against MCMC and tested on question answering benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: An Isotropic Approach to Efficient Uncertainty Quantification with Gradient Norms
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an efficient method for quantifying predictive uncertainty in large pretrained neural networks by approximating uncertainty through gradient norms and an isotropic assumption on parameter covariance. This approach allows estimation of epistemic uncertainty as the squared gradient norm and aleatoric uncertainty as the Bernoulli variance from a single forward-backward pass without modifying the model or requiring training data. The method is validated against Markov Chain Monte Carlo estimates on synthetic problems, showing improved accuracy with larger models.

The isotropy assumption is supported by theoretical results on large network spectral properties and avoids distortions introduced by covariance estimates from non-training data. Applying this uncertainty quantification to question answering benchmarks reveals that combined uncertainty estimates perform well on tasks involving conflicting plausible answers but are less effective for factual recall, indicating that parameter-level uncertainty captures different information than traditional self-assessment methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.29466v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing methods for quantifying predictive uncertainty in neural networks are either computationally intractable for large language models or require access to training data that is typically unavailable. We derive a lightweight alternative through two approximations: a first-order Taylor expansion that expresses uncertainty in terms of the gradient of the prediction and the parameter covariance, and an isotropy assumption on the parameter covariance. Together, these yield epistemic uncertainty as the squared gradient norm and aleatoric uncertainty as the Bernoulli variance of the point prediction, from a single forward-backward pass through an unmodified pretrained model. We justify the isotropy assumption by showing that covariance estimates built from non-training data introduce structured distortions that isotropic covariance avoids, and that theoretical results on the spectral properties of large networks support the approximation at scale. Validation against reference Markov Chain Monte Carlo estimates on synthetic problems shows strong correspondence that improves with model size. We then use the estimates to investigate when each uncertainty type carries useful signal for predicting answer correctness in question answering with large language models, revealing a benchmark-dependent divergence: the combined estimate achieves the highest mean AUROC on TruthfulQA, where questions involve genuine conflict between plausible answers, but falls to near chance on TriviaQA's factual recall, suggesting that parameter-level uncertainty captures a fundamentally different signal than self-assessment methods.

items.title: Study analyzes Claude Code architecture and compares it with OpenClaw and Hermes Agent, identifying design principles and future directions for AI agent systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today's and Future AI Agent Systems
items.summary:
A recent study examines the architecture of Claude Code, an AI agentic coding tool capable of running shell commands, editing files, and calling external services for users. By analyzing its publicly available source code and comparing it with two other open-source AI agent systems, OpenClaw and Hermes Agent, the research identifies key human values such as decision authority, safety, security, and adaptability that shape their design. The study outlines thirteen design principles and highlights differences in runtime and context management approaches among the three systems.

Claude Code centers on a simple loop that interacts with the model and tools, supported by complex surrounding systems including a multi-mode permission system, context management pipeline, extensibility mechanisms, and session storage. In contrast, OpenClaw and Hermes Agent adopt different strategies for safety, access control, and runtime architecture. The paper concludes by proposing six open design directions for future AI agent systems, informed by recent empirical, architectural, and policy research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.14228v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Claude Code is an agentic coding tool that can run shell commands, edit files, and call external services on behalf of the user. This study describes its architecture by analyzing the publicly available source code and comparing it with two independent open-source AI agent systems, OpenClaw and Hermes Agent, that answer many of similar or even the same design questions. Our analysis identifies five human values, philosophies, and needs that motivate the architecture: human decision authority, safety, security, and privacy, reliable execution, capability amplification, and contextual adaptability. We then trace them through thirteen design principles to implementation choices. The core of the system is a simple while-loop that calls the model, runs tools, and repeats. Most of the code, however, lives in the systems around this loop: a permission system with seven modes and an ML-based classifier, a five-layer compaction pipeline for context management, four extensibility mechanisms (MCP, plugins, skills, and hooks), a subagent delegation and orchestration mechanism, and append-oriented session storage. Comparisons with OpenClaw and Hermes Agent show that the same design questions produce different answers across three deployment contexts. Claude Code emphasizes per-action safety, OpenClaw emphasizes perimeter-level access, and Hermes renders per-action approvals across many surfaces. At the runtime layer, Claude Code uses a single CLI loop, OpenClaw embeds the runtime within a gateway control plane, and Hermes uses one process whose role is set by its entry point. At the context and extension layer, Claude Code extends the context window, OpenClaw registers gateway-wide capabilities, and Hermes provides pluggable memory and model backends. We finally identify six open design directions for future agent systems, grounded in recent empirical, architectural, and policy literature.

items.title: Researchers present ResearchClawBench, a benchmark evaluating autonomous scientific research across 40 tasks in 10 domains, revealing current AI agents' limited re-discovery capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ResearchClawBench: A Benchmark for End-to-End Autonomous Scientific Research
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced ResearchClawBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate the autonomous scientific research capabilities of AI agents across 40 tasks spanning 10 scientific domains. Each task is based on a real published paper and includes related literature and raw data, with the target paper concealed during evaluation. The benchmark uses expert-curated rubrics to assess the AI's ability to re-discover scientific findings while allowing for new discoveries. Testing seven autonomous research agents and seventeen large language models (LLMs) revealed that current AI systems struggle with reliable re-discovery, with the top-performing agent achieving an average score of 21.5 out of a possible 26.5.

The evaluation highlighted common failure points such as mismatches in experimental protocols, evidence inconsistencies, and missing core scientific elements. ResearchClawBench offers a reproducible framework to measure progress toward fully autonomous scientific research, providing a valuable tool for advancing AI capabilities in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.07591v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI coding agents are increasingly used for scientific work, but their end-to-end autonomous research capability remains difficult to verify. We present ResearchClawBench, a benchmark for evaluating autonomous scientific research across 40 tasks from 10 scientific domains. Each task is grounded in a real published paper, provides related literature and raw data, and hides the target paper during evaluation. Expert-curated multimodal rubrics decompose the target scientific artifacts into weighted criteria, enabling evaluation of target-paper-level re-discovery while leaving room for new discovery. We evaluate seven autonomous research (auto-research) agents under a unified protocol and seventeen native LLMs through the lightweight ResearchHarness. Current systems remain far from reliable re-discovery: the strongest autonomous agent, Claude Code, averages 21.5, and the strongest ResearchHarness LLM, Claude-Opus-4.7, averages 20.7, with an LLM frontier mean of only 26.5. Error analysis shows that failures concentrate in experimental protocol mismatch, evidence mismatch, and missing scientific core. ResearchClawBench provides a reproducible evaluation frontier for measuring progress toward autonomous scientific research.

items.title: Researchers develop CreativityNeuro to steer language model weights, improving divergent thinking and reducing mode collapse without additional training data or fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CreativityNeuro: Steering Language Model Weights to Improve Divergent Thinking and Reduce Mode Collapse
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced CreativityNeuro, a new technique that enhances divergent thinking in large language models by steering their weights without requiring additional training data or fine-tuning. This method improves creativity-related performance on various tasks, including vocabulary-based and open-ended assessments, while also reducing the models' tendency to generate repetitive responses, known as mode collapse. CreativityNeuro outperforms activation steering by generalizing better to diverse creative tasks, offering a promising approach to boost creativity in language models.

Evaluations demonstrated that CreativityNeuro increased performance on the Divergent Association Task by up to 14 percentile points and showed significant improvements in originality, surprise, and creativity in large-scale human assessments. Unlike activation steering, which performed well only on specific tasks, CreativityNeuro's weight-space steering effectively transfers to more open-ended and longer-form creative tasks, highlighting its versatility and effectiveness without the need for retraining or gradient-based fine-tuning.

items.title: Researchers develop DiffusionGemma-26B, a diffusion language model for interactive radiology report drafting with faster decoding and any-order text infill capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Discrete Diffusion Language Models for Interactive Radiology Report Drafting
items.summary:
Researchers have developed DiffusionGemma-26B, a diffusion-based language model designed for medical tasks like drafting radiology reports. Unlike traditional autoregressive models that generate text sequentially, this model denoises text bidirectionally, allowing faster decoding and flexible text infilling in any order. It matches or outperforms a comparable autoregressive model on medical visual question answering benchmarks while offering a unique capability for interactive report editing.

The model's any-order infill feature enables radiologists to fix parts of a report and have the model complete the text between those segments, addressing common issues of terseness and inconsistency in clinical documentation. This approach leverages the inherent advantages of diffusion models over autoregressive ones, providing a more efficient and adaptable tool for clinical report generation.

items.title: Researchers propose Procedural Memory Distillation to improve language model training by converting cross-episode signals into reusable memory, boosting performance on Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Procedural Memory Distillation: Online Reflection for Self-Improving Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Procedural Memory Distillation (PMD), a new training method for language models that captures and reuses procedural knowledge across multiple episodes. Unlike traditional reinforcement learning approaches that update policies based only on individual episode outcomes, PMD distills cross-episode signals into a reusable memory that is integrated into the model's parameters, enhancing its ability to internalize strategies and behavioral patterns. This approach was tested on Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B models, showing significant performance improvements on benchmarks like SCIKNOWEVAL and LIVECODEBENCH compared to previous methods.

PMD organizes procedural memory at three abstraction levels—raw trajectories, self-reflected strategies, and higher-level behavioral patterns—extracted online from the model's own experiences. A memory-conditioned self-teacher uses this accumulated knowledge to guide the model's learning, enabling a co-evolution process where the policy and memory continuously update each other. Empirical results demonstrate that freezing either the memory or policy components reduces performance, highlighting the importance of their interaction in achieving the observed gains.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01480v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), along with recent selfdistillation variants such as SDPO, evaluates each rollout against a verifier and updates the policy from that episode-level signal. However, the richer procedural information in the rollout is rarely retained or reused. Across episodes and epochs, the model repeatedly encounters related problems under a changing policy, producing cross-episode signals that episode-local updates cannot capture: which strategies consistently pass verification, which failure modes persist, which patterns recur. We propose Procedural Memory Distillation (PMD), which converts these crossepisode signals into reusable procedural memory and distills it into the policy's weights during training. This memory functions as a training scaffold, absorbed into the policy itself, yielding a memory-free model at inference. PMD organizes the memory at three levels of abstraction: raw trajectories, self-reflected strategies and lessons, and higher-level behavioral patterns that recur across problems, all extracted online from the model's own trajectories. A memory-conditioned self-teacher draws on the accumulated experience to supervise the student on its own rollouts, enabling student to progressively internalize procedural knowledge within its parameters. The central design principle is co-evolution: the policy generates rollouts that update the memory, and memory shapes the supervision that updates the policy. Empirically, across Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B, PMD improves over SDPO by 3.8-5.5% on SCIKNOWEVAL and 7.9-13.6% on LIVECODEBENCH. Co-evolution powers these gains: freezing either the memory or the policy trails PMD by more than 10% across SCIKNOWEVAL domains.

items.title: Researchers propose Semi-CoT, a semi-supervised chain-of-thought learning framework using unlabeled questions to generate pseudo reasoning supervision with high precision on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Reasoning under Limited Supervision: Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Semi-CoT, a semi-supervised learning framework that leverages unlabeled questions to generate high-precision pseudo reasoning chains for large language models. This approach extends traditional chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning by using multiple pseudo-CoTs per question and selecting those with low semantic entropy as reliable training signals, thereby enhancing the model's reasoning capabilities beyond inference-time prompting.

Pilot experiments on benchmarks such as AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith demonstrate that Semi-CoT achieves pseudo-answer precision between 91.36% and 100%. While it yields modest improvements on some datasets, results vary, indicating that effective use of unlabeled data for pseudo supervision requires further refinement in demonstration selection and training methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as an effective approach for activating latent reasoning capabilities in large language models. However, most existing CoT methods use reasoning chains mainly as inference-time prompts, while the generated reasoning traces are rarely reused as semi-supervised learning signals. In this report, we define \textbf{Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning} and propose \textbf{Semi-CoT}, a simple framework that uses unlabeled questions to construct pseudo reasoning supervision. Semi-CoT samples multiple pseudo-CoTs for each unlabeled question, estimates answer-level semantic entropy, and selects low-entropy reasoning chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations. This extends the self-training view of CoT from inference-time refinement to semi-supervised pseudo-supervision. Pilot experiments on AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith show that the entropy gate selects high-precision pseudo-CoTs, with pseudo-answer precision ranging from $91.36\%$ to $100\%$. Semi-CoT also gives small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, while AQuA shows negative transfer and MultiArith reaches a ceiling. These results suggest that unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo reasoning signals, but their effective use still requires stronger demonstration selection or student training.
