items.title: Researchers introduce OPINE-World, an LLM agent that learns object-centric programmatic world models online using ontology-error-guided exploration, solving 20 of 25 ARC-AGI-3 benchmark games without per-game training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OPINE-World: Programmatic World Modeling with Ontology-error-Prioritized Interactive Exploration
items.summary:
Researchers have developed OPINE-World, a large language model (LLM) agent that learns object-centric programmatic world models through interactive exploration guided by ontology error. This approach combines two cooperating agents—one interacting with the environment and the other synthesizing code-based models verified through replay and planning. OPINE-World was tested on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, which challenges agents to acquire skills without prior knowledge of object vocabulary, goals, or action semantics, and successfully solved 20 out of 25 games without per-game training, achieving an action-efficiency score of 78.4 compared to human performance.

Unlike traditional deep network-based world models that require extensive data and struggle to generalize, OPINE-World uses program synthesis refined by counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS) to efficiently learn reusable models. Its exploration strategy prioritizes reducing ontology error, a Bayesian measure of how well the hypothesized object types fit the environment, enabling flexible hypothesis testing in pixel-rendered settings where object structures are not predefined.

This work demonstrates a promising direction for building adaptive agents capable of learning complex environments with limited data and no task-specific training, potentially advancing the development of more generalizable artificial intelligence systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01531v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning how an environment behaves from interaction is central to building agents that adapt to unfamiliar tasks. World models learned with deep networks are flexible but data-hungry and transfer poorly beyond their training distribution. Program-synthesized world models, written as source code by LLMs and refined through counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS), are instead data-efficient and reusable, yet they have been demonstrated mainly on structured-state worlds with a given object vocabulary, and a single program search does not scale to pixel-rendered environments whose object structure must be hypothesized flexibly. We introduce OPINE-World, an LLM agent that learns an object-centric programmatic world model online from interaction. OPINE-World couples two cooperating agents in a loop of hypothesis and test, one acting in the environment and one synthesizing the model in code with replay verification and model-based planning, and it steers exploration with a Bayesian measure of object-type adequacy we call ontology error. We evaluate OPINE-World on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark for skill-acquisition efficiency in which the object vocabulary, the goal, and the action semantics are withheld. OPINE-World solves 20 of 25 games without per-game training and reaches an action-efficiency score of 78.4 against the human baseline.

items.title: Researchers propose PASE, a neuro-symbolic framework using LLMs and neural-symbolic world models to verify and optimize cloud recovery plans, reducing system recovery time by over 40% [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Safe and Adaptive Cloud Healing: Verifying LLM-Generated Recovery Plans with a Neural-Symbolic World Model
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PASE, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) with neural-symbolic world models to improve fault detection and recovery in cloud-based AI systems. PASE treats recovery as a program synthesis task, using an LLM to generate structured recovery plans, which are then verified through simulation by a neural-symbolic model. A meta-prompt optimizer trained via deep reinforcement learning guides the LLM to produce optimal recovery strategies dynamically.

This approach creates a tightly coupled reason-plan-verify-adapt loop that surpasses traditional methods by enabling context-aware recovery beyond predefined actions. Experiments on real-world cloud fault data show that PASE reduces system recovery time by over 40% and enhances fault detection accuracy, particularly in unknown fault scenarios. The framework represents a significant advancement in autonomous system management by combining LLM reasoning, model-based verification, and meta-learned guidance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As the scale and complexity of cloud-based AI systems continue to escalate, ensuring service reliability through rapid fault detection and adaptive recovery has become a critical challenge. While existing approaches integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) for semantic understanding and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for policy optimization, they often rely on sequential, loosely coupled architectures that underutilize the generative and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. In this paper, we propose a paradigm shift with PASE, a Planning-Aware Semantic self-healing engine, a novel fault self-healing framework that reconceptualizes recovery as a neuro-symbolic program synthesis task. PASE employs an LLM as a core Plan Synthesis Engine to generate structured recovery plans from a library of semantic primitives. A Neural-Symbolic World Model verifies plan feasibility through simulation, while a Meta-Prompt Optimizer, trained via DRL, learns to generate optimal prompts that guide the LLM's planning process. This tight reason-plan-verify-adapt loop enables dynamic, context-aware recovery strategy generation beyond predefined action spaces. Experiments on a real-world cloud fault injection dataset demonstrate that PASE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, reducing average system recovery time by over 40% and improving fault detection accuracy in unknown fault scenarios. Our framework advances autonomous system management by unifying LLM-based reasoning with model-assisted verification and meta-learned guidance.

items.title: Researchers introduce COMFYCLAW, a self-evolving skill harness for ComfyUI image generation workflows that improves agent reliability and outperforms verifier-only baselines across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: COMFYCLAW: Self-Evolving Skill Harnesses for Image Generation Workflows
items.summary: Researchers have developed COMFYCLAW, a self-evolving skill harness designed to improve the reliability and performance of agents managing image generation workflows in ComfyUI. This system treats workflow construction as typed graph editing, uses a vision-language model to identify and correct visual errors, and evolves a skill library by learning from past executions and feedback. COMFYCLAW outperforms baseline models across multiple benchmarks and is preferred by human evaluators, demonstrating the effectiveness of skill evolution in enhancing agent capabilities for recurring visual tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents are increasingly used to construct workflows and assist humans in completing recurring tasks more efficiently. As these workflows become repeated and domain-specific, agent memory and reusable skills become increasingly important: agents should be able to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs. We study this problem in workflow-based image generation and introduce COMFYCLAW, an agentic skill evolution harness for controlling ComfyUI workflows. COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes tools organized by construction stage, automatically reverts invalid edits, and uses a region-level vision-language model (VLM) verifier to translate visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. The framework further evolves a progressively disclosed skill library, where trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from previous runs are distilled into reusable Agent Skills. Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotations further show that annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution. Our results suggest that skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

items.title: Researchers find Diffusion Language Models internally encode latent timestep representations related to denoising progress, enabling modulation of model confidence and entropy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Subliminal Clocks: Latent Time Modelling in Diffusion Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have discovered that Diffusion Language Models (DLMs), a new alternative to autoregressive models, internally encode a latent representation related to the diffusion timestep, which corresponds to the progress of denoising. This latent signal can be extracted from the models' internal activations and used to modulate the model's confidence and entropy by steering it along a specific low-dimensional subspace.

The study reveals that although DLMs are not explicitly conditioned on timesteps, they still maintain an interpretable and structured representation of denoising progress within their residual streams. By analyzing the geometry of this representation, the researchers shed light on how these models process and utilize this internal timing information during generation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01774v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models. Unlike standard diffusion-based approaches, DLMs are not explicitly conditioned on a timestep, raising a natural question: do these models internally represent denoising progress, and how is such information used downstream? In this work, we show that DLMs do in fact encode a latent representation related to the diffusion timestep within their residual streams. We find that this signal can be reliably extracted using probes across layers, indicating that denoising progress is decodable from internal activations. We further demonstrate that steering the model along a low-dimensional subspace associated with the inferred timestep allows us to systematically modulate its notion of denoising progress, leading to predictable changes in model confidence and entropy. Finally, we analyse the geometry of the identified representation, showing that it exhibits structured and interpretable properties in activation space, and shedding light on how such a signal is processed by these models.

items.title: Researchers release Pre-Flight, a 300-question benchmark evaluating large language models on aviation operational knowledge, finding top models reach 82.7% accuracy versus 95% expert level [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Pre-Flight: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Aviation Operational Knowledge
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Pre-Flight, a new open-source benchmark consisting of 300 multiple-choice questions designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on aviation operational knowledge. The benchmark covers topics such as international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, and complex operational scenarios, with questions developed and reviewed by aviation professionals. Testing various commercial and open-source models revealed that the best-performing model achieved 82.7% accuracy, compared to an expert reference level of approximately 95%, indicating a significant gap in model reliability for aviation-specific tasks.

Pre-Flight aims to address the limitations of general-purpose benchmarks by focusing on the high-stakes, regulated aviation domain where safe and accurate reasoning is critical. The dataset, evaluation tools, and results are publicly available, and the benchmark is integrated into the community evaluations package of the Inspect framework. The researchers emphasize that domain-specific evaluation is essential for the responsible deployment of generative AI in non-safety-critical aviation operations, highlighting the need for continued improvement in model performance before broader adoption.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations, from documentation and training generation to customer facing assistants. General purpose benchmarks do not measure whether a model reasons safely and correctly about aviation specific operational knowledge, and the high stakes, regulated nature of the domain makes that gap consequential. We present Pre-Flight, an open source benchmark of 300 multiple choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with experience in air traffic management, ground operations and commercial flying. We evaluate a range of contemporary commercial and open weight models using the Inspect evaluation framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple choice protocol, and we maintain the leaderboard on a rolling basis as new models are released. Against an informal expert reference of around 95%, obtained from a low sample quiz of aviation professionals at a conference, even the strongest model evaluated (released in 2026) reaches 82.7%, having improved only gradually from roughly 75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap below expert level reliability therefore remains. We release the dataset, the evaluation harness and the results, and the benchmark is available within the community evaluations package distributed with inspect_evals. We argue that domain specific evaluation of this kind is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non safety critical aviation operations.

items.title: Researchers introduce STEER, a gradient-guided attack exploiting multilingual safety gaps in large language models, achieving up to 96.7% success on open-source 8B-parameter models and transferring to GPT-4o-mini [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement
items.summary:
Researchers have developed STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that exploits gaps in multilingual safety training of large language models (LLMs). STEER identifies words that trigger model refusals and translates them into low-resource languages to bypass safety mechanisms while maintaining harmful intent. Testing on six open-source 8B-parameter models showed attack success rates up to 96.7%, and the method also transferred to GPT-4o-mini with a 35.5% success rate, indicating a broader vulnerability beyond specific architectures.

The study highlights that safety training focused mainly on English does not reliably generalize to other languages or mixed-language inputs, creating an epistemic gap where models may produce harmful outputs. The authors suggest that enhancing multilingual safety requires more comprehensive alignment across languages and mechanisms to detect and abstain from out-of-distribution inputs to prevent exploitation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety training for large language models (LLMs) is conducted predominantly in English, leaving uncertain how well safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and mixed-language code-switching. We show that this creates an epistemic gap in which models confidently generate harmful responses for inputs that fall outside the distribution of their safety training. To study this phenomenon, we introduce STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing most strongly to the model's refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Across six open-source 8B-parameter models, STEER achieves attack success rates of up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG). The resulting prompts also transfer to GPT-4o-mini, achieving a 35.5% attack success rate without requiring access to the target model, suggesting that the underlying weakness is not specific to a single architecture. These findings demonstrate that safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. We argue that improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that explicitly detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

items.title: Researchers introduce SkillCoach, a self-evolving rubric framework for evaluating and improving agentic skill-use in LLM agents by analyzing skill selection, following, composition, and reflection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SkillCoach: Self-Evolving Rubrics for Evaluating and Enhancing Agentic Skill-Use
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SkillCoach, a self-evolving rubric framework designed to evaluate and improve the use of skills by large language model (LLM) agents. SkillCoach addresses challenges in skill repositories where overlapping skills complicate reliable skill use, and where traditional final outcome verification is insufficient for thorough evaluation and training. The framework assesses agent behavior across four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection, separating process quality from mere task success.

SkillCoach generates skill-grounded process rubrics from real agent rollouts and uses these rubrics to supervise the selection of high-quality training trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that these evolved rubrics enhance evaluation accuracy, reveal failures that final outcome measures miss, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only approaches, thereby supporting more effective agentic skill use.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01874v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Skills are becoming a reusable operational layer for LLM agents, encoding SOPs, domain rules, tool workflows, scripts, and validation routines. In realistic skill repositories, overlapping skills make reliable skill-use difficult. Final verifier success is too coarse for both evaluation and training, since an agent may pass through trial and error while selecting distractor skills, skipping required steps, composing workflows incorrectly or omitting final checks. We introduce SkillCoach, a self-evolving rubric framework for evaluating and enhancing agentic skill-use. The evolved rubrics further serve as process supervision for selecting high-quality training trajectories. Experiments show that evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.

items.title: Researchers propose Spec-AUF training method to improve masked block drafters by focusing cross-entropy loss on accepted token prefixes, boosting performance on Qwen3-8B benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Spec-AUF: Accept-Until-Fail Training under Train-Inference Misalignment for Masked Block Drafters
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Spec-AUF, a training method designed to improve masked block drafters used in speculative decoding for autoregressive generation. This approach focuses the cross-entropy loss on the accepted token prefixes rather than the entire predicted block, aligning training more closely with inference behavior where only the longest accepted prefix is committed. Applied to the Qwen3-8B model, Spec-AUF enhanced the average emitted token length across multiple benchmarks, demonstrating consistent performance gains without altering the inference pipeline or requiring auxiliary objectives.

Spec-AUF addresses the mismatch between training and inference in block drafters, which traditionally use full-block cross-entropy loss despite discarding tokens after the first rejection during decoding. By limiting supervision to the prefix up to the first predicted failure, Spec-AUF approximates prefix-sensitive learning in mask-only drafters that lack input-side conditioning. Experiments showed that this focused loss support improves decoding efficiency and effectiveness, with additional findings indicating that standard position-decay weighting becomes less impactful once Spec-AUF truncates the loss support.

The method's simplicity and compatibility with existing drafter architectures suggest it could be broadly applicable for enhancing speculative decoding performance. Its ability to increase emitted token length and improve decoding quality without complicating the inference process may influence future developments in efficient autoregressive generation models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01893v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting a block of tokens that the target model verifies left-to-right, committing only the longest accepted prefix. Block (DLM-style) drafters predict the whole block in parallel, which is fast but trained with a full-block cross-entropy that supervises every position against the gold continuation -- even though inference discards every token after the first rejection. Recent acceptance-aware objectives patch this by reweighting the full-block loss; we instead use teacher-forced learning as a motivation for how supervision should concentrate on the accepted prefix. A mask-only block drafter has no input-side channel for gold-prefix conditioning, so AUF approximates that prefix-sensitive supervision on the loss side by keeping the cross-entropy support only through the drafter's first predicted failure. AUF is a single, detached change to the CE support -- no auxiliary objective, no verifier rollouts, and no change to the inference pipeline or the exactness contract. Within fixed drafter backbones and serving settings on Qwen3-8B, AUF raises the DFlash drafter's average emitted length $\tau$, averaged over six benchmarks, from 2.40 to 2.61, with a gain on every benchmark, and transfers to Domino's two-branch head (2.56 to 2.68). Two findings sharpen the picture: the decay-only baseline reaches higher token accuracy on the shared block mask yet decodes worse, and on DFlash, once AUF truncates the support, the standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.

items.title: Researchers propose ScopeEdit, a scope-aware online editor for multimodal large language models that controls edit propagation boundaries to improve cross-modal transfer and edit stability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Multimodal Knowledge Edit-Scoped Generalization for Online Recursive MLLM Editing
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced ScopeEdit, a novel online editor designed for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that manages the boundaries of knowledge edits to enhance cross-modal transfer and maintain edit stability. Unlike existing editors that focus mainly on reliability and long-term stability, ScopeEdit controls how edits propagate semantically, ensuring that changes affect relevant modalities without unintended spillover. This approach addresses the challenge of balancing instance-level edit success with broader cross-modal consistency and containment.

ScopeEdit operates by splitting each update into two branches: a modality-local absorption branch that stabilizes the edit within a specific modality, and an evidence-gated shared generalization branch that allows cross-modal propagation only when visual and textual evidence align. Both branches use orthogonal low-rank spaces and efficient computational techniques to keep the editing overhead constant. Extensive testing across various benchmarks, model architectures, and real-world scenarios demonstrated that ScopeEdit improves the trade-off between effective cross-modal knowledge transfer and limiting unintended effects, while preserving reliability, stability, and efficiency in online editing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01978v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online multimodal knowledge editing requires injecting a continual stream of visual-textual corrections into multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with bounded overhead and minimal disruption to unrelated behaviors. Existing editors mainly emphasize edit reliability and long-horizon stability, but rarely control the semantic boundary of each edit. Our pilot analyses of post-edit behaviors and internal neuronal activities reveal a scope gap behind reliable edits: instance-level success neither guarantees transfer to valid cross-modal variants nor prevents leakage to unrelated inputs, while edit-related cross-modal responses concentrate in deeper semantic layers. Therefore, we formulate Edit-Scoped Generalization, reframing online MLLM editing from merely correcting an instance to controlling the propagation boundary of each edit. To this end, we propose ScopeEdit, a scope-aware online editor that decomposes each update into a modality-local absorption branch and an evidence-gated shared generalization branch. The local branch supports stable edit absorption, whereas the shared branch enables cross-modal propagation only when visual and textual evidence are sufficiently aligned. Both branches perform scope-separated write geometries in orthogonal low-rank spaces and maintain branch-wise preconditioners via Sherman--Morrison recursions, yielding constant per-edit overhead. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks, long-horizon edit streams, MLLM backbones, real-world VLKEB scenarios, and complex vision-language architectures show that ScopeEdit consistently improves the trade-off between in-scope cross-modal transfer and out-of-scope locality, while preserving edit reliability, stability and online efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/lab-klc/ScopeEdit.

items.title: Researchers introduce PACE, a proxy benchmark framework that predicts agentic LLM performance using a small subset of non-agentic evaluation instances, reducing evaluation cost by over 99% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PACE: A Proxy for Agentic Capability Evaluation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PACE, a proxy benchmark framework designed to predict the performance of agentic large language models (LLMs) using a small, carefully selected subset of non-agentic evaluation instances. This approach significantly reduces the cost and time required for evaluation, cutting expenses by over 99% compared to traditional agentic benchmarks like SWE-Bench and GAIA. PACE constructs proxy benchmarks by selecting instances from existing non-agentic tests that best correlate with agentic benchmark outcomes, enabling accurate performance predictions through regression models.

The framework combines two instance-selection strategies—target-relevance local selection and globally informative global selection—to curate a compact subset of evaluation tasks. Experiments involving 14 models across four agentic benchmarks and 19 non-agentic benchmarks demonstrated that PACE-Bench, the resulting proxy benchmark, predicts agentic scores with high accuracy, achieving a mean absolute error under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, and approximately 85% accuracy in pairwise model ranking. This method allows practitioners to reliably estimate agentic capabilities during model development and selection without the extensive resources typically required for full agent evaluations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluating LLM agents on benchmarks like SWE-Bench and GAIA can be expensive, time-consuming, and requires complex infrastructure. A single evaluation can cost thousands of dollars and take days to complete. In contrast, non-agentic LLM benchmarks that test individual capabilities (e.g., reasoning, code generation) are fast and cheap to run. In this paper, we investigate whether performance on expensive agentic benchmarks can be accurately predicted by the performance on a small, carefully selected subset of atomic evaluation instances. We introduce PACE, a framework that constructs proxy benchmarks by selecting instances from existing non-agentic evaluations whose aggregate scores most reliably predict model performances on agentic benchmarks. Given a pool of candidate instances spanning atomic capabilities, PACE fits a regression that maps a model's scores on a compact subset of source instances to its score on the target agentic benchmark. The subset itself is curated by combining two complementary instance-selection strategies, target-relevance local selection and globally informative global selection. We apply PACE to the 4 target agentic benchmarks in this paper, which yields PACE-Bench, the concrete proxy benchmark that we evaluate in the paper. Experiments across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks show that PACE-Bench predicts agentic scores with leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) mean absolute error (MAE) under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, and pairwise model-ranking accuracy around 85%, all at much less than 1% of the full agentic evaluation cost. We further analyze the selected proxy instances, revealing which skills each agentic benchmark uniquely demands. PACE enables practitioners to obtain reliable estimates of agentic performance during model development, selection, and routing, without the overhead of full agent evaluation.

items.title: Researchers propose Maven, a reinforcement learning framework with editable evidence memory that rewards intermediate evidence-state transitions for improved long-context reasoning in Llama and Qwen models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evidence-State Rewards for Long-Context Reasoning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Maven, a reinforcement learning framework designed to enhance long-context reasoning in language models like Llama and Qwen. Maven improves the process by maintaining an editable evidence memory and rewarding intermediate evidence-state transitions, rather than focusing solely on final answers or static evidence extraction. This approach allows the models to better locate, revise, and synthesize evidence distributed across lengthy inputs.

Maven assigns rewards based on the contribution of actions such as adding, linking, or dropping evidence, which helps optimize the navigation through evidence states. Evaluations on benchmarks including LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER demonstrate that Maven outperforms traditional reinforcement learning methods and evidence-identification baselines by producing more comprehensive evidence sets and reducing the retention of irrelevant information.

The findings suggest that reinforcement learning strategies that focus on stateful evidence navigation can significantly improve long-context reasoning capabilities in large language models, offering a more effective alternative to one-shot evidence extraction methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02073v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-context reasoning requires models to locate, revise, and synthesize evidence distributed across lengthy inputs. Existing long-context RL methods usually reward final answers or static evidence extraction, offering little feedback on how intermediate actions change the model's evidence state. We propose Maven, a reinforcement learning framework with an editable evidence memory. Maven defines an answer-conditioned evidence-state value and rewards action-level state transitions: add actions are credited by marginal gain and hindsight contribution, link actions by evidence synergy, and drop actions by improved answer support after removing misleading evidence. These rewards are assigned to the corresponding action spans in GRPO. Across Llama and Qwen models on LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER, Maven outperforms outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines, producing more sufficient evidence sets and lower distractor retention. Our results show that long-context RL benefits from optimizing stateful evidence navigation rather than one-shot evidence extraction.

items.originalTitle: SUNTA: Hierarchical Video Prediction with Surprise-based Chunking
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced SUNTA, a hierarchical video prediction model that uses surprise-based chunking to improve long-horizon predictions in 2D and 3D environments. Unlike previous models that rely on fixed-length or similarity-based chunking, SUNTA determines chunk boundaries based on prediction errors, which better reflect when extended context is needed. This approach addresses challenges such as hierarchical collapse during training and the lack of surprise signals during open-loop prediction by employing a decoupled training strategy and using internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric.

Experiments demonstrate that SUNTA significantly outperforms existing baselines by maintaining accurate video predictions over 250 timesteps, whereas other models' accuracy deteriorates within the first 10 timesteps. This advancement highlights the potential of surprise-driven chunking in enhancing the temporal segmentation and prediction capabilities of hierarchical state-space models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hierarchical state-space models (HSSMs) offer a promising approach to long-horizon prediction by segmenting sequences into temporal chunks. However, their performance hinges on how chunk boundaries are determined. While prior HSSMs typically rely on fixed-length chunking or similarity-based boundary detection, these methods often misalign with the intrinsic temporal structure of the data. We argue that chunking should instead be driven by prediction errors, which more directly indicate when longer-range context becomes necessary. Nevertheless, integrating surprise-based chunking into HSSMs introduces critical challenges, including hierarchical collapse during end-to-end training and the absence of surprise signals during open-loop prediction. To address these issues, we propose Surprise-based Nested Temporal Abstraction (SUNTA), a method that employs a decoupled training strategy to preserve surprise signals and uses internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric to determine chunk boundaries within imagined rollouts. Experiments on video prediction tasks in 2D and 3D environments demonstrate that SUNTA outperforms baselines, uniquely maintaining accurate predictions over 250 timesteps, whereas all baselines degrade within the first 10 timesteps.

items.title: Researchers evaluate GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro on five clinician-authored clinical reasoning tasks using a detailed rubric, finding critical criteria pass rates below 42% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A rubric-based controlled comparison of frontier language models on expert-authored clinical reasoning tasks
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a detailed evaluation of three advanced language models—GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro—using five clinician-authored clinical reasoning tasks across four medical specialties. Each task was assessed with a comprehensive rubric containing 184 criteria, revealing that the models achieved mean pass rates below 47%, with critical criteria pass rates ranging from only 32.4% to 41.7%. Notably, over half of the critical criteria were unmet by any model, highlighting significant challenges in clinical reasoning performance.

The study employed a rigorous, weighted rubric developed from expert clinical answers to ensure precise assessment of model outputs. While lower-stakes criteria were passed at rates between 80% and 90%, the models struggled with high-priority clinical requirements. Additionally, three automated language model raters closely matched expert evaluations, demonstrating the potential for scalable and reliable assessment methods.

These findings underscore the current limitations of frontier language models in handling complex clinical reasoning tasks and suggest the need for further development. The evaluation framework introduced offers a scalable and defensible approach that could evolve into a large-scale benchmark to better measure and improve medical AI performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiple-choice medical benchmarks are increasingly saturated, and recent rubric-based evaluations such as HealthBench have shown that open-ended clinical performance is far from solved - its "Hard" subset top score remains 32%. We present a small, deliberately difficult evaluation dataset of five clinician-authored clinical scenarios spanning four specialties (anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, and obstetrics), each accompanied by an atomic, weighted, MECE rubric (25-62 criteria per task; 184 criteria total) authored from a clinician-drafted golden answer. We evaluate three frontier models: GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Mean rubric pass rates were 0.47 (Claude), 0.39 (GPT), and 0.37 (Gemini). The central finding is an inversion of clinical priority: the highest-weighted (weight-5, critical) criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7%, while low-stakes weight-1 criteria passed at 80-90%. 56 of 108 critical (weight-5) criteria (52%) were satisfied by no model. Three LLM autoraters reproduced expert met/not-met labels on 92.8-94.7% of 552 graded criteria. We position this as a methods-and-preliminary-findings contribution: the five tasks demonstrate a scalable, defensible pipeline ready to develop into a large-scale benchmark.

items.title: Researchers propose Purified OPSD method to improve long chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs by isolating and filtering reference-induced shortcuts using pointwise mutual information [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Purified OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation Without Losing How to Think
items.summary:
Researchers have identified limitations in the on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) method for improving long chain-of-thought (long-CoT) reasoning in large language models (LLMs). They found that OPSD often leads to rote memorization of reference-specific shortcuts rather than enhancing transferable reasoning skills, which can destabilize the models' reflective reasoning capabilities. To address this, they propose a purified OPSD approach that isolates and filters out these reference-induced shortcuts using a reference-only teacher model and pointwise mutual information (PMI) to create a more effective supervision signal.

This two-step method first separates the non-transferable component of the teacher's supervision by conditioning on the reference alone, then uses PMI to transform the residual signal into a target distribution that the student model can learn from without inheriting shortcuts. Experiments on multiple long-CoT models and datasets demonstrate that this purified OPSD consistently improves performance over both the base models and standard OPSD, while maintaining the models' natural epistemic behavior during training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving LLM reasoning, where a privileged teacher with access to reference solutions provides token-level supervision on the student's own generated trajectories. However, we find that OPSD consistently fails on long chain-of-thought (long-CoT) reasoning models, yielding at best marginal gains while destabilizing the reflective reasoning capability these models depend on. Through a novel decomposition of the teacher's supervision signal, we identify the root cause: the teacher's supervision is dominated by a reference-induced component that drives rote memorization of reference-specific shortcuts, while the question-conditioned, inference-transferable component is ignored or actively opposed. Based on this diagnosis, we propose a two-step solution. First, we construct a reference-only teacher (the same model conditioned on the reference without the question) to isolate the non-transferable component of the supervision signal; the residual after subtracting this component captures the question-conditioned, inference-transferable correction. Second, we use pointwise mutual information (PMI) as the mechanism to transform this residual into a well-formed PMI target distribution that the student can directly distill from, filtering out the reference-induced shortcut. Experiments on four long-CoT models across two datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over both the base model and standard OPSD, while preserving the models' natural epistemic behavior throughout training.

items.title: Researchers introduce AgenticSTS, a bounded-memory testbed for long-horizon LLM agents using typed retrieval in Slay the Spire 2 with a public benchmark and reproducible methodology [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AgenticSTS: A Bounded-Memory Testbed for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed AgenticSTS, a bounded-memory testbed designed to improve long-horizon decision-making in large language model (LLM) agents. Unlike traditional methods that append all past interactions to each prompt, AgenticSTS uses typed retrieval to assemble fresh user messages for each decision, keeping prompts concise and allowing isolated analysis of memory components. This approach was tested in Slay the Spire 2, a complex deck-building game requiring numerous strategic decisions, where current LLMs struggle to win at low difficulty levels compared to human players.

The testbed includes a public benchmark with 298 completed game trajectories, condition tags, and analysis tools, enabling reproducible research on how explicit memory layers affect LLM agent performance. Initial experiments showed that enabling strategic skills improved win rates, though results are preliminary. This work provides a validated methodology and resources for studying memory management in long-horizon LLM agents, addressing challenges in maintaining effective context over extended interactions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory for a long-horizon LLM agent is a contract about what each future decision is allowed to see. The simplest contract appends past observations, tool calls, and reflections to every prompt, which makes prior context easy to access but also turns it into a jumbled mixture in which the effect of any single memory component is hard to isolate. We introduce and instrument an alternative bounded contract: every decision is made from a fresh user message assembled by typed retrieval, with no raw cross-decision transcript appended. The prompt thus stays bounded across runs of any length, and any single layer can be ablated in isolation. We instantiate the contract in Slay the Spire 2, a closed-rule stochastic deck-building game whose runs require hundreds of tactical and strategic decisions. A public online benchmark of frontier LLMs on the same game reports zero wins at the lowest difficulty across five configurations, and the developer-reported human win rate at the same difficulty is 16%; the task is hard but not saturated. Within our harness, a fixed-A0 ablation shows the largest observed difference when triggered strategic skills are enabled: the no-store baseline wins 3/10 games and adding the skill layer 6/10. At this sample size the comparison is directional rather than statistically decisive (Fisher exact p\approx0.37); a cross-backbone probe and public accumulating-context baselines are reported as operational comparisons rather than controlled tests of the contract variable itself. We release a reproducible testbed: 298 completed trajectories with condition tags, frozen memory/skill snapshots, prompt records, and analysis scripts -- an agent design and a validated, reusable methodology for studying how explicit memory layers shape long-horizon LLM-agent decisions.

items.title: Researchers adapt Recursive Feature Machine to rapidly identify multi-dimensional refusal subspaces in Qwen 2.5 and Qwen 3 large language models, improving efficiency and performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Fast Multi-dimensional Refusal Subspaces via RFM-AGOP
items.summary:
Researchers have adapted the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm to quickly identify multi-dimensional refusal subspaces in large language models (LLMs) such as Qwen 2.5 and Qwen 3. This advancement addresses the challenge of computationally expensive methods previously used to extract complex behaviors like refusal to answer harmful queries, which exist in multi-dimensional activation spaces rather than single linear directions. The adapted RFM, enhanced with probe-informed initialization, can identify these subspaces within seconds, improving both efficiency and performance on reasoning and non-reasoning models.

The study demonstrates that RFM not only speeds up subspace identification but also outperforms alternative methods in ablation tasks. The researchers plan to further investigate the relationships between subspaces identified by different techniques. If validated, RFM could become a cost-effective and scalable tool to complement existing methods for monitoring and steering LLM behaviors, enhancing safety and interpretability in these models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02396v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Steering and monitoring activations in Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for both safety and interpretability. Early work assumed behaviours are encoded along single linear directions, but recent findings suggest complex behaviours, such as the refusal to answer harmful queries, live in multi-dimensional subspaces. However, existing methods for extracting these subspaces are computationally expensive, which becomes prohibitive on reasoning models who produce long reasoning traces. By adapting the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm -- which can be computed efficiently -- with a probe-informed initialization, we are able to identify the multi-dimensional refusal subspace in seconds, on reasoning (Qwen 3) and non-reasoning (Qwen 2.5) models. While RFM allows for faster subspace identification, it also showed better performances on the ablation task than its alternatives. More work is planned to better understand the relations between subspaces found by different methods. If confirmed, RFM could be a cheap and scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods in LLMs.

items.title: Study evaluates GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, and GLM for automated grading of Linux/bash exams using a four-level cognitive taxonomy, finding Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric prompts achieves highest human-AI agreement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Automated grading of Linux/bash examinations using large language models: a four-level cognitive taxonomy approach
items.summary:
A study evaluated four leading Large Language Models—GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, and GLM—for their ability to grade Linux/bash command-line exam responses using a four-level cognitive taxonomy. This taxonomy ranges from basic information retrieval to advanced system management tasks. The models were tested on 1,200 student responses with two types of prompts: a minimal baseline and a rubric-enhanced version. Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the highest agreement with human graders, demonstrating strong potential for AI-assisted grading in computing education.

The study found that grading accuracy declined as question complexity increased, with the largest discrepancies occurring at higher taxonomy levels. Across all models, the quality of the rubric prompts had a greater impact on grading agreement than the choice of model provider. These findings establish a framework for identifying which exam questions are suitable for automated grading and which require human review, while also providing evaluation protocols and prompt templates to support scalable and reliable grading.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02432v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scalable and reliable grading of command-line examinations remains a challenge in computing education, where rising enrolments make manual marking difficult and rule-based autograders cannot handle partial credit, equivalent solutions, or syntactic variation. The study adopts a four-level cognitive taxonomy that combines cognitive complexity and operational impact, ranging from information retrieval (L1) and basic file manipulation (L2) to structural operations (L3) and advanced system management (L4). Gemini~3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the highest human-AI agreement (ICC(3,1) = 0.888, MAE = 0.10, Bland-Altman bias = -0.014). Agreement declined consistently as taxonomy level increased, with the largest discrepancies at higher levels. Across all models, rubric quality had a larger effect than provider choice, with structured prompts consistently improving agreement. These results show that question complexity is a reliable predictor of the difficulty LLMs face in grading accurately, and they establish a principled, taxonomy-based framework for determining which questions are suitable for AI-assisted grading and which require human review, while also providing a transferable evaluation protocol and prompt templates.

items.title: Researchers introduce EvoPolicyGym benchmark to evaluate autonomous policy evolution in interactive RL environments, with GPT-5.5 achieving top performance across 16 tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EvoPolicyGym: Evaluating Autonomous Policy Evolution in Interactive Environments
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced EvoPolicyGym, a new benchmark designed to evaluate autonomous policy evolution in interactive reinforcement learning environments. This benchmark tests how agents iteratively improve executable policies within a fixed interaction budget, providing a controlled setting to assess autonomous policy refinement. GPT-5.5 demonstrated the strongest overall performance, ranking in the top two across all 16 tested environments.

EvoPolicyGym offers detailed diagnostics beyond simple leaderboard scores, analyzing how agents allocate resources and translate feedback into policy adjustments. The findings highlight that successful autonomous policy evolution relies on discovering mechanisms suited to specific tasks and refining policies effectively under limited feedback, rather than merely achieving isolated task successes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly expected to improve executable policies through feedback, yet existing evaluations often collapse this process into a final score or confound it with open-ended software-engineering progress. We introduce Autonomous Policy Evolution, a controlled evaluation setting in which a harness-model agent repeatedly edits an executable policy system under a fixed interaction budget. We instantiate this setting in EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark built from compact interactive RL environments that evaluates how agents iteratively improve explored policies. On the EvoPolicyGym suite, GPT-5.5 achieves the strongest aggregate rank score and top-two performance on all 16 environments. Beyond leaderboard results, EvoPolicyGym also provides trajectory-level diagnostics that distinguish how agents allocate budget, convert feedback into parametric tuning. These analyses show that strong autonomous policy evolution depends not only on isolated task wins, but on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback.

items.title: Researchers present TokenScope, an interactive tool for token-level explainability and interpretability in code generation by large language models, combining decoding-time signals with structural program analysis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TokenScope: Token-Level Explainability and Interpretability for Code-Oriented Tasks in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed TokenScope, an interactive tool designed to enhance understanding of how large language models (LLMs) make token-level decisions during code generation. TokenScope integrates decoding-time signals with structural program analysis, providing detailed token-level metrics, attention patterns, and structural information to facilitate in-depth exploration of model behavior.

The tool supports features such as interactive token replacement, counterfactual branching, and code-aware aggregation using abstract syntax trees. By combining fine-grained uncertainty measures with interactive mechanisms, TokenScope enables systematic investigation of alternative generation paths and improves interpretability for both researchers and practitioners working with decoder-based LLMs in code-oriented tasks.

While recent tools provide insights into model internals or generation outcomes, they often lack decoding-time signals, fine-grained uncertainty measures, and interactive mechanisms for exploring alternative generation paths. We present TokenScope, an interactive interpretability and analysis tool for decoder-based LLMs that exposes token-level metrics, attention patterns, and structural information during generation. By unifying decoding-time signals with structural program analysis, TokenScope enables systematic investigation of LLM behaviour during code generation.

items.title: Researchers propose ProvenanceGuard, a provenance-based framework that reduces misalignment errors in LLM agents' tool use from up to 42.9% to 1.8% across benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Safeguarding LLM Agents from Misalignment through Provenance Analysis
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced ProvenanceGuard, a provenance-based framework designed to reduce misalignment errors in large language model (LLM) agents when using tools. Misalignment occurs when an agent's tool invocation deviates from the user's intent, potentially causing harmful outcomes. ProvenanceGuard analyzes the agent's proposed actions for alignment with the user's input before execution, significantly lowering misalignment error rates from up to 42.9% to as low as 1.8% across benchmarks.

The framework formalizes misalignment detection by verifying whether a proposed tool call is supported by traceable evidence within the agent's context. Tested on two benchmarks, Agent-SafetyBench and WorkBench, and across ten backbone LLMs, ProvenanceGuard outperformed existing LLM-as-a-judge methods by reducing errors and intervention burdens without increasing unnecessary interventions. These results highlight the effectiveness of structured, provenance-based reasoning in safeguarding LLM agents against misalignment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLM agents gain increasing access to powerful tools, ensuring that their actions are aligned with the user's intent becomes critical. When an agent's proposed tool invocation deviates from the user's intent -- a phenomenon called misalignment -- it may lead to harmful consequences that are difficult to undo. Existing runtime guardrails rely on an LLM-as-a-judge paradigm that lacks a systematic framework for reasoning about alignment, often producing judgments that are inconsistent or difficult to audit. Motivated by provenance analysis, we propose a provenance-based conceptual framework that formalizes misalignment detection as determining whether a proposed tool call is supported by traceable evidence in the agent's context. Building on this framework, we propose ProvenanceGuard, a multi-stage pipeline that analyzes the agent's action for three types of misalignment before the selected tool is executed and only allows the action to take place when it is considered aligned with the user's input query. We evaluated our proposed approach on two different benchmarks, Agent-SafetyBench and WorkBench, across 10 backbone LLMs. Compared to the LLM-as-a-judge baseline, ProvenanceGuard reduces error rate on misaligned traces from 42.9% to 1.8% on Agent-SafetyBench and from 32.1% to 17.3% on WorkBench, while reducing intervention burden on task-successful traces from 30.5% to 12.8% and introducing no statistically significant increase in unnecessary interventions on aligned traces. These results demonstrate that structured, provenance-based reasoning provides an effective and practical foundation for safeguarding LLM agents from misalignment.

items.title: Researchers propose Kara, a sliding-window KV cache compression method for reasoning LLMs that reduces memory usage and improves decoding throughput, demonstrated in the KvLLM inference framework [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Kara: Efficient Reasoning LLM Serving via Sliding-Window KV Cache Compression
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Kara, a sliding-window key-value (KV) cache compression method designed to improve the efficiency of reasoning language models that generate long chain-of-thought sequences. Kara addresses limitations in existing compression techniques by selectively compressing only the most recent context during decoding, using bidirectional attention to identify important KV pairs and expanding them into flexible-sized chunks. This approach reduces memory usage and enhances decoding throughput.

Kara is integrated into KvLLM, an inference framework built on vLLM with PagedAttention, which further optimizes KV cache management. Experiments demonstrate that Kara and KvLLM consistently improve performance by lowering memory overhead and increasing output speed without significant information loss, offering a promising solution for efficient large language model serving.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01237v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning language models often generate long chain-of-thought (CoT), which accumulates a massive KV cache during the decoding phase and incurs high decoding latency and limited throughput. To address these issues, KV cache compression has emerged as a promising technique for reducing memory overhead by selectively removing unimportant KV pairs while preserving useful ones for subsequent decoding. Nevertheless, we identify two key limitations in existing KV cache compression methods: 1) their threshold-triggered compression policy may provide limited throughput improvement or even reduce throughput, and may fully eliminate KV pairs from certain blocks of the sequence, potentially worsening information loss. 2) they typically retain either isolated KV pairs or fixed-size chunks with rigid boundaries, failing to preserve important flexible-sized chunks at arbitrary token positions. To overcome these limitations, we propose Kara, a sliding-window KV cache compression method that performs decoding-time compression by operating only on the recently generated context. Kara leverages bidirectional attention to score and select informative KV pairs in the window. To enable flexible preservation of important semantic information, we design a Token2Chunk module to expand a subset of selected KV pairs into chunks. Furthermore, we adapt Kara to PagedAttention and develop KvLLM, an inference framework built upon vLLM, which reduces KV cache memory usage and effectively improves output throughput. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent performance improvements of proposed Kara and KvLLM.

items.title: Researchers propose SPARCLE, a speaker-aware grapheme representation model using contrastive learning to improve text-to-speech quality and reduce word error rates in low-resource settings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SPARCLE: SPeaker-aware Aligned Representations via Contrastive Language Embeddings
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced SPARCLE, a speaker-aware grapheme representation model designed to enhance text-to-speech (TTS) systems, particularly in low-resource settings. Unlike traditional phoneme-based approaches that depend on grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) systems and often miss speaker-specific acoustic nuances, SPARCLE enriches graphemes with precise acoustic information by aligning them with Wav2Vec2 acoustic representations conditioned on speaker identity using contrastive learning. This approach serves as a replacement for G2P systems and has demonstrated significant improvements, halving word error rates in extreme low-resource scenarios compared to standard grapheme-based models.

items.title: Researchers find BPE tokenization fragments safety-critical words, enabling character-level attacks that bypass alignment in five major LLM families [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Breaking Safety at the Token Boundary: How BPE Tokenization Creates Exploitable Gaps in LLM Alignment
items.summary:
Researchers have discovered that Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenization in large language models (LLMs) fragments safety-critical words into sub-word pieces, creating vulnerabilities that allow character-level attacks to bypass safety alignment. This issue was tested across five major LLM families, where targeted perturbations flipped refusal triggers on a high percentage of harmful prompts, often resulting in genuinely harmful outputs. The study found that existing public alignment datasets do not include intentionally fragmented inputs, which contributes to this gap in safety.

The research involved detailed analysis including activation patching and targeted mutation experiments, pinpointing the disruption to specific layers and safety-related words. Attempts to defend against these attacks using various training methods showed limited success, with some approaches causing a global collapse that increased refusals on benign prompts. To better evaluate defenses, the researchers introduced a new diagnostic tool called Conv-Benign. Their findings highlight a structural weakness in current LLM safety mechanisms linked to tokenization, suggesting that addressing this fragmentation is necessary but not sufficient for robust alignment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01239v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Character-level perturbations bypass safety alignment in modern LLMs despite leaving prompts human-readable. We identify and test a central structural mechanism: BPE tokenization fragments safety-critical words into sub-word pieces, and the three public alignment datasets we surveyed contain no intentionally fragmented inputs. The mechanism is a chain, tested end-to-end on five model families (Qwen-3-4B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B). An optimization targeting safety-token fragmentation flips the first-token refusal trigger on 80-100% of refused HarmBench prompts, with 48% of those flips producing genuinely harmful outputs (per-model 29-65%; gap-vs-behavior ROC-AUC 0.66-0.98, pooled 0.84). Activation patching localizes the disrupted signal to the last ${\sim}30\%$ of layers; an alignment-data scan finds zero fragmented prompts among 30,000 examples (positive-control recall $\geq 99\%$ at attack-relevant intensities); and targeted-mutation experiments isolate safety words as the disruption locus. On the defense side, a 68-cell grid (55 trained checkpoints) shows that no DPO configuration achieves seed- and pool-stable ASR closure on the three families with closed pool-size confounds. SFT trained on fragmented prompts closes ASR on 3/5 families but only via global collapse that raises refusal on benign prompts as well, indicating the missing distribution is necessary but not sufficient under the LoRA-16 recipe we tested. To distinguish selective repair from global collapse, we introduce Conv-Benign, a candidate paired diagnostic. All ASR claims are 3-judge-calibrated (cell rankings stable across judges; absolute levels $\pm$18pp; see App.~B.13).

items.title: Researchers find prompt framing causes inflated count-based F1 scores in LLM error detection without improved span localization, based on tests of six models over 4,290 responses [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Prompt Framing Distorts Count-Based Evaluation of LLM Error Detection: Evidence from Numeric Anchoring
items.summary:
A recent study reveals that count-based F1 scores, commonly used to evaluate large language model (LLM) error detection, can increase significantly without actual improvement in accurately locating error spans, a phenomenon termed F1 Inflation. Researchers introduced ErrorBench, a stress-test protocol assessing six LLMs across five prompt conditions using 4,290 responses from CoNLL-2014 passages. The results showed that anchored prompts caused notable F1 Inflation, with increases up to 0.79 points under standard scoring and 0.96 under strict matching criteria.

Further testing with the ERRANT 3.0.0 pipeline confirmed these findings, showing that prompt framing led to a substantial rise in count-based F1 scores but only a minimal increase in span-aware metrics. The study also observed that models like GPT and Claude, which follow instructions closely, produced larger count responses compared to the Gemini family. These findings suggest that evaluations of LLM proofreading and document review should avoid relying solely on pre-populated error counts and instead incorporate span-aware metrics alongside count-based measures to provide a more accurate assessment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Count-based F1 is widely used as a proxy for LLM error-detection quality, but this paper shows that it can rise dramatically without a corresponding improvement in span localization, a gap termed F1 Inflation. The paper introduces ErrorBench, a controlled stress-test protocol for prompt-induced count distortion. ErrorBench evaluates six contemporary LLMs under five prompt conditions over 4,290 responses from 143 CoNLL-2014 passages. Under CoNLL-2014 M2-style scoring, anchored prompts produce up to 0.79 points of F1 Inflation, and up to 0.96 under strict matching. A 100-passage replication using the official ERRANT 3.0.0 pipeline and multi-reference scoring reproduces the pattern: averaged over six models, the Blind-to-Anchored prompt shift raises Count-F1 by +0.21 while raising multi-reference ERRANT F0.5 by only +0.04. The study finds larger count responses in highly instruction-compliant GPT/Claude systems and smaller responses in the Gemini family under this stress-test protocol. The findings suggest that LLM proofreading and document-review evaluations should avoid pre-populated error counts and should report span-aware metrics alongside count-based metrics.

items.title: Researchers propose RAGP, a prompt compression method using Lévy walk-guided graph pruning on multiplex graphs, outperforming existing LLM and vision-based compression on LongBench tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mapping Text to Multiplex Graph: Prompt Compression as L\'evy Walk-Guided Graph Pruning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced RAGP, a novel prompt compression method that models text as a multiplex graph to capture both local syntactic dependencies and global semantic relations. By applying redundancy-aware graph pruning guided by Lévy walks, RAGP efficiently identifies non-redundant information across dense and sparse graph structures. This approach outperforms existing large language model-based and vision-based compression techniques on LongBench tasks, achieving higher scores at greater compression ratios.

RAGP represents text tokens or sentences as nodes connected by edges reflecting attention-based and semantic dependencies, enabling a more nuanced representation than traditional flat token sequences. The use of Lévy walks balances local and global exploration in the graph, improving the selection of essential nodes. Experimental results demonstrate that RAGP achieves an average score of 49.3 at a 4x compression ratio, surpassing methods like LongLLMLingua, which scores 48.8 at 3x compression. The method's code has been made publicly available for further research and application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01241v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing prompt compression methods treat text as flat token sequences, failing to capture the distributed nature of important information, which is often spread across multiple locations and connected through both local syntactic dependencies and global semantic relations. Such relational structure is naturally represented as a graph, where tokens or sentences become nodes and their dependencies become edges. To this end, we propose RAGP, which formulates prompt compression as Redundancy-Aware Graph Pruning on a multiplex graph that jointly models fine-grained attention-based dependencies and coarse-grained semantic relations. To efficiently identify non-redundant nodes in this heterogeneous structure (dense local subgraphs and sparse global connections), we employ Levy walks whose heavy-tailed step distribution naturally balances local exploitation with global exploration. Experiments on LongBench show that RAGP achieves an average score of 49.3 under a 4x compression ratio, outperforming existing LLM-based compression methods, such as LongLLMLingua, which attains 48.8 at a 3x compression ratio. Besides, RAGP also surpasses state-of-the-art vision-based text compression paradigms on multiple tasks. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RAGP-B0CB.

items.title: Researchers present ExPerT, a framework that personalizes LLM responses to users' domain expertise using query text and keystroke dynamics, reducing expertise inference error by 65.7% in a 40-participant study [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ExPerT: Personalizing LLM Responses to Users' Domain Expertise via Query-Wise Semantic and Keystroke Behavioral Cues
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ExPerT, a framework that personalizes large language model (LLM) responses based on users' domain expertise for each query. By combining semantic analysis of query text with behavioral cues from keystroke dynamics, ExPerT adapts the detail, terminology, and complexity of responses to better match user expertise. A study involving 40 participants and over 1,200 queries showed that ExPerT reduced expertise inference errors by 65.7% compared to existing methods and increased user satisfaction by 17.5% on a five-point scale.

ExPerT includes two main components: a semantic-behavioral expertise inference module that interprets both the content and typing behavior of queries, and an expertise-conditioned response generator that tailors the output accordingly. This approach addresses limitations of prior personalization techniques that relied solely on static profiles or text signals, which often failed to capture variations in user expertise across different queries.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01242v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by end users, yet existing personalization methods relying on static profiles or text-only signals fail to capture query-specific expertise variation. We present ExPerT, a query-wise personalization framework that adapts LLM responses to users' query domain expertise by combining semantic and behavioral cues. ExPerT consists of two key components: (i) a semantic-behavioral expertise inference module that jointly interprets query text and keystroke dynamics via in-context LLM prompting, and (ii) an expertise-conditioned response generation that adapts the level of detail, terminology, and conceptual complexity. Our user study with 40 participants and 1270 queries demonstrated that ExPerT reduced expertise inference error by 65.7% compared to the strongest baseline (MAE = 0.398 vs. 1.162) and improved response satisfaction by 17.52% (from 3.71 to 4.36) on a 5-point Likert scale.

items.originalTitle: Structuring the Space of Sociotechnical Alignment
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a human-centered framework to better define and evaluate sociotechnical alignment in AI, focusing on the social desirability of AI behavior. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01250v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sociotechnical alignment concerns the social desirability of AI behavior and is thus inherently normative, not merely technical. While NLP research increasingly addresses its technical aspects, it often leaves underspecified what such "social desirability" entails. We argue that this reflects a fundamental gap: the absence of a systematic way to specify how sociotechnical alignment defines, justifies, and evaluates socially desirable AI behavior. To address this gap, we introduce a human-centered framework for specifying sociotechnical alignment. We draw on social-scientific accounts of sociobehavioral desirability to ground the basis for behavioral desirability judgments and use this framework to analyze how alignment is specified in practice. Our systematic literature review identifies recurring patterns: normative concepts grounding desirability judgments are often unspecified or conflated with alignment targets for (desired) system behavior, target populations are underdefined, and design choices are rarely theoretically justified. These findings point to a lack of conceptual specificity that limits cumulative progress. We therefore offer recommendations that link social-scientific frameworks to alignment design choices, supporting more conceptually precise approaches to sociotechnical alignment.

items.title: Researchers benchmark 13 federated learning algorithms and 10 knowledge distillation objectives for 3D point cloud classification, revealing performance drops under non-IID data and recommending label-free distillation evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Benchmarking Federated Learning and Knowledge Distillation for Point Cloud Classification
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a comprehensive benchmark evaluating 13 federated learning (FL) algorithms and 10 knowledge distillation (KD) objectives for 3D point cloud classification, focusing on privacy-sensitive and resource-limited environments. Their study, involving 504 training runs on ModelNet40 and a clinical craniosynostosis dataset, found that FL performance significantly declines under extreme non-IID label distributions compared to centralized models. They also demonstrated that KD effectively compresses models, producing smaller and faster students that often match or exceed teacher performance.

The study revealed a critical evaluation issue when combining FL and KD: using hard-label cross-entropy on a labeled proxy dataset can misleadingly inflate student accuracy, masking poor federated teacher quality. Instead, label-free distillation objectives better reflect the true performance of the federated teacher. Based on these findings, the researchers recommend evaluating FL-KD pipelines with label-free distillation to ensure accuracy metrics accurately represent federated model quality rather than proxy label effects.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01272v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deploying 3D point cloud analysis in privacy-sensitive, resource-constrained settings faces two barriers: data cannot be centralized, and models must run on limited edge hardware. We present a multi-seed benchmark jointly evaluating federated learning (FL) and knowledge distillation (KD) for 3D point cloud classification. It spans 13 FL algorithms and 10 KD objectives (a 130-pair cross-product) across 504 training runs, evaluated on ModelNet40 and a clinical craniosynostosis dataset. We report three findings. First, under extreme non-IID label skew, standalone FL degrades sharply: on ModelNet40, the strongest method reaches 76.32% against a 92.26% centralized reference; on clinical data, the best reaches 75.83% against 100%. Second, distillation successfully compresses the teacher into a student 74.51% smaller and roughly twice as fast at inference, often matching or surpassing the teacher. Third, the combined pipeline exposes an evaluation pitfall: when distillation keeps a hard-label cross-entropy term on a labeled proxy split, a collapsed federated teacher (8.50%) paired with Logit-MSE still yields a 92.94% student. This 84.4-point gap reflects the proxy labels rather than the federated model, reusing the very labels whose privacy motivated federation. Objectives without hard labels instead track teacher quality ($r \approx 0.99$) and collapse when the teacher does. We therefore recommend evaluating FL-KD pipelines with label-free distillation so reported accuracy reflects the federated teacher, not the proxy.

items.title: Researchers propose a domain knowledge-based temporal-spatial graph convolution network for ECG recognition, achieving 88.1% average F1 score and outperforming state-of-the-art models on a nine-category Chinese ECG dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Domain Knowledge Based Temporal-Spatial Graph Convolution Network for ECG Recognition
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a novel domain knowledge-based temporal-spatial graph convolution network to improve electrocardiograph (ECG) recognition. By incorporating key PRQST landmark points and modeling both spatial and temporal relationships within and between ECG cycles, the model achieved an average F1 score of 88.1% on a nine-category Chinese ECG dataset, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods. This approach enhances interpretability and detection performance, particularly for rare ECG categories.

The model uses a double-stream directed graph structure where spatial graphs capture positional relationships among key ECG points, and temporal graphs represent dependencies across adjacent cycles in extended sequences. Experimental validation on the First Chinese ECG Intelligent Competition dataset demonstrated the effectiveness of integrating domain knowledge into the graph convolution framework, leading to improved classification accuracy across common and rare ECG types.
