items.title: Researchers present Decomposer, a framework that converts symbolic MIDI music into executable Strudel programs using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to improve reconstruction and code readability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Decomposer: Learning to Decompile Symbolic Music to Programs
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Decomposer, a framework that converts symbolic MIDI music into executable programs written in Strudel, a music programming language. This approach addresses the challenge of recovering high-level musical instructions from performances by translating MIDI inputs into readable and editable code that can faithfully reconstruct the original music when executed. Decomposer uses a two-stage training process involving supervised fine-tuning on a synthetic dataset and reinforcement learning to optimize both reconstruction accuracy and code readability.

The framework tackles the scarcity of paired MIDI and Strudel code data by creating Strudel-Synth, a synthetic corpus for initial training, and then refines the model using unpaired MIDI data with reinforcement learning. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world MIDI benchmarks demonstrate that Decomposer outperforms existing closed-source large language models in MIDI reconstruction fidelity while generating more readable and diverse code compared to heuristic converters.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Musical performance involves executing a set of high-level musical instructions, yet recovering those instructions from the performance is a challenging inverse problem. We present Decomposer, a post-training framework for symbolic music decompilation: the task of recovering executable, editable music programs from symbolic music. We instantiate the task as MIDI-to-Strudel decompilation, where the model takes symbolic MIDI as input and produces a program in Strudel, a music programming language, that reconstructs the input when executed. The task poses two challenges: Strudel is a low-resource language with little naturally paired MIDI-code data, and optimizing faithful reconstruction of MIDI alone can collapse to unreadable note-by-note transliteration. We address these challenges in two stages. First, we construct Strudel-Synth, a synthetic corpus of paired Strudel programs and rendered MIDI, and use it for supervised fine-tuning. Second, we refine the model with reinforcement learning on unpaired MIDI, optimizing rewards for both MIDI reconstruction faithfulness and code readability. Our evaluation across synthetic and real-world MIDI benchmarks shows that Decomposer achieves substantially higher MIDI reconstruction faithfulness than closed-source LLMs while producing more readable and diverse code than the heuristic converter.

items.title: Researchers evaluate cluster-based semantic chunking for Retrieval-Augmented Generation on academic theses and find it does not outperform simpler chunking methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Academic Texts
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated whether cluster-based semantic chunking enhances retrieval and answer quality in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems compared to fixed-size and recursive chunking methods. The study focused on long, structured academic theses and used the Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment (RAGAs) framework to measure performance. Results showed that cluster-based chunking did not outperform simpler chunking strategies under the tested conditions.

The evaluation revealed variability in performance between fixed and document-specific questions, likely influenced by document formatting and preprocessing. Additionally, the faithfulness metric based on RAGAs demonstrated limited reliability in this context, suggesting challenges in assessing answer quality for complex academic texts using current methods.

items.title: Researchers introduce Rank-Then-Act, a reward-free control framework using vision-language models and correlation-based reinforcement learning for video demonstration tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Rank-Then-Act: Reward-Free Control from Frame-Order Progress
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Rank-Then-Act (RTA), a novel framework that enables learning control policies from expert video demonstrations without relying on environment rewards. RTA uses a Vision-Language Model trained offline to score progress based on the temporal order of shuffled video frames, emphasizing visual semantics over time cues. Instead of using this scorer as a direct reward, the method employs a correlation-based reward function that measures the Spearman rank correlation between predicted progress and actual frame order, providing a stable and scale-invariant learning signal.

The framework was tested on both discrete and continuous control tasks, including PyBoy games and robotic environments like MetaWorld. RTA consistently matched or outperformed existing video-based reward learning approaches and demonstrated effective transferability across different tasks using a single pretrained progress scorer. This approach suggests that leveraging correlation-structured supervision from video-derived ordinal signals can serve as a scalable alternative to traditional reward design in reinforcement learning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Rank-Then-Act (RTA), a framework for learning control policies from expert video demonstrations without environment rewards. RTA trains a Vision-Language Model (VLM) offline as a progress-based ordinal scorer, using a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective over shuffled frame sequences, which forces the model to recover temporal ordering from visual semantics rather than trivial time cues. Importantly, instead of using the scorer directly as a scalar reward model, we propose a correlation-based reward function for reinforcement learning: at each interaction window, we compute the Spearman rank correlation between predicted progress rankings and true temporal indices, yielding a bounded, scale-invariant learning signal. This design decouples reward learning from absolute calibration and enables stable transfer across tasks and environments. We evaluate RTA on discrete control benchmarks (PyBoy: Catrap, Kirby) and continuous control tasks (PointMaze, MetaWorld). RTA consistently matches or outperforms prior video-based reward learning methods and rank-based baselines, while demonstrating strong cross-task reuse of a single pretrained progress scorer. Our results suggest that correlation-structured supervision over video-derived ordinal signals is sufficient for policy learning, offering a scalable alternative to explicit reward design.

items.title: Researchers propose SABER, a semantic-aligned brain network analysis framework using multi-scale hypergraphs to integrate LLM-derived semantics for improved brain disease diagnosis on ABIDE and ADHD-200 datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SABER: A Semantic-Aligned Brain Network Analysis Framework via Multi-scale Hypergraphs
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SABER, a novel brain network analysis framework that integrates semantic information derived from large language models (LLMs) to enhance brain disease diagnosis. This approach incorporates region-of-interest (ROI) level semantics through global self-attention to enrich brain network representations and constructs multi-scale hypergraphs to capture complex functional interactions. A decision-level semantic alignment mechanism further allows patient-specific textual embeddings to directly influence predictions without altering the underlying network structure.

Tests on public datasets, including ABIDE and ADHD-200, show that SABER achieves state-of-the-art diagnostic performance with improved stability and interpretability, especially in scenarios with limited sample sizes. This framework addresses limitations of previous methods that treated LLM semantics only as auxiliary inputs, enabling a more integrated and robust use of semantic knowledge in brain disease classification.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01901v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective brain disease diagnosis requires the synergy of brain connectivity patterns and high-level semantic knowledge. Existing methods, however, largely treat semantics from large language models (LLMs) as auxiliary features or supervision, limiting their direct role in decision-making and constraining classification stability and robustness. To overcome this, we propose a semantic-aligned brain network framework that actively integrates LLM-derived semantics into the prediction process. Specifically, ROI-level semantics are first incorporated via global self-attention to enrich node representations and provide whole-brain context. Multi-scale hypergraphs are then constructed to explicitly model functional subnetworks and multi-ROI interactions, addressing the locality limitations of traditional GNNs and capturing high-order dependencies. Finally, a decision-level semantic alignment mechanism selectively injects patient-specific textual embeddings into graph representations, enabling semantics to directly guide predictions without perturbing the underlying network structure. Experiments on public brain network datasets ABIDE and ADHD-200 demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, enhanced stability, and improved interpretability, particularly in small-sample settings.

items.title: Researchers propose population-based multi-objective training for discriminators in semi-supervised GANs, improving classification accuracy and training stability on MNIST with limited labels [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Population-Based Multi-Objective Training of Discriminators for Semi-Supervised GANs
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a population-based evolutionary training method for semi-supervised generative adversarial networks (SSL-GANs) that treats discriminator learning as a multi-objective optimization problem. This approach maintains a population of discriminators ranked by Pareto dominance, allowing the exploration of trade-offs between classification accuracy and real/fake discrimination, rather than combining these objectives into a single loss function. The method aims to enhance both the classifier accuracy and the quality of generated samples in SSL-GANs.

Experiments on the MNIST dataset with limited labeled data demonstrate that this multi-objective strategy improves training stability and robustness compared to existing SSL-GAN baselines. Among the variants tested, an elitist strategy consistently achieved the highest classification accuracy, highlighting the benefits of maintaining diverse discriminator populations during training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semi-supervised generative adversarial networks (SSL-GANs) can exploit large unlabeled datasets while retaining a classifier in the discriminator, but their training is often unstable. This paper proposes a population-based evolutionary training strategy in which discriminator learning is formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem. Instead of aggregating the supervised and unsupervised components of the SSL objective into a single scalar loss, the method maintains a population of discriminators ranked by Pareto dominance, enabling the exploration of different trade-offs between classification accuracy and real/fake discrimination. This formulation aims to improve both roles of SSL-GANs: learning accurate classifiers and training generators capable of producing realistic samples. We analyze several variants, including an elitist strategy and a mono-objective ablation, to assess the role of multi-objective selection. Experiments on MNIST with limited labels show improved training robustness compared to SSL-GAN and CE-SSL-GAN state-of-the-art baselines, while the elitist variant consistently achieves the highest classification accuracy.

items.title: Researchers present TUDUM, a Turkish-thinking reasoning pipeline for Qwen3.5-27B using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on 15,991 Turkish examples with mixed benchmark results [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TUDUM: A Turkish-Thinking Reasoning Pipeline for Qwen3.5-27B
items.summary:
Researchers have developed TUDUM, a pipeline designed to adapt the Qwen3.5-27B language model for Turkish reasoning tasks. Unlike models that translate Turkish prompts into English for internal processing, TUDUM aims to maintain explicit reasoning in Turkish by training the model to generate Turkish-language reasoning traces. The approach involves supervised fine-tuning on nearly 16,000 Turkish reasoning examples followed by reinforcement learning in a Turkish mathematics environment, resulting in mixed performance outcomes.

The supervised fine-tuning phase made the model's reasoning more concise and consistently Turkish but led to a decrease in benchmark accuracy. Subsequent reinforcement learning partially restored mathematical performance on some tests but did not improve all benchmarks or surpass the original model's overall average. The researchers present TUDUM as a transparent pipeline and evaluation framework for Turkish reasoning rather than a state-of-the-art solution. The step-50 model from this project has been made publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents TUDUM (T\"urk\c{c}e D\"u\c{s}\"unen \"Uretken Model), a project pipeline for adapting a Qwen-family 27B thinking model toward Turkish reasoning. The central problem is not only to answer Turkish prompts in Turkish, but to make the explicit reasoning trace itself Turkish. A thinking model may translate a Turkish prompt into an English-centered internal or visible scratchpad, solve the problem mostly in English, and only localize the final answer. TUDUM instead treats the generated <think>...</think> block as a trainable behavior. The pipeline starts from the project base checkpoint unsloth/Qwen3.5-27B, applies supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on 15,991 Turkish reasoning examples using LoRA adapters, and then applies GRPO-family reinforcement learning on a proxy-filtered Turkish mathematics environment. The results are mixed. SFT made the model shorter and more consistently Turkish in its reasoning behavior, with large reductions in average response length and thinking exhaustion, but reduced benchmark accuracy. RL recovered some mathematical performance, especially AIME24 at the best early checkpoint, yet did not uniformly improve all benchmarks and did not exceed the base model on the reported Macro-6 average. The contribution is therefore best framed as a technically honest Turkish-thinking reasoning pipeline and evaluation, not as a claim of state-of-the-art Turkish reasoning. The released step-50 model is publicly available.

items.title: Researchers release AIriskEval-edu-db2 dataset with 1,639 K-12 educational explanations and annotations for training LLM auditors on pedagogical risk assessment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AIriskEval-edu: New Dataset for Risk Assessment in AI-mediated K-12 Educational Explanations
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced AIriskEval-edu-db2, a dataset designed to train and evaluate large language model (LLM) auditors for assessing pedagogical risks in K-12 educational content. The dataset includes 1,639 explanations from 170 ScienceQA questions across science, language arts, and social sciences, featuring both human-written and LLM-generated explanations that simulate various pedagogical risk profiles. It incorporates a detailed risk rubric covering factual accuracy, depth, relevance, appropriateness for students, and ideological bias, along with 785 explanations annotated for explainability and risk localization validated by expert teachers.

The team conducted validation experiments comparing state-of-the-art proprietary models with a lightweight local Llama 3.1 8B model to assess their performance in detecting pedagogical risks and providing explainability. Results suggest that fine-tuning on AIriskEval-edu-db2 enables locally deployable models to approach or surpass more powerful models while maintaining privacy, offering a promising approach for educational auditing and assessment tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work introduces AIriskEval-edu-db2, a new dataset designed to train and evaluate auditors based on LLMs for an explainable pedagogical risk assessment in instructional content for grades K-12. The dataset comprises 1,639 explanations from 170 curated ScienceQA questions, covering science, language arts, and social sciences. For each question, the dataset includes an explanation written by a human teacher alongside 11 explanations generated by LLM-simulated teacher profiles associated with distinct pedagogical risks. We propose a comprehensive risk rubric aligned with established educational standards that covers five complementary dimensions: factual precision, depth and completeness, focus and relevance, student-level appropriateness, and ideological bias. A key contribution is the addition of 785 explanations with structured explainability annotations, including risk localization and risk description. The annotations are produced through a semi-automatic process with expert teacher validation. Finally, we present validation experiments comparing state-of-the-art proprietary models with a lightweight local Llama 3.1 8B model in both the pedagogical risk detection and the explainability assessment. These experiments evaluate whether supervised fine-tuning on AIriskEval-edu-db2 enables a locally deployable model to approach or outperform stronger frontier models while preserving privacy in educational auditing and assessment tasks.

items.originalTitle: Conditional Co-Ablation: Recovering Self-Repair Backups in Transformer Circuits
items.summary: Researchers have developed Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a new method to identify and recover backup components in transformer models that self-repair when primary components are removed. This approach improves the detection of backup units by measuring how the effect of ablating remaining units changes after removing a primary set, revealing interactions missed by traditional single-unit scoring. Applied to GPT-2-small and other models ranging from 124 million to 7 billion parameters, CoAx significantly enhances backup-head recovery and supports repair-aware pruning and capability knockout.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mechanistic interpretability often relies on component-level interventions to discover how a model produces a behavior. This guides attribution, capability knockout, and model pruning downstream to operate by scoring each unit by the effect of ablation in isolation. Such first-order scoring is natural when component importance is additive, but becomes misleading when a transformer self-repairs: after a primary component is removed, a dormant backup can take over, muting the primary's measured effect while the backup itself appears irrelevant on the intact model. We recast this failure as a recovery task, conditional circuit completion, and introduce Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a label-free, output-grounded score that asks how much each remaining unit's ablation effect grows once a primary set has been removed. This conditional growth exposes the second-order interaction that single-unit scores discard. On the GPT-2-small IOI circuit, CoAx raises backup-head recovery from 0.33 to 0.91 ROC-AUC, outperforming all baselines, including self-repair-aware gradient scores (best 0.82); counterfactual patching verifies that the recovered heads causally carry the repair. The same label-free procedure transfers to induction across eight models. Beyond discovery, the recovered backups correct self-repair-masked attribution, identify the components required for capability knockout, and yield repair-aware structured pruning scaling from 124M to 7B. Component importance is therefore not merely an isolated-unit property: in robust circuits, the components that matter can become visible only under the interventions that make them necessary.

items.title: Researchers analyze three LLMs' responses to science skepticism across climate, vaccines, and evolution, finding varied robustness patterns that do not indicate sycophantic retreat but differ by model and domain [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Robust for the Wrong Reasons: The Representational Geometry of LLM Robustness to Science Skepticism
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated three open instruction-tuned large language models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B) on their responses to skepticism about established scientific consensus in climate change, vaccines, and evolution. Contrary to concerns that these models might sycophantically retreat from consensus when faced with doubt, the study found distinct response patterns: Llama increased consensus assertion, Qwen softened its tone while maintaining its stance, and Mistral often did not respond. These behaviors were linked to differences in how the models represent skepticism signals internally.

The study combined behavioral analysis with techniques like linear probing and activation patching to understand the models' internal representations. It revealed that robustness to skepticism varies by model and domain, with some models showing weakened rebuttals in critical areas like vaccines under skeptical pressure. The authors propose a taxonomy distinguishing active from accidental robustness and caution that behavioral responses alone cannot determine whether a model truly understands skepticism or simply fails to detect it.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01951v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted on contested scientific questions, raising the concern that they will sycophantically retreat from established consensus when a user signals doubt -- drifting toward a false balance that treats settled science as one view among several. We test this across three open instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B), three consensus-science domains (climate, vaccines, evolution), and single- and multi-turn settings, combining behavioral measurement with linear probing and activation patching. We do not observe sycophantic retreat. Instead, models show three distinct policies under the same skeptical pressure: reactive assertion, where consensus assertion increases rather than decreases (Llama); surface hedging, where tone softens while the position holds (Qwen); and non-response (Mistral). Pairwise judgments confirm the reactive shift is stance, not style (63.6%, p=.007), and a decomposition identifies increased consensus assertion, not false balance, as its driver (beta=+0.042 per dose, p<1e-77). Linear probes localize the divergence to middle layers -- perfect separation in Llama and Qwen versus 72% in Mistral, with non-overlapping confidence intervals -- indicating the non-responsive model does not linearly represent the skepticism signal at all. Crucially, this robustness does not transfer: it attenuates across domains and, in the safety-critical vaccine domain, can reverse, with myth-rebuttal weakening under skeptical pressure. We synthesize these into a four-way taxonomy separating active from accidental robustness, and argue that behavioral evaluation alone cannot distinguish a model that resists skepticism because it understands the signal from one that only appears to resist because it fails to perceive it.

items.title: Researchers benchmark 16 vision-language models on medical image quality assessment across seven corruption types and five severity levels, finding pixelation and metadata bias reduce reliability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Assessing VLM Reliability for Medical Image Quality Evaluation Under Corruption and Bias
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated 16 vision-language models (VLMs) for medical image quality assessment (MIQA) using the MediMeta-C dataset, testing across seven types of image corruption and five severity levels. They found that pixelation significantly reduced model performance, while brightness changes had minimal impact. The study also revealed that textual metadata, such as institutional prestige and equipment age, influenced model scores, indicating potential biases.

The analysis showed that pixelation, often used to protect patient privacy, compromises the reliability of VLMs in assessing image quality, highlighting a trade-off between privacy and diagnostic accuracy. Additionally, the sensitivity of models to contextual metadata suggests limited objectivity and raises concerns about privacy and bias in automated medical image evaluation. These findings underscore the need for balancing privacy protection with objective quality assessment before deploying VLMs in clinical settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01973v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly applied in medical tasks such as pathology description, report generation, and visual question answering. Medical Image Quality Assessment (MIQA) supports diagnostic accuracy and patient safety by determining whether images meet the standards required for clinical decision-making. Automating MIQA with VLMs may reduce workload, but their behavior under real-world conditions, where images may be degraded or textual context may affect judgments, should be further explored before deployment. We benchmark VLMs on medical image quality using the MediMeta-C dataset zero-shot across seven corruption types and five severity levels. We evaluate sensitivity to degradation patterns, the effect of corruptions on embedding geometry, and whether textual attributes (demographics, expertise, infrastructure, institution) alter scores. Across 16 VLMs and seven modalities, pixelation produced the largest score reductions (mean -20.58%, up to -34.4% for OCT), whereas brightness had limited effect (-0.81%). Embedding displacement was associated with score changes. Same-family models showed correlations of 0.67-0.83; some produced increases up to +31% for corrupted mammography. Textual attributes affected scores: institutional prestige raised them +17.15%, and equipment age lowered them -14.7%. The largest changes were +95.62% (InternVL-8B) and -37.7% (MedGemma). Current VLMs show limitations for medical image quality assessment. Pixelation, a privacy-preserving transformation, reduces performance, indicating a trade-off between patient privacy and reliability. Sensitivity to contextual metadata indicates limited objectivity and marks metadata as a privacy and bias source. Privacy protection and objective quality assessment are related requirements for use.

items.title: Study compares nine lightweight CNNs on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet, finding newer models offer selective gains in accuracy and efficiency under resource constraints [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Do Newer Lightweight CNNs Perform Better Under Resource Constraints? A Controlled Multigenerational Study of Architecture, Initialization, Training Budget, and Efficiency
items.summary:
A recent study evaluates nine lightweight convolutional neural networks (CNNs) across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet datasets to assess their predictive accuracy and deployment efficiency under resource constraints. The research compares models on metrics including top-1 accuracy, parameter count, computational cost, latency, and memory usage, revealing that newer CNN architectures offer selective improvements rather than consistent gains across all measures. EfficientNetV2-S achieved the highest accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, while RepViT-M1.0 led on Tiny ImageNet, but EfficientNet-B0 demonstrated a strong balance of accuracy and efficiency, appearing on all evaluated Pareto frontiers as a competitive intermediate option.

The study also highlights that MobileNetV3-Small is the fastest and most efficient in terms of computational cost, outperforming MobileNetV4-Conv-S in accuracy despite lower resource use. SqueezeNet1.1, while having the fewest parameters and lowest memory allocation, showed substantially weaker accuracy. The findings emphasize that computational metrics like GMACs do not reliably predict inference latency across different hardware, underscoring the complexity of evaluating model performance in practical deployment scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.01984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Newer lightweight convolutional neural networks are often presented as improving predictive performance and deployment efficiency, but such claims require controlled evaluation. This study compares nine lightweight CNN model packages across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet under a shared downstream protocol. We report top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency on an NVIDIA L4 and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU, peak PyTorch CUDA allocated tensor memory, and point estimate Pareto frontiers. EfficientNetV2-S achieves the highest observed top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 at 97.57% and 86.98%, while RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet at 79.87%. EfficientNet-B0 remains within 0.22, 0.85, and 1.79 percentage points of the best result on the three datasets while using approximately 79% fewer parameters and 86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S. It also appears on every evaluated accuracy and resource Pareto frontier, making it the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget option. MobileNetV3-Small has the lowest GMAC count, is the fastest model under both CPU thread settings, and records higher observed accuracy than MobileNetV4-Conv-S on all three datasets. Under random initialization, it leads MobileNetV4-Conv-S by 2.55, 1.76, and 0.99 points, with paired test-set intervals excluding zero for the fixed trained models. EfficientNet-B0 remains 3.29, 10.10, and 17.54 points below its pretrained counterpart after 100 epochs of scratch training, despite requiring about five times the recorded training time. SqueezeNet1.1 has the fewest parameters and lowest peak CUDA allocation, but substantially weaker accuracy. Latency rankings differ sharply between the L4 and CPU environments, showing that GMACs alone do not predict measured inference performance. Overall, newer designs provide selective rather than universal gains

items.title: Researchers introduce OpenSafeIntent benchmark to evaluate AI model safety across benign, dual-use, and malicious prompt variants, revealing calibration failures and brittleness in intent-sensitive completions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenSafeIntent: Evaluating Intent-Calibrated Safe Completion Across Dual-Use Prompt Sets
items.summary: Researchers have introduced OpenSafeIntent, a new benchmark designed to evaluate AI model safety by testing how models respond to prompts with varying intents—benign, dual-use, and malicious—while keeping the underlying task constant. This approach reveals whether models can appropriately calibrate their assistance based on intent rather than simply appearing safe on average. The study found that many models fail to maintain safety across different intent variants, exhibit brittle behavior when prompts are paraphrased, and do not consistently provide safe responses on risky topics.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safe completion requires models to provide useful assistance without enabling harm, but this behavior is difficult to evaluate with isolated prompts. We introduce OpenSafeIntent, a benchmark of controlled prompt-sets that vary intent while holding the underlying task fixed. Each datapoint contains benign, dual-use, and malicious variants of the same task. This design lets us evaluate whether models calibrate assistance across intent shifts, rather than merely appearing safe on average. Across a broad model suite, we find that prompt-level safety hides important failures: models often fail to remain safe across matched intent variants, dual-use behavior is brittle under paraphrase, high-level answers on risky topics are not reliably safe, and responses that reframe ambiguous requests into safer tasks are substantially less likely to cross the safety boundary. Our results suggest that safe completion should be evaluated as intent-calibrated behavior over controlled task variants, not as a single safety-helpfulness tradeoff over independent prompts.

items.title: Researchers introduce SPLIT benchmark to evaluate empathy and cultural grounding in English and Ukrainian LLM responses, finding performance drops in some models and weak human-AI evaluator agreement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SPLIT: Cross-Lingual Empathy and Cultural Grounding in English and Ukrainian LLM Responses
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced SPLIT, a 500-prompt benchmark designed to evaluate large language models' (LLMs) ability to generate emotionally grounded responses in English and Ukrainian across five categories related to crisis situations. The study assessed three diverse LLMs on empathetic accuracy, linguistic naturalness, and cultural grounding, revealing that some models' performance declined when switching to Ukrainian, while others remained stable. Additionally, the research found weak agreement between human and AI evaluators on empathy and naturalness, with greater divergence on cultural grounding, highlighting that producing text in Ukrainian does not necessarily equate to providing culturally appropriate emotional support.

The SPLIT benchmark aims to fill a gap in evaluating LLMs' cross-lingual empathy and cultural sensitivity, especially in low-to-mid-resource languages during crisis contexts. By comparing model responses in English and Ukrainian, the study underscores the challenges of maintaining empathetic and culturally grounded communication across languages. The findings suggest the need for more culturally tailored benchmarks and emphasize the importance of human-centered evaluation methods to better assess emotional support capabilities in multilingual AI systems.

items.title: Researchers propose Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization to improve AI evaluation and training in spatially correlated domains, reducing data leakage and hidden stratification [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond the Performance Illusion: Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization for Spatially Correlated Domains
items.summary:
Researchers have identified that the common assumption of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data splits in AI performance evaluation often fails in spatially and temporally correlated domains such as aerial surveillance, precision agriculture, and medical imaging. This failure leads to data leakage, where correlated samples appear in both training and validation sets, inflating performance metrics, and hidden stratification, where errors in minority subpopulations are masked by overall metrics. To address these challenges, the researchers propose a unified framework combining Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning (SASP) to create validation splits that minimize leakage while maintaining class balance, and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization (CDRO), a training method that stabilizes optimization under these stricter splits.

Testing across multiple benchmarks shows that this approach improves generalization, provides more reliable confidence calibration, and reveals failure modes that traditional random-split evaluations fail to detect. This work offers a significant advancement in evaluating and training AI systems in spatially correlated settings, enhancing the reliability and robustness of their performance assessments.

items.title: Researchers propose SA-HGNN, a Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network model for EEG-based depression recognition capturing hierarchical brain network structures and reducing noise [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SA-HGNN: Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network for EEG-Based Depression Recognition
items.summary: Researchers have developed a new model called Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network (SA-HGNN) to improve EEG-based depression recognition by accurately capturing the hierarchical structure of brain networks affected by depression. The model features three key components: a Sample-Adaptive Graph Construction module that creates personalized brain network topologies, hyperbolic graph convolution to better represent latent hierarchical relationships, and an Attention Pooling module that reduces noise in EEG signals. Experiments on public EEG datasets demonstrate that SA-HGNN outperforms existing methods in both resting-state and task-related scenarios, showing robustness to noise and effectiveness in identifying abnormal brain connectivity patterns associated with depression.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02063v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been widely used to capture spatial functional connectivity patterns to improve electroencephalography (EEG)-based depression recognition performance. However, the functional connectivity of brain networks in patients with depression exhibits an inherent hierarchical structure, making it difficult to capture accurate connection patterns. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel model named Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network (SA-HGNN), which aims to accurately extract the authentic hierarchical structure of depression-affected brain networks. Specifically, the proposed model comprises three core modules. First, a Sample-Adaptive Graph Construction module dynamically constructs personalized brain network topologies to capture more complex spatial relationships within the brain network. Second, hyperbolic graph convolution is employed to overcome the representation bottlenecks of Euclidean space, leveraging hyperbolic geometry to precisely capture latent hierarchical relationships within the brain network. Finally, an Attention Pooling module adaptively filters out highly redundant noise channels in EEG signals, effectively mitigating the interference of inherent noise on the authentic hierarchical topology. Extensive experiments on public EEG datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method across resting-state and task-related paradigms, validating its robustness to noise and efficacy in capturing abnormal functional connectivity patterns in brain networks of patients with depression.

items.title: Researchers present kNNGuard, a training-free LLM guardrail using hidden activations and multi-layer kNN for faster, configurable safety classification across six domains [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: kNNGuard: Turning LLM Hidden Activations into a Training-Free Configurable Guardrail
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced kNNGuard, a training-free guardrail system for large language models (LLMs) that detects unsafe, off-topic, or adversarial prompts by leveraging hidden activations from an off-the-shelf LLM. Using a small labeled bank of 50 safe and unsafe prompts, kNNGuard applies multi-layer k-nearest neighbors (kNN) classification combining activation-space and embedding-space scores. It achieves competitive or superior performance compared to fine-tuned state-of-the-art guardrails across six domains while operating significantly faster, with up to 10 times speed improvement over fine-tuned classifiers.

kNNGuard requires no gradient updates or fine-tuning, and domain adaptation is simplified to updating the labeled prompt bank, which can be constructed in under 10 seconds. The study also explores the effects of system prompts, layer selection, and integration into production LLM pipelines, highlighting kNNGuard as a configurable, low-latency safety mechanism suitable for diverse applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in domains requiring guardrails to detect unsafe, off-topic, or adversarial prompts. Existing guardrails predominately rely on fine-tuning to build classifiers, which often suffer from low generalization and high inference latency. We present kNNGuard, a training-free guardrail that utilizes the activation space of an off-the-shelf LLM. Given a small bank of 50 safe and unsafe prompts, kNNGuard extracts hidden activations and performs multi-layer kNN fusing activation-space and embedding-space scores for classification. Across six domains spanning topical and security prompts, kNNGuard achieves competitive or superior F1 compared to fine-tuned state-of-the-art guardrails while running 2.7x faster than the best comparable guardrail, and 10x faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier without gradient updates or fine-tuning. Domain adaptation requires only updating the labeled bank, which can be constructed in under 10 seconds and several orders of magnitude faster than established guardrails. We also analyze the impact of system prompts, layer selection, and integration into production LLM pipelines as a configurable, low-latency guardrail.

items.title: Researchers propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART) and ART-RL for continuous-time control and reinforcement learning to improve timestep allocation in diffusion sampling, enhancing sample quality and generalization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ART for Diffusion Sampling: Continuous-Time Control and Actor-Critic Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control method designed to optimize timestep allocation in score-based diffusion sampling. ART treats the speed of the sampling clock as a control variable, enabling adaptive timesteps that improve sample quality compared to traditional uniform or fixed schedules. To implement this, they developed ART-RL, a reinforcement learning approach that learns optimal timestep schedules through Gaussian policies, effectively turning schedule learning into a continuous-time control problem.

The team demonstrated that ART-RL's randomized formulation is equivalent to ART at the optimization level, with its optimal policy recovering the best time-warping rate. Experiments across various settings, including image generation, showed that ART-RL can be integrated into existing diffusion samplers by adjusting only the timestep grid, consistently enhancing sample quality without altering other components. Additionally, the learned schedules generalize well across different sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, and pipelines, indicating broad applicability and robustness.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study timestep allocation for score-based diffusion sampling, where a learned reverse-time dynamics is discretized on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted schedules are standard choices, but they rely on fixed prescriptions and can therefore be suboptimal. To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change by treating the speed of the sampling clock as the control, so that a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in the original diffusion time. Based on a leading-order Euler error surrogate, ART provides a principled objective for allocating timesteps along the sampling trajectory. To solve this deterministic control problem, we introduce ART-RL, an auxiliary randomized formulation with Gaussian policies that turns schedule learning into a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem. We prove that the randomized ART-RL formulation is equivalent to ART at the optimizer level, in the sense that its optimal Gaussian policy recovers the optimal ART time-warping rate through its mean. We further establish policy evaluation and policy improvement characterizations and derive trajectory-based moment identities that yield implementable actor--critic updates for learning the schedule. Across experiments ranging from controlled low-dimensional settings to image generation, ART-RL can be plugged into existing diffusion samplers by changing only the timestep grid, consistently improving sample quality over strong baseline schedules at matched budgets while leaving the rest of the sampling pipeline unchanged. The learned schedules also exhibit broad generalization, transferring without retraining across sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.

items.title: Researchers develop deep neural network and ensemble machine learning models to predict early-stage Alzheimer's disease and identify key biomarkers using ADNI data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Predicting Early Stages Of Alzheimer's Disease And Identifying Key Biomarkers Using Deep Artificial Neural Network And Ensemble Of Machine Learning Methodologies
items.summary:
Researchers have developed machine learning models, including a deep neural network and an ensemble of classifiers, to predict early-stage Alzheimer's disease and identify key biomarkers using data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). The study addresses challenges such as missing data and class imbalance by applying iterative imputation and Borderline SVM-SMOTE, respectively, and uses feature selection methods to focus on important predictors. The models' performance was evaluated using metrics like precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC to determine the most effective approach for early diagnosis.

The research integrates clinical details, neuropsychological test scores, and neuroimaging measures to improve detection accuracy. By comparing multiple machine learning techniques, including Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, LightGBM, and an artificial neural network, the study aims to enhance early identification of Alzheimer's disease, which is crucial since early symptoms often resemble normal aging and current treatments are limited. Identifying significant biomarkers could support better management and timely intervention for patients.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02142v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Alzheimers disease (AD) is a brain disorder that develops slowly and mainly affects memory, thinking, language, and daily activities. It is one of the most common causes of dementia and creates many difficulties for patients as well as their families. In the early stage, the symptoms are often mild and may look like normal ageing. For this reason, many people are diagnosed late, when the disease has already progressed. At present, there is no complete cure for AD. Still, early detection can help doctors manage the condition better and take suitable steps at the right time. In this study, a machine learning model is proposed to detect the early stages of Alzheimers disease using clinical details, neuropsychological test scores, and neuroimaging-related measures. The data used in this work is collected from the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). As the dataset has missing values, iterative imputation is applied to fill them. The dataset also has class imbalance, which is handled using Borderline SVM-SMOTE. After that, feature selection is carried out using wrapper-based and embedded methods so that only important features are used for training. The selected features are divided into training and testing sets, and feature scaling is applied. A stacking ensemble model is developed using Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, and LightGBM as base classifiers. Along with this, an artificial neural network is also trained on the same dataset. The performance of these models is compared using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC. This study aims to find the best classifier and also identify important biomarkers that may help in the early diagnosis of Alzheimers disease.

items.title: Researchers propose Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder to capture sequential inference in neural network weight spaces, improving INR classification accuracy by 10% on CIFAR-100-INR [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Dynamic Neural Graph Encoding of Inference Processes in Deep Weight Space
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder), a novel method that represents neural network parameters as dynamic graphs to capture the sequential, layer-by-layer inference process in neural networks. This approach addresses challenges in analyzing high-dimensional weight spaces by preserving the temporal dynamics of neural processing. Using DNG-Encoder, they developed INR2JLS, a framework for downstream tasks such as classifying Implicit Neural Representations (INRs), achieving a roughly 10% improvement in classification accuracy on the CIFAR-100-INR dataset compared to previous methods.

The DNG-Encoder's ability to model the sequential nature of neural inference distinguishes it from existing techniques that often overlook this aspect. By encoding the temporal progression of neural network layers, the method enhances the analysis and processing of weight spaces, which are typically complex and high-dimensional. This advancement demonstrates significant performance gains across multiple tasks involving implicit neural representations.

items.title: Researchers analyze challenges of using LLMs as judges in multilingual and low-resource language settings, finding inconsistent evaluations and overreliance on single models, and offer recommendations for NLP community [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Challenges and Recommendations for LLMs-as-a-Judge in Multilingual Settings and Low-Resource Languages
items.summary:
Researchers have examined the challenges of using large language models (LLMs) as evaluators, or "judges," in multilingual and low-resource language contexts. Their analysis of 650 ACL Anthology papers revealed that only a small fraction focus on these settings, and among those, evaluations often show inconsistent results, an overreliance on single LLMs, and insufficient human validation. The study highlights the limitations of LLMs in less-resourced languages and the risks of overtrusting their judgments in diverse linguistic environments.

The researchers provide detailed insights into current practices and emphasize the need for more robust evaluation methods when applying LLMs as judges beyond English. They conclude with recommendations aimed at guiding the natural language processing community to improve the reliability and fairness of LLM-based evaluations in multilingual and low-resource scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has become the dominant evaluation paradigm for many natural language generation tasks, due to shortcomings of conventional metrics and high correlations with human judgment, albeit mostly in English. There are now attempts to extend LLM-as-a-Judge to multilingual settings including low-resource languages. However, LLMs have limited proficiency in low-resource languages, and there is often no adequate human validation in these settings. To highlight the scope of the problem and current practices, we explore the use of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators in ACL Anthology papers focusing on multilingual settings and low-resource languages across a diverse set of tasks. Out of 650 papers mentioning LLM-as-a-judge, only 33 of them focus on low-resource or multilingual settings. Our in-depth analysis of these papers indicates inconsistent evaluation outcomes, a tendency to overtrust LLM judgments in multilingual settings, and the widespread reliance on a single judge model per study. To help the NLP community further, we conclude with recommendations about how to use LLM-as-a-Judge in multilingual and low-resource settings.

items.title: Researchers find that in offline reinforcement learning, the structure of pessimism impacts generalization more than its amount, with symmetric value functions improving outcomes in contextual MDPs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Generalization in offline RL: The structure is more important than the amount of pessimism
items.summary:
Researchers have found that in offline reinforcement learning (RL), the structure of pessimism in value functions plays a more critical role in generalization than the degree of pessimism itself. Their study shows that a symmetric, overly pessimistic value function can generalize better in contextual Markov decision processes (CMDPs) than a mildly pessimistic but non-symmetric one. This challenges the notion that excessive conservatism inherently limits generalization.

The team explains that the structure of pessimism is influenced by the dataset coverage and that enforcing symmetry in value functions may require techniques like data augmentation (DA). They propose applying DA through a consistency loss during policy extraction rather than traditional offline training on augmented datasets. Their theoretical insights were empirically validated using IQL and CQL algorithms in a rotationally symmetric reacher environment, demonstrating improved generalization outcomes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While pessimism counteracts overestimation bias in offline reinforcement learning (RL), being overly conservative has been associated with hindering certain forms of generalization. However, in this paper we demonstrate that being overly pessimistic does not inherently prevent optimal generalization in contextual MDPs (CMDPs). Instead, we argue successful generalization depends not on the amount of pessimism, but whether the pessimistic structure respects the underlying symmetries of the optimal solution. We prove that a mildly pessimistic, non-symmetric value function can generalize worse than an overly pessimistic, symmetric one. In offline RL, the structure of the pessimism is determined by the structure of the dataset coverage. As such, enforcing a symmetric value function can be non-trivial, and might require techniques such as data augmentation (DA). Inspired by our theoretical results, we argue that DA can best be applied through a consistency loss during policy extraction, rather than the common practice of (regular) offline training on an augmented dataset. This is empirically validated using IQL and CQL on a rotationally symmetric reacher environment.

items.title: Researchers propose Self-Gating Attention to reduce time and memory complexity in transformer-based time series forecasting, improving inference efficiency on nine real-world datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-Gating Attention for Efficient Time Series Forecasting
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Self-Gating Attention (SGA), a new attention mechanism designed to improve the efficiency of transformer-based time series forecasting. SGA reduces the time and memory complexity from quadratic to linear by using a shared learnable matrix combined with an input-dependent residual component, avoiding the costly query and key projections typical in standard self-attention. This approach addresses redundancy in attention patterns observed in many real-world time series data.

The team integrated SGA into various forecasting models and tested it on nine diverse real-world datasets, including electricity, finance, weather, and medical monitoring. Results demonstrated that SGA enhances inference speed and memory usage while maintaining competitive forecasting accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art attention methods. These findings suggest SGA offers a practical solution for resource-constrained or high-throughput forecasting applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transformer architectures have shown strong potential in time series forecasting, where multi-head self-attention is widely used to capture temporal dependencies across historical timestamps. However, standard self-attention has quadratic time and memory complexity with respect to the look-back length. This cost may limit its use in resource-constrained or high-throughput forecasting systems, where fast and memory-efficient inference is important. Through qualitative and quantitative analyses, we observe that self-attention maps in time series forecasting often contain redundant patterns across different timestamps. This phenomenon can be related to the repeated temporal patterns and relatively stable temporal correlations in many real-world time series. Motivated by this observation, we propose Self-Gating Attention (SGA), a plug-and-play attention mechanism that represents the attention score with a shared learnable matrix and an input-dependent residual component. The shared matrix captures common attention patterns, while the residual component captures input-dependent variations. In this way, SGA avoids the query and key projections used in standard attention score computation, leading to linear time and score-matrix memory complexity with respect to the look-back length. We integrate SGA into several forecasting backbones and compare it with standard self-attention and lightweight attention variants on nine publicly available real-world datasets covering electricity, finance, weather, medical monitoring, human activity, and climate records. The results show that SGA improves inference efficiency on public benchmarks while maintaining competitive forecasting performance against state-of-the-art attention mechanisms. These benchmark results provide deployment-oriented evidence.

items.title: Researchers propose SkillFuzz, an execution-free fuzzing approach using contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search to detect over 1,000 implicit intents in open skill marketplaces for LLM-based agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SkillFuzz: Fuzzing Skill Composition for Implicit Intents Discovery in Open Skill Marketplaces
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced SkillFuzz, a novel execution-free fuzzing method designed to detect implicit intents arising from the interaction of skills in open marketplaces for Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents. These agents use reusable skills guided by natural-language instructions to automate software engineering tasks, but when skills are combined, they may unintentionally redirect the agent toward undesired objectives. SkillFuzz addresses this challenge by treating implicit-intent discovery as a fuzzing problem over skill compositions, using structured skill contracts and contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search to efficiently identify potentially conflicting skill interactions without requiring execution environments.

In testing across representative skill-marketplace workloads, SkillFuzz discovered over 1,000 distinct implicit intents within a fixed query budget and confirmed more than 80% of the highest-risk flagged compositions during execution-time validation. The approach outperformed alternative search strategies by identifying significantly more high-severity implicit intents while exploring only a fraction of the possible pairwise skill interactions, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving the safety and reliability of skill marketplaces for LLM-based agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02345v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents increasingly automate software engineering tasks through reusable skills, natural-language instruction documents that guide planning and execution. Open skill marketplaces enable users to assemble agents by co-activating community-contributed skills, but marketplace operators typically audit skills in isolation. As a result, individually benign skills may interact to redirect an agent toward unintended objectives, which we term implicit intents. Detecting such intents is challenging because the effect emerges only through skill composition, execution environments are often unavailable at admission time, and the space of possible co-activations grows exponentially with marketplace size. In this paper, we formulate implicit-intent discovery as a fuzzing problem over skill compositions, where skill compositions are the unit under test, planning artifacts expose agent intent before execution, and deviations from a skill-free baseline serve as a differential oracle. Based on this formulation, we propose skillfuzz, the first execution-free testing approach that extracts structured skill contracts and uses contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search to prioritize potentially conflicting compositions. Across representative skill-marketplace workloads, skillfuzz discovers over 1,000 distinct implicit intents under a fixed query budget, confirms more than 80% of the highest-risk flagged compositions during execution-time validation, and identifies substantially more high-severity implicit intents than alternative search strategies while exploring only a fraction of the pairwise interaction space they require.

items.title: Researchers propose bounded old-state modulation for Self-Modulating Quantum Fast-Weight Programmers to stabilize long-sequence quantum sequence modeling and improve robustness [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Stable Self-Modulating Quantum Fast-Weight Programmers with Bounded Memory Gates
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a bounded old-state modulation technique for Self-Modulating Quantum Fast-Weight Programmers (QFWPs) to enhance stability and robustness in long-sequence quantum sequence modeling. QFWPs store temporal information in variational-circuit parameters, and the self-modulating variant uses input-dependent gates for updating fast weights, but its unbounded old-state multiplier can cause divergence over long sequences. The proposed method applies a bounded, sign-preserving tanh gate to the recurrent memory branch, preventing divergence while maintaining update mechanisms.

The team evaluated this approach on quantum-dynamics forecasting tasks and telecommunication activity prediction, finding that old-state modulation consistently improves performance over standard QFWPs. Bounding the old-state gate eliminated long-sequence divergence and enhanced overall robustness. These results highlight accumulated-memory modulation as the key factor in self-modulating QFWPs and demonstrate that bounded gating is an effective stabilization strategy for quantum sequence models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02363v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum Fast-Weight Programmers (QFWPs) store temporal information in dynamically programmed variational-circuit parameters rather than in nonlinear recurrent hidden states, offering a practical route to quantum sequence modeling. Self-Modulating QFWP improves this framework by using input-dependent gates for both new fast-weight updates and the accumulated fast-weight state, but its unbounded old-state multiplier can diverge in long-sequence regimes. We propose a bounded old-state modulation rule that applies a sign-preserving tanh gate only to the recurrent memory branch while leaving the additive update and new-update modulation unchanged. We evaluate standard QFWP, full Self-Modulating QFWP, Only-New, and Only-Old variants on two CUDA-Q quantum-dynamics forecasting tasks and on Milan SMS telecommunication activity prediction. The quantum-dynamics results show that old-state modulation is the most consistent source of improvement over Standard QFWP, and that bounding the old-state gate removes long-sequence divergence while improving aggregate robustness. On Milan SMS forecasting, the original unbounded Self-Modulating QFWP converges across the tested grid and shows its clearest gains at longer input windows, with behavior close to the Only-Old ablation. These findings identify accumulated-memory modulation as the key mechanism of Self-Modulating QFWP and bounded old-state gating as a targeted stabilization strategy.

items.title: Researchers find LLM personas have dual components: frame-robust aggregated traits and frame-dependent geometric features, based on GPT-4o psychometric analysis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Dual Nature of LLM Persona: Aggregated Tendencies and Frame-Dependent Geometry
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed large language model (LLM) personas using psychometric questionnaires and found that persona expression consists of two distinct components: frame-robust aggregated traits, such as Big Five personality scores, and frame-dependent geometric features captured by correlation structures. By manipulating question orderings in GPT-4o simulations of American and Chinese-American personas, they observed that aggregated traits remain relatively stable despite randomization, while geometric features collapse under frame misalignment but recover significantly when frames align.

This study reveals that persona geometry is not an intrinsic property but depends on the framing of questions, encoding information beyond what aggregate scores capture. The findings propose a dual-nature framework for evaluating LLM personas, emphasizing the need for frame-aware assessments and challenging traditional views of static personality traits.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02368v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Evaluations of LLM personas via psychometric questionnaires typically rely on aggregate scores, discarding within-instance correlation structure. We test whether this geometric structure is intrinsic or frame-dependent. Constructing within-instance correlation matrices from IPIP-50 responses, we analyze geometry on SPD manifolds under manipulated question orderings in GPT-4o simulating American and Chinese-American personas. We find that persona expression comprises two dissociable components: aggregated features (Big Five scores) degrade under randomization (21% drop) but are frame-robust; geometric features (SPD manifold) collapse under frame misalignment (42% drop) but recover substantially (to 84%) under shared frames, surpassing aggregated features (76%). This collapse-recovery pattern reveals that persona geometry is not intrinsic but a frame-dependent coordination pattern encoding information invisible to aggregation. Our findings establish a dual-nature framework for LLM personas, frame-dependent geometry versus frame-robust aggregates, necessitating frame-aware evaluation and challenging static trait conceptions.

items.title: Researchers propose literary analysis frameworks to develop culturally literate AI addressing global textuality, monolingualism, and untranslatability in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: World Wide Models: Literary Tools for Cultural AI
items.summary:
Researchers propose a framework that integrates literary analysis methods to enhance the cultural literacy of large language models (LLMs). The study highlights how LLMs represent a new, large-scale, automated, and predominantly monolingual form of cultural interaction, and argues that tools from literary disciplines—such as comparative literature, narratology, critical theory, and translation studies—are essential for developing AI that can interpret texts with greater nuance and cultural awareness.

The framework connects contemporary debates in critical theory with the challenges of structural monolingualism in AI, and suggests applying world literature approaches to address issues of global textuality, including macrostructure, circulation, and untranslatability. This interdisciplinary approach aims to foster pluralistic interpretations and more sophisticated textual models in AI, bridging the gap between literary scholarship and AI development.

items.title: Researchers propose NeuFS, a neuron-aware active few-shot learning framework for LLMs that uses internal neuron activation patterns to improve sample selection and outperform existing methods on reasoning and text classification tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Neuron-Aware Active Few-Shot Learning for LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced NeuFS, a neuron-aware active few-shot learning framework designed to enhance large language models (LLMs) by leveraging internal neuron activation patterns for selecting valuable unlabeled samples. Unlike traditional methods that rely on output-level signals such as predictive entropy or semantic similarity, NeuFS focuses on the models' internal dynamics to identify diverse and informative samples, particularly those prone to hallucination. This approach aims to reduce human annotation costs while improving performance in specialized domains.

NeuFS employs a dual-criteria selection strategy that ensures sample diversity through neuron pattern coverage and prioritizes challenging examples by measuring neuron consensus. Experiments across three datasets demonstrate that NeuFS outperforms existing active few-shot learning baselines in reasoning and text classification tasks. Further analysis confirms that internal neuron activations provide a more effective and principled signal for sample selection compared to external embeddings, highlighting the framework's potential to advance few-shot learning techniques for LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02423v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Active Few-Shot Learning (AFSL) adapts LLMs to specialized domains by identifying the most valuable unlabeled samples for annotation and use as few-shot demonstrations, effectively reducing human annotation costs while promoting high performance. However, existing methods typically rely on output-level signals for sample identification, such as predictive entropy or semantic similarities with test-time data based on external embeddings, which often overlook models' internal dynamics, which could pinpoint specific knowledge gaps. To bridge this gap, we propose NeuFS, a Neuron-Aware Active Few-Shot Learning framework that shifts the selection paradigm from output-level proxies to models' internal dynamics. NeuFS utilizes neuron activation patterns to represent sample directly, and includes a dual-criteria selection strategy that: (1) ensures few-shot sample diversity with neuron patterns for broader example coverage, while (2) prioritizing on identifying informative and challenging few-shot samples LLMs tend to hallucinate by quantifying neuron consensus. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate that NeuFS excels in both reasoning and text classification tasks, outperforming existing AFSL baselines. Ablation studies further highlight that internal neuron activations provide a more principled and effective selection signal than external embeddings, validating the superiority of the proposed NeuFS.

items.title: Researchers propose QFedAgent, a quantum-classical personalized federated learning framework for multi-agent activity recognition achieving 97.7% accuracy with 10x parameter reduction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: QFedAgent: Quantum-Enhanced Personalized Federated Learning for Multi-Agent Activity Recognition
items.summary:
Researchers have developed QFedAgent, a hybrid quantum-classical personalized federated learning framework designed for multi-agent activity recognition. This approach addresses challenges in federated learning caused by heterogeneous, non-independent, and non-identically distributed multimodal sensor data in multi-agent systems. By integrating a variational quantum circuit fusion module, QFedAgent models interactions between accelerometer and gyroscope data using quantum state encoding and entanglement, significantly reducing the number of parameters required compared to classical methods.

The quantum fusion module uses only 72 quantum rotation parameters, compared to 33,000 parameters in traditional multi-layer perceptron-based fusion, achieving about a tenfold reduction in total parameters. Experiments on the OPPORTUNITY dataset with subject-based non-IID partitions demonstrated that QFedAgent achieves a mean test accuracy of 97.7%, showing that quantum-enhanced fusion can maintain competitive performance while improving parameter efficiency in federated learning for robotic sensing applications.

items.title: Researchers propose Neuron On-Policy Self-Distillation framework using neuron activations for annotation-free LLM training, improving in-domain performance and cross-domain generalization in specialized domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Neuron-Aware Data Selection for Annotation-Free LLM Self-Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Neuron On-Policy Self-Distillation (Neuron-OPSD), a novel framework for training large language models (LLMs) without relying on human-labeled data or real-world interaction feedback. This approach uses internal neuron activations to guide the selection of training data and the construction of teacher contexts, enabling on-policy distillation from the teacher distribution without any ground-truth labels. Neuron-OPSD aims to improve performance in specialized domains while maintaining generalization across different domains and reducing calibration errors seen in previous annotation-free methods.

The framework addresses challenges in post-training LLM adaptation where expert annotations are costly or unavailable, particularly in specialized fields. Unlike prior methods that suffer from out-of-domain performance degradation or inflated calibration errors, Neuron-OPSD leverages a data-centric strategy that enhances in-domain task accuracy and preserves cross-domain robustness. This method is especially relevant for scenarios where online interaction or external supervision is impractical, distinguishing itself from offline reinforcement learning approaches that depend on logged, reward-labeled data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) without real-world interaction feedback or human-labeled supervision remains challenging, particularly in specialized domains where expert annotations are costly to obtain. Recent annotation-free self-evolution methods address this by using the model's own outputs as supervision signals, constructing a teacher via additional context and aggregating predictions across multiple rollouts through majority voting to produce pseudo-labels. items.title: Researchers present OrbitQuant, a data-agnostic quantizer for image and video diffusion transformers that enables post-training quantization without per-modality tuning and achieves state-of-the-art results at low-bit settings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OrbitQuant: Data-Agnostic Quantization for Image and Video Diffusion Transformers
items.summary:
Researchers have developed OrbitQuant, a novel data-agnostic quantizer designed for image and video diffusion transformers (DiTs) that enables efficient post-training quantization without the need for per-modality tuning. OrbitQuant uses a normalized, rotated basis with a randomized permuted block-Hadamard rotation to stabilize activation distributions across different timesteps, prompts, and layers, allowing a single quantization codebook to be applied universally. This approach reduces inference costs while maintaining high-quality generation.

The method extends to weight quantization by integrating the rotation into the weights, which cancels out during computation, leaving only a forward rotation on activations at runtime. OrbitQuant has demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks, including FLUX.1, Z-Image-Turbo, Wan 2.1, and CogVideoX, achieving effective low-bit quantization and advancing the practical use of PTQ for image diffusion transformers to configurations like W2A4 with usable generation quality.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02461v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diffusion transformers (DiTs) achieve state-of-the-art image and video generation, but their multi-step sampling and growing parameter count make inference expensive. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is the natural remedy, yet DiT activations shift across timesteps, prompts, and guidance branches, forcing prior methods to re-fit calibration data for every new checkpoint or modality. We present OrbitQuant, a data-agnostic weight-activation quantizer that bypasses range estimation by quantizing in a normalized, rotated basis. In this basis, a randomized permuted block-Hadamard (RPBH) rotation concentrates each coordinate around one fixed, known marginal regardless of the input, so a single Lloyd-Max codebook serves all timesteps, prompts, and layers of a given input dimension. We extend the same quantizer to weight rows offline, absorbing the rotation into the weights so that it cancels inside each linear layer and only a forward rotation on the activations remains at runtime. The same recipe transfers from image to video with no per-modality tuning. Across FLUX.1, Z-Image-Turbo, Wan 2.1, and CogVideoX, it sets the state of the art for PTQ at several low-bit settings. It also pushes PTQ of image diffusion transformers to W2A4 with usable generation quality.

items.title: Researchers introduce TestEvo-Bench, a live benchmark for test and code co-evolution with 1,255 tasks from 152 Java projects, evaluating AI agents on test generation and update success rates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TestEvo-Bench: An Executable and Live Benchmark for Test and Code Co-Evolution
items.summary:
Researchers have developed TestEvo-Bench, a live benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents on the co-evolution of software tests and code. The benchmark includes 1,255 tasks from 152 open-source Java projects, divided into two tracks: test generation, where agents create new tests to reflect updated software behavior, and test update, where agents modify existing tests to align with code changes. Each task is linked to real commit histories and supports execution-based metrics such as pass rate and coverage, enabling a more accurate assessment of an agent's understanding of code-test relationships.

TestEvo-Bench continuously updates with new tasks mined from software repositories, allowing evaluations to focus on data beyond a model's training period to minimize data leakage. Experiments with four state-of-the-art AI agents combining advanced harnesses and foundation models showed success rates up to 77.5% for test generation and 74.6% for test updates. However, performance declines on the most recent tasks and under constraints limiting computational resources per task, highlighting ongoing challenges in automated test maintenance.
