items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02469v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Software tests and code evolve together: a code change should be followed by new or updated tests that record the new software behavior. Yet existing test generation and update benchmarks often isolate the test from the code change, and rely on static metadata that does not verify whether a test is executable or semantically tied to the code change. This makes it difficult to evaluate whether a test automation agent understands how a code change should propagate into the test suite. We introduce TestEvo-Bench, a benchmark of test and code co-evolution tasks mined from software repositories, with two tracks: in test generation, the agent shall write new tests to capture the new software behavior; in test update, the agent shall adapt failing existing tests to the changed software behavior. Each task is anchored to a real commit history and packaged with environment configuration to support execution-grounded metrics such as pass rate, coverage, and mutation score. TestEvo-Bench is also a live benchmark: each task records the timestamp of the test and code changes, and new tasks are periodically mined by our automated pipeline, so evaluation can be restricted to tasks postdating a model's training cutoff to reduce data leakage risk. The current snapshot contains 746 test generation and 509 test update tasks, curated from 59,950 candidate co-evolution records across 152 open-source Java projects. We experiment with four state-of-the-art agents that combine strong harnesses (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and SWE-Agent) with strong foundation models (Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro). Results show that they achieve up to 77.5% success rate on test generation and 74.6% on test update. However, success rate is materially lower on the most recent benchmark tasks and drops significantly under limited per-task cost.

items.title: Researchers compare SOAP, Muon, and hybrid optimizers to Adam for training machine learning interatomic potentials, finding faster convergence and higher accuracy especially under partial force supervision [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Adam: SOAP and Muon for Faster, Label-Efficient Training of Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
items.summary:
Researchers have evaluated new matrix-structured optimizers—Muon, SOAP, and a hybrid SOAP-Muon—against the commonly used Adam optimizer for training machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs). Their study shows that these alternative optimizers, particularly SOAP and SOAP-Muon, achieve faster convergence and higher accuracy when training NequIP and Allegro MLIP models, especially under conditions of partial force supervision. Muon provides some improvement but is less effective than the other two.

The findings highlight that while much focus has been on model architectures and datasets, the choice of optimizer has been largely overlooked in MLIP training. This research suggests that selecting the right optimizer can significantly enhance training efficiency and model performance, marking an important consideration for future MLIP development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02499v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have become a hallmark of AI for scientific simulation. While efforts on new architectures and datasets have led to increasingly accurate and general models, the choice of optimizer for training has largely remained unexplored, defaulting to Adam and its variants in the community. Here, we implement and systematically compare a class of recently proposed matrix-structured optimizers, including Muon, SOAP, and the hybrid SOAP-Muon, for training NequIP and Allegro MLIP models. We find that these optimizers can substantially outperform Adam in both convergence speed and final accuracy. SOAP and SOAP-Muon emerge as robust and consistently strong methods, while Muon only provides partial gains relative to Adam. The improvements are particularly pronounced under partial force supervision. Our results indicate that optimizer choice is an overlooked yet impactful design axis for MLIPs.

items.title: Researchers introduce DemoPSD, a self-distillation framework that mitigates privileged information leakage and preserves exploration in large language model training, outperforming prior methods on scientific benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DemoPSD: Disagreement-Modulated Policy Self-Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed DemoPSD, a new self-distillation framework designed to improve the training of large language models (LLMs) by addressing the issue of privileged information leakage and preserving exploration during learning. DemoPSD selectively blends teacher and student model outputs using a reverse-KL barycenter target, which balances guidance from the teacher with the student's own reasoning capabilities. This approach mitigates overfitting to in-domain data and prevents the student model from relying on shortcuts unavailable during testing.

The framework adaptively adjusts the influence of the teacher at each token position based on the discrepancy between teacher and student distributions. Experiments on scientific benchmarks across multiple fields demonstrate that DemoPSD outperforms existing methods like GRPO and SDPO, maintaining higher training entropy and showing robust generalization to out-of-distribution tasks. The method offers a promising direction for enhancing LLM reasoning and cross-domain performance while reducing reliance on privileged information.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a practical method for training large language models (LLMs) to reason, where a single model acts as both the teacher and the student with different levels of information access. However, recent studies have found that the teacher's dense token-level supervision, conditioned on privileged information, can lead to overfitting to in-domain patterns, suppress exploration, and hurt cross-domain generalization, while also introducing a more fundamental issue: *privileged information leakage*, where the student encodes answer-dependent shortcuts that are unavailable at test time. We introduce **DemoPSD**, a novel framework that resolves such problems through the idea of *selective adoption of teacher guidance*. Instead of fitting the full teacher distribution, DemoPSD steers the student toward a *reverse-KL barycenter target*, a weighted geometric combination of the teacher and student distributions, that naturally balances learning from the teacher with preserving the student's own reasoning capacity. We measure the difference between their distributions and use such a discrepancy to adaptively control the blending at each token position. We provably show that DemoPSD achieves **(1)** *leakage attenuation*, i.e., effective mitigation of privileged information leakage; and **(2)** *exploration preservation*, i.e., preservation of exploration capacity under dense token-level distillation. Extensive experiments on SciKnowEval across four scientific fields show that DemoPSD outperforms both GRPO and SDPO while maintaining higher training entropy and robustly generalizing to out-of-distribution GPQA benchmarks.

items.originalTitle: Reasoning LLM Improves Speaker Recognition in Long-form TV Dramas
items.summary:
Researchers have developed DramaSR-LRM, a large reasoning language model designed to improve speaker recognition in long-form TV dramas by integrating auditory, linguistic, and visual information. This approach addresses the challenge of accurately attributing spoken lines to characters, which is crucial for understanding complex storylines. The team also introduced DramaSR-532K, a large-scale benchmark dataset with 532,000 annotated dialogue lines from over 900 characters, to support this task.

DramaSR-LRM autonomously combines multimodal contextual evidence to enhance attribution accuracy, particularly excelling in cases with short utterances where traditional acoustic methods struggle. Experimental results show that this model significantly outperforms existing baselines. The researchers plan to make all data and code publicly available to facilitate further research in this area.

items.title: Researchers propose MAGIK framework enabling reinforcement learning agents to transfer knowledge to analogous tasks via imagination-based analogy mapping without target environment interaction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MAGIK: Mapping to Analogous Goals via Imagination-enabled Knowledge Transfer
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MAGIK, a new framework designed to enable reinforcement learning (RL) agents to transfer knowledge to similar tasks without needing to interact with the new environment. MAGIK uses an imagination-based mechanism to map elements of a target task to their counterparts in a previously learned source task, allowing the agent to apply its existing policy directly. This approach addresses the common challenge in RL where agents require extensive retraining even for structurally related tasks.

The team tested MAGIK on custom MiniGrid and MuJoCo tasks, demonstrating effective zero-shot transfer with only a few human-labeled examples. Compared to existing methods, MAGIK offers a novel and efficient way to achieve knowledge transfer through analogy mapping, potentially reducing the time and data needed for RL agents to adapt to new but related tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2506.01623v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Humans excel at analogical reasoning - applying knowledge from one task to a related one with minimal relearning. In contrast, reinforcement learning (RL) agents typically require extensive retraining even when new tasks share structural similarities with previously learned ones. In this work, we propose MAGIK, a novel framework that enables RL agents to transfer knowledge to analogous tasks without interacting with the target environment. Our approach leverages an imagination mechanism to map entities in the target task to their analogues in the source domain, allowing the agent to reuse its original policy. Experiments on custom MiniGrid and MuJoCo tasks show that MAGIK achieves effective zero-shot transfer using only a small number of human-labelled examples. We compare our approach to related baselines and highlight how it offers a novel and effective mechanism for knowledge transfer via imagination-based analogy mapping.

items.title: Researchers find human psychological imagination networks show consistent cross-population structure that large language models fail to replicate across architectures and scales [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Psychological Imagination Networks Show Cross-Population Centrality and Clustering Alignment in Humans That Large Language Models Fail to Replicate
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed mental imagery vividness across diverse human populations and large language models (LLMs) to compare the relational structure of imagined scenarios. Using psychological network analysis on data from two validated questionnaires, they found consistent network patterns and community structures among humans from different regions, while LLMs failed to replicate these patterns across various architectures and scales. This suggests that human imagination networks reflect embodied memory organization that LLMs, trained solely on language, do not capture.

The study involved 2,743 participants from Florida, Poland, and London, and six LLMs including Gemma3 and Llama models. Human networks showed strong correlations in centrality measures and meaningful clustering aligned with sensory modalities and scene contexts. In contrast, LLMs produced weak correlations and often degenerate single-cluster structures, regardless of model size or conversational context.

These findings imply that the representational structure underlying human imagination is shaped by embodied experience and memory, which current language-based models cannot reproduce. This highlights a fundamental difference between human cognitive processes and synthetic language models, with implications for future AI development and understanding of mental imagery.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2510.04391v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mental imagery vividness is a stable individual trait, yet whether imagined scenarios share relational structure across human and synthetic large language model (LLM) populations remains unknown. We applied psychological network analysis to vividness ratings from two validated questionnaires: the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ-2) and the Plymouth Sensory Imagery Questionnaire (PSIQ), across geographically and linguistically distinct human samples (Florida, Poland, and London; total N = 2,743) and six large language models (LLMs; Gemma3-12B/27B, their quantization-aware counterparts, Llama3.3-70B, and Llama4-16x17B). Imagination networks were constructed as regularized partial correlation graphs, with node centrality and community structure compared across populations using Pearson correlations and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI). Human networks showed robust cross-population centrality correlations for expected influence, strength, and closeness (r = 0.31-0.93), and community detection recovered clusters aligned with VVIQ-2 scene contexts (ARI = 0.27-0.40) and PSIQ sensory modalities (ARI = 0.87-1.0). Betweenness centrality was unstable across all populations, consistent with its sensitivity to individual experiential history. LLMs failed to replicate human network structure: LLM-human centrality correlations were weak and largely non-significant after correction, and most LLM configurations produced degenerate single-cluster topologies (median ARI = 0). This failure was consistent across model architectures, parameter scales (12B-272B), and conversational conditions. We posit that these findings may be driven by human imagination networks reflecting memory organization accumulated through embodied experience, a representational structure that linguistic training alone does not reproduce regardless of model scale and conversational memory.

items.title: Researchers introduce BuilderBench, a benchmark with a robot simulator and 50+ tasks to test AI agents' embodied reasoning and exploration skills in building structures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: BuilderBench: The Building Blocks of Intelligent Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced BuilderBench, a new benchmark designed to advance AI agent training focused on open-ended exploration and embodied reasoning. BuilderBench features a robot simulator and a suite of over 50 tasks requiring agents to build diverse structures using physical blocks, testing their understanding of physics, mathematics, and long-term planning. The benchmark challenges AI agents to learn through interaction and experimentation rather than relying solely on mimicry or existing data.

The benchmark provides agents with a target structure and allows multiple episodes for interaction, encouraging the development of skills through trial and error. Experiments with state-of-the-art language model-based agents and reinforcement learning algorithms revealed that these models struggle to solve the more complex tasks, highlighting their limited exploration capabilities. BuilderBench aims to stimulate research into scalable learning mechanisms that enable agents to acquire new skills through experience and interaction.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2510.06288v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Today's AI models learn primarily through mimicry and refining, so it is not surprising that they struggle to solve problems beyond the limits set by existing data. To solve novel problems, agents should acquire skills by exploring and learning through experience. Finding a scalable learning mechanism for developing agents that learn through interaction remains a major open problem. In this work, we introduce BuilderBench, a benchmark to accelerate research into agent training that centers open-ended exploration. BuilderBench requires agents to learn how to build any structure using blocks. BuilderBench is equipped with (1) a simulator of a robot interacting with various physical blocks, and (2) a task-suite with over 50 diverse target structures that are carefully curated to test an understanding of physics, mathematics, and long-horizon planning. Agents are provided with a target structure at the start, and can interact with the environment for multiple episodes to experiment and learn various skills for building the structure. Solving these tasks requires \emph{embodied reasoning} in a way that is not reflected in words but rather in actions, experimenting with different strategies and piecing them together. Our experiments with multiple state-of-the-art frontier language model based agents and tabula rasa reinforcement learning algorithms show that these agents cannot solve any of the non-trivial tasks in the BuilderBench. Our analysis throws light on the lack of exploration abilities in these models.

items.title: Researchers release PreScience dataset and benchmark for scientific forecasting using 502K AI research papers and introduce LACER, an LLM-based evaluation metric [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PreScience: A Dataset and Benchmark for Scientific Forecasting
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced PreScience, a comprehensive dataset and benchmark designed to evaluate AI systems' ability to forecast scientific advancements. The dataset encompasses 502,000 papers, including 98,000 recent AI research articles, along with detailed metadata such as author histories, citations, and topic labels. PreScience supports seven tasks related to scientific forecasting, including contribution generation and citation prediction, and features baselines from simple heuristics to advanced language models. Additionally, the team developed LACER, a new evaluation metric based on large language models that better aligns with human judgments for assessing generated scientific contributions.

The researchers used PreScience to generate a synthetic corpus of papers over a 12-month period, finding that AI-generated research tends to be less diverse and novel compared to human-authored work from the same timeframe. The dataset and accompanying code have been made publicly available to support further research in scientific forecasting and AI evaluation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.20459v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Can AI systems trained on the existing scientific record forecast the advances that will follow? We introduce PreScience, a dataset and benchmark for scientific forecasting built around 98K recent AI research papers, together with companion papers covering author publication histories and citation links, yielding 502K papers in total. The resulting paper records include titles, abstracts, disambiguated author identities, influential references, topic labels, citation trajectories, and metadata snapshotted to respect temporal cutoffs. We instantiate seven exemplar tasks: five paper-anchored tasks -- contribution generation, collaborator prediction, prior work selection, citation count prediction, and future combination prediction -- and two aggregate topic trend forecasting variants. We develop baselines ranging from simple heuristics and embedding methods to frontier language models and agentic systems, and introduce LACER, an LLM-based metric for evaluating similarity of generated contribution descriptions that agrees better with human judgments than existing metrics. Finally, we compose task models to generate a 12-month synthetic corpus and find that the resulting papers are systematically less diverse and less novel than human-authored research from the same period. We release the PreScience dataset (https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/prescience) and code (https://github.com/allenai/prescience).

items.title: Researchers propose conformal policy control method to safely regulate new AI behaviors using probabilistic calibration with finite-sample guarantees across diverse applications [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Conformal Policy Control
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new method called conformal policy control to safely regulate the behavior of AI agents exploring new actions in high-stakes environments. This approach uses a safe reference policy as a probabilistic regulator to calibrate how aggressively a new, untested policy can act, ensuring adherence to a user-defined risk tolerance. Unlike previous methods, it does not require assumptions about the correct model class or hyperparameter tuning and provides finite-sample guarantees even for complex loss functions.

The method applies conformal calibration on data from the safe policy to balance exploration and safety, preventing harmful violations of constraints that could lead to an agent being taken offline. Experiments across diverse applications, including natural language question answering and biomolecular engineering, demonstrate that safe exploration is achievable from the outset and can enhance performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.02196v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An agent must try new behaviors to explore and improve. In high-stakes environments, an agent that violates safety constraints may cause harm and must be taken offline, curtailing any future interaction. Imitating old behavior is safe, but excessive conservatism discourages exploration. How much behavior change is too much? We show how to use any safe reference policy as a probabilistic regulator for any optimized but untested policy. Conformal calibration on data from the safe policy determines how aggressively the new policy can act, while provably enforcing the user's declared risk tolerance. Unlike conservative optimization methods, we do not assume the user has identified the correct model class nor tuned any hyperparameters. Unlike previous conformal methods, our theory provides finite-sample guarantees even for non-monotonic bounded loss functions, and it introduces a new policy control setting. Our experiments on applications ranging from natural language question answering to biomolecular engineering show that safe exploration is not only possible from the first moment of deployment, but can also improve performance.

items.title: Researchers present a conformal interpretability framework for temporal concepts in LLM agents, enabling early failure detection and performance improvement in interactive environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Actions to Understanding: Conformal Interpretability of Temporal Concepts in LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a conformal interpretability framework to analyze the temporal evolution of concepts within Large Language Model (LLM) agents operating in interactive environments. This framework uses step-wise reward modeling combined with conformal prediction to statistically label internal model representations as successful or failing at each step. By training linear probes on these representations, the study identifies latent directions in the model's activation space that correspond to notions of success, failure, or reasoning drift, enabling early failure detection and performance improvement.

The framework was tested on two simulated environments, ScienceWorld and AlfWorld, where temporal concepts were found to be linearly separable and aligned with task success. Preliminary results also indicate that steering the model along identified successful directions can enhance the agent's performance. This approach offers a principled method for interpreting and intervening in LLM-based agents, contributing to the development of more trustworthy autonomous language models in complex interactive settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.19775v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents capable of reasoning, planning, and acting within interactive environments. This paper presents a framework for interpreting the temporal evolution of concepts in LLM agents through a step-wise conformal lens. We introduce the conformal interpretability framework for temporal tasks, which combines step-wise reward modeling with conformal prediction to statistically label model's internal representation at each step as successful or failing. The proposed approach, thus, offers a principled method for early failure detection as well as intervention in LLM-based agents, paving the path towards trustworthy autonomous language models in complex interactive settings.

items.title: Researchers propose LGMT, a logic-grounded metamorphic testing framework using first-order logic to evaluate reasoning reliability of six state-of-the-art large language models, revealing hidden defects missed by traditional benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LGMT: Logic-Grounded Metamorphic Testing for Evaluating the Reasoning Reliability of LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LGMT (Logic-Grounded Metamorphic Testing), a new framework that uses first-order logic to evaluate the reasoning reliability of large language models (LLMs). Unlike traditional static benchmarks, LGMT tests models by generating logically equivalent variations of problems and checking for consistent reasoning, revealing hidden defects in six state-of-the-art LLMs that previous evaluations missed. This approach highlights the models' sensitivity to subtle changes and challenges the adequacy of current evaluation methods.

LGMT constructs semantically invariant test cases based on formal logical equivalences and detects reasoning errors through cross-case consistency checks without relying on predefined answers. Experiments showed that advanced prompting techniques only partially address these issues, indicating that LLM evaluation should focus more on robustness under logical transformations rather than isolated correctness.

The framework offers a scalable and principled method for diagnosing reasoning failures in LLMs, suggesting a shift in how their logical reasoning capabilities are assessed and potentially guiding future improvements in model development and evaluation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.23965v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve strong performance on logical reasoning benchmarks, yet their reliability remains uncertain. Existing evaluations rely on static benchmarks, which fail to assess robustness under logically equivalent transformations and often overestimate reasoning capability. We propose LGMT (Logic-Grounded Metamorphic Testing), an oracle-free framework that leverages first-order logic (FOL) to evaluate LLM reasoning. By deriving metamorphic relations from formal logical equivalences, LGMT constructs semantically invariant test cases and detects reasoning defects through cross-case consistency checking. Experiments on six state-of-the-art LLMs show that LGMT exposes substantial hidden defects missed by traditional reference-based evaluations. We further find that models are particularly sensitive to symbol-level and conclusion-level variations, and that advanced prompting such as Few-shot CoT only partially mitigates these issues. These results suggest that LLM evaluation should move beyond isolated correctness toward robustness under logical invariance. LGMT provides a principled and scalable approach for diagnosing reasoning failures.

items.title: Researchers propose a policy-based reinforcement learning method for the 20 Questions game that learns optimal question selection without relying on a knowledge base and outperforms entropy-based systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Playing 20 Question Game with Policy-Based Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a policy-based reinforcement learning method for the 20 Questions game that enables the questioner agent to learn optimal question selection strategies through continuous interaction with users. Unlike previous approaches, this method does not rely on a predefined knowledge base and is robust to noisy answers, improving the system's ability to accurately guess the object within 20 questions. Experimental results demonstrate that this reinforcement learning approach outperforms traditional entropy-based systems and performs competitively in noise-free simulation environments.

The proposed method incorporates a reward network to provide more informative feedback during training, facilitating the learning process. This approach addresses the challenges posed by the complexity and variability of the game environment, allowing the questioner to adapt its strategy dynamically without prior knowledge of the objects involved.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:1808.07645v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The 20 Questions (Q20) game is a well known game which encourages deductive reasoning and creativity. In the game, the answerer first thinks of an object such as a famous person or a kind of animal. Then the questioner tries to guess the object by asking 20 questions. In a Q20 game system, the user is considered as the answerer while the system itself acts as the questioner which requires a good strategy of question selection to figure out the correct object and win the game. However, the optimal policy of question selection is hard to be derived due to the complexity and volatility of the game environment. In this paper, we propose a novel policy-based Reinforcement Learning (RL) method, which enables the questioner agent to learn the optimal policy of question selection through continuous interactions with users. To facilitate training, we also propose to use a reward network to estimate the more informative reward. Compared to previous methods, our RL method is robust to noisy answers and does not rely on the Knowledge Base of objects. Experimental results show that our RL method clearly outperforms an entropy-based engineering system and has competitive performance in a noisy-free simulation environment.

items.title: Researchers propose 3DGSim, a learned 3D simulator that captures physical interactions from multi-view RGB videos using particle-based representations and Gaussian splatting for realistic scene reconstruction and dynamics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning 3D-Gaussian Simulators from RGB Videos
items.summary:
Researchers have developed 3DGSim, a learned 3D simulator that captures physical interactions directly from multi-view RGB videos without relying on privileged information like depth data or particle tracking. This end-to-end framework integrates 3D scene reconstruction, particle dynamics prediction, and video synthesis using a particle-based representation and Gaussian splatting to generate realistic novel view renderings. By jointly training inverse rendering and dynamics forecasting, 3DGSim encodes physical properties into latent features, enabling it to model diverse behaviors such as rigid, elastic, and cloth-like dynamics with realistic lighting effects.

3DGSim employs components like MVSplat for latent particle representation, a Point Transformer for dynamics prediction, and a Temporal Merging module for consistent temporal aggregation. This approach overcomes limitations of previous methods that required strong inductive biases or ground truth 3D information, allowing the model to generalize to unseen multibody interactions and novel scene edits while maintaining spatial and temporal consistency.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2503.24009v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Realistic simulation is critical for applications ranging from robotics to animation. Learned simulators have emerged as a possibility to capture real world physics directly from video data, but very often require privileged information such as depth information, particle tracks and hand-engineered features to maintain spatial and temporal consistency. These strong inductive biases or ground truth 3D information help in domains where data is sparse but limit scalability and generalization in data rich regimes. To overcome the key limitations, we propose 3DGSim, a learned 3D simulator that directly learns physical interactions from multi-view RGB videos. 3DGSim unifies 3D scene reconstruction, particle dynamics prediction and video synthesis into an end-to-end trained framework. It adopts MVSplat to learn a latent particle-based representation of 3D scenes, a Point Transformer for particle dynamics, a Temporal Merging module for consistent temporal aggregation and Gaussian Splatting to produce novel view renderings. By jointly training inverse rendering and dynamics forecasting, 3DGSim embeds the physical properties into point-wise latent features. This enables the model to capture diverse physical behaviors, from rigid to elastic, cloth-like dynamics, and boundary conditions (e.g. fixed cloth corner), along with realistic lighting effects that also generalize to unseen multibody interactions and novel scene edits.

items.title: Researchers present MetaTT, a Tensor Train adapter framework for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of pre-trained transformers, demonstrating competitive performance on single-task and multi-task language modeling benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MetaTT: A Global Tensor-Train Adapter for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MetaTT, a Tensor Train adapter framework designed for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of pre-trained transformer models. MetaTT uses a shared tensor train to factorize transformer sub-modules, allowing its parameter count to scale with the sum rather than the product of key structural dimensions, resulting in a more compact adapter. The framework demonstrates competitive performance compared to existing methods like LoRA on both single-task and multi-task language modeling benchmarks.

The design of MetaTT includes indexing across layers, matrix types, and optionally heads and tasks, enhancing its flexibility. Additionally, the researchers developed a rank adaptive optimizer inspired by the DMRG method from many-body physics, which, when integrated with AdamW, improves optimization performance for a specified target rank. These advancements suggest MetaTT as an effective approach for efficient transformer fine-tuning with promising optimization capabilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2506.09105v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present MetaTT, a Tensor Train (TT) adapter framework for fine-tuning of pre-trained transformers. MetaTT enables flexible and parameter-efficient model adaptation by using a single shared TT to factorize transformer sub-modules. This factorization indexes key structural dimensions, including layer and matrix type, and can optionally incorporate heads and tasks. This design allows MetaTT's parameter count to scale with the sum, rather than the product, of the modes, resulting in a substantially more compact adapter. Our benchmarks compare MetaTT with LoRA along with recent state-of-the-art matrix and tensor decomposition based fine-tuning methods. We observe that when tested on single-task standard language modeling benchmarks, MetaTT achieves competitive parameter efficiency to accuracy tradeoff. We further demonstrate that MetaTT performs competitively when compared to state-of-the-art methods on multi-task learning. Finally, we leverage the TT decomposition to design a rank adaptive optimizer inspired by the DMRG method from many-body physics. Our results demonstrate that integrating this approach with AdamW enhances optimization performance for a specified target rank.

items.title: Researchers introduce MedRepBench, a benchmark with 1,925 Chinese medical report images for structured report interpretation and patient-facing explanation evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MedRepBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Medical Report Interpretation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MedRepBench, a new benchmark dataset comprising 1,925 de-identified Chinese medical report images designed to advance structured interpretation and patient-facing explanation in medical report understanding. The benchmark focuses on extracting structured fields from reports and generating explanations grounded strictly in the report content, primarily evaluating end-to-end vision-language models (VLMs) and including a controlled text-only setting to approximate upper performance bounds.

MedRepBench covers diverse medical departments, patient demographics, and acquisition formats, and provides two evaluation protocols: an objective metric measuring field-level recall and a subjective LLM-based scoring of factuality, interpretability, and reasoning quality. The researchers also present a baseline model that improves recall by up to 6% and analyze limitations of OCR plus language model pipelines, highlighting the need for robust vision-based approaches. The dataset and evaluation tools are publicly available for further research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2508.16674v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Medical report understanding from real-world document images is essential for generating patient-facing explanations and enabling structured information exchange in clinical systems. Existing VLMs and LLMs have shown strong performance on document understanding, but structured understanding of medical reports remains insufficiently benchmarked. Therefore, we introduce MedRepBench, a benchmark with 1,925 de-identified Chinese medical report images spanning diverse departments, patient demographics, and acquisition formats. In MedRepBench, we mainly focus on report-grounded interpretation rather than evaluating diagnostic reasoning, treatment recommendation, or the integration of patient history. The interpretation is defined as structured extraction of report fields (e.g., item, value, unit, reference range, abnormal flag) plus a patient-facing explanation grounded strictly in the report content. The benchmark primarily evaluates end-to-end VLMs, and also includes a controlled text-only setting (high-quality OCR + LLM) to approximate an upper bound when character recognition errors are minimized. Our evaluation framework provides two complementary protocols: (1) an objective protocol measuring field-level recall of structured items, and (2) an automated subjective protocol that uses an LLM-based judge to score factuality, interpretability, and reasoning quality under a fixed prompt. Using the objective metric as a reward signal, we also provide a lightweight GRPO-based alignment baseline for a mid-sized VLM, which improves field-level recall by up to 6%. Finally, we analyze practical limitations of OCR+LLM pipelines, including layout-related errors and additional system latency, showing the need for robust end-to-end vision-based medical report understanding. The dataset and evaluation resources are publicly available on https://huggingface.co/datasets/MedRepBench/MedRepBench.

items.title: Researchers introduce PsySET benchmark to evaluate effectiveness and trustworthiness of psychological steering in large language models across emotion and personality domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Psychological Steering in LLMs: An Evaluation of Effectiveness and Trustworthiness
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced PsySET, a new benchmark designed to evaluate the effectiveness and trustworthiness of psychological steering in large language models (LLMs) across emotion and personality domains. The study tested four different LLMs using various steering methods such as prompting, fine-tuning, and representation engineering. Results showed that prompting is generally effective but limited in controlling intensity, while vector injections offer finer control at the cost of some output quality.

The research also assessed the trustworthiness of these steered models by examining factors like safety, truthfulness, fairness, and ethics, revealing potential side effects and behavioral changes. For example, inducing positive emotions like joy can reduce robustness to adversarial factuality and increase bias, whereas anger increases toxicity but improves resistance to data leakage. This work provides the first comprehensive evaluation of emotion and personality steering in LLMs, offering valuable insights for their use in socially interactive applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2510.04484v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The ability to control LLMs' emulated emotional states and personality traits is an essential step in enabling rich, human-centered interactions in socially interactive settings. We introduce PsySET, a Psychologically-informed benchmark to evaluate LLM Steering Effectiveness and Trustworthiness across the emotion and personality domains. Our study spans four models from different LLM families paired with various steering strategies, including prompting, fine-tuning, and representation engineering. Our results indicate that prompting is consistently effective but limited in intensity control, whereas vector injections achieve finer controllability while slightly reducing output quality. Moreover, we explore the trustworthiness of steered LLMs by assessing safety, truthfulness, fairness, and ethics, highlighting potential side effects and behavioral shifts. Notably, we observe idiosyncratic effects; for instance, even a positive emotion like joy can degrade robustness to adversarial factuality, lower privacy awareness, and increase preferential bias. Meanwhile, anger predictably elevates toxicity yet strengthens leakage resistance. Our framework establishes the first holistic evaluation of emotion and personality steering, offering insights into its interpretability and reliability for socially interactive applications.

items.title: Researchers propose CreativityPrism, a scalable cross-domain framework evaluating 17 large language models on creativity across divergent thinking, creative writing, and logical reasoning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CreativityPrism: A Cross-Domain Evaluation Framework for Large Language Model Creativity
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced CreativityPrism, a scalable evaluation framework designed to assess the creativity of large language models (LLMs) across multiple domains, including divergent thinking, creative writing, and logical reasoning. The framework measures creativity along three dimensions: quality, novelty, and diversity, using eight tasks and automated evaluation methods validated against human judgments. This approach addresses the limitations of previous evaluations that were either domain-specific or heavily reliant on human input, hindering scalability and comprehensive assessment.

The study evaluated 17 state-of-the-art LLMs using CreativityPrism, revealing that while leading large-scale models outperform open-source models in creative writing and logical reasoning by about 15%, they do not show significant advantages in divergent thinking tasks. Additionally, the analysis found that strong performance in one creative dimension or domain does not necessarily translate to others, with novelty often showing weak or negative correlations with other metrics. These findings highlight the importance of a multi-dimensional, cross-domain framework like CreativityPrism for a meaningful evaluation of LLM creativity.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2510.20091v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Creativity is often seen as a hallmark of human intelligence. While large language models(LLMs) are increasingly perceived as generating creative text, there is still no cross-domain and scalable framework to evaluate their creativity across diverse scenarios. Existing methods of LLM creativity evaluation either heavily rely on humans, limiting speed and scalability, or are fragmented across different domains and different definitions of creativity. To address this gap, we propose CreativityPrism, an evaluation and analysis framework that consolidates eight tasks from three domains: divergent thinking, creative writing, and logical reasoning, into a taxonomy of creativity that emphasizes three dimensions: quality, novelty, and diversity of LLM generations. The framework is designed to be scalable with reliable automatic evaluation judges that have been validated against human annotations. We evaluate 17 state-of-the-art (SoTA) LLMs on CreativityPrism and find that while frontier-scale LLMs dominate creative writing and logical reasoning tasks by a .10 (or 15%) lead over locally-deployable open models, they offer no significant advantage in divergent thinking, a domain much less explored in existing post-training regimes. Our analysis also shows that high performance in one creative dimension or domain rarely generalizes to others; specifically, novelty metrics often show weak or negative correlations with other metrics. This fragmentation confirms that a cross-domain, multi-dimensional framework like CreativityPrism is essential for any meaningful assessment of LLM creativity.

items.title: Researchers present a computational framework using deep learning and LLM Claude 3.5 to model human neurophysiological and cognitive adaptation across altered gravity environments for spaceflight [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Gravity-Awareness: Deep Learning Models and LLM Simulation of Human Awareness in Altered Gravity
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a computational framework that uses deep learning and the large language model Claude 3.5 to simulate human neurophysiological and cognitive adaptation to altered gravity environments, such as those encountered in spaceflight. The framework includes two components: CorticalG, a neural network predicting gravity-dependent changes in EEG patterns, and PhysioG, which models physiological responses like heart rate variability and motor control. Additionally, Claude 3.5 generates narratives describing subjective experiences across different gravity conditions, including zero gravity and partial gravity on the Moon and Mars.

This approach is based on open-access data from altered-gravity studies, particularly parabolic flights, and integrates quantitative physiological modeling with simulated subjective awareness. It offers a novel tool for predicting human performance and resilience in space environments, potentially aiding the design of future space exploration missions by providing insights into how the brain and body adapt to varying gravitational forces.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2511.05536v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Earth s gravity fundamentally shapes human behaviour. The brain encodes this force as an internal model of gravity, enabling the prediction and interpretation of gravitational effects during perception and action. Understanding how this model adapts to altered gravity is critical for predicting human performance in spaceflight. We present a computational framework for modelling neurophysiological adaptation across diverse gravitational environments. The framework has two components trained on open-access data from altered-gravity studies, particularly parabolic flights. The first component (CorticalG) employs a lightweight multilayer perceptron neural network to predict gravity-dependent changes in EEG frequency bands, estimating cortical state under different gravitational loads. The second component (PhysioG) uses independent Gaussian process models to capture broader physiological responses, including heart rate variability, electrodermal activity, and motor control. To complement the quantitative modelling, we simulated subjective experience across gravitational environments using the Large Language Model (LLM) Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Physiological outputs prompted the model to generate narratives describing alertness, bodily awareness, and cognitive state across zero gravity, partial gravity of the Moon and Mars, and hypergravity. This framework provides a novel approach for investigating human adaptation to spaceflight. It offers a predictive tool to assess performance and resilience, supporting the design of future space exploration missions.

items.title: Researchers propose a theoretical framework for evaluation-aligned training signals in multi-LLM agent systems, unifying game-theoretic attribution with process reward modeling for improved cooperation and error correction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Who Gets the Reward & Who Gets the Blame? Evaluation-Aligned Training Signals for Multi-LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a theoretical framework to improve training signals in multi-agent systems using large language models (LLMs). This framework integrates cooperative game-theoretic attribution with process reward modeling to translate system-level evaluations into detailed, agent- and message-level feedback. The approach generates local, signed, and credit-conserving signals that fairly allocate rewards in successful interactions and identify errors for corrective actions in failures, promoting cooperation and reducing redundancy or sabotage.

Unlike previous methods that relied solely on attribution or step-level labels, this new framework produces bounded and cooperative signals compatible with reinforcement or preference-based post-training. It offers a unified and auditable pathway from global system evaluation to local supervision, enhancing the training of multi-LLM agents. The contribution is conceptual, providing a foundation and training signals, with empirical validation planned for future research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2511.10687v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) in multi-agent systems (MAS) have shown promise for complex tasks, yet current training methods lack principled ways to connect system-level evaluation with agent- and message-level learning. We propose a theoretical framework that unifies cooperative game-theoretic attribution with process reward modeling to transform system evaluation to agent credit to response-level signals. Unlike prior approaches that rely only on attribution (Shapley) or step-level labels (PRM), our method produces local, signed, and credit-conserving signals. In success cases, Shapley-based credit assignment fairly allocates outcomes across agents and is refined into per-message rewards that promote cooperation while discouraging redundancy or sabotage; in failure cases, first-error localization yields repair-aware preferences that penalize harmful steps while rewarding corrective attempts. The resulting signals are bounded, cooperative, and directly compatible with reinforcement- or preference-based post-training, providing a unified and auditable pathway from global evaluation to local supervision in LLM multi-agent training. Our contribution is conceptual: we present a theoretical foundation and training signals, leaving empirical validation for future work.

items.title: Researchers propose Locality-Aware Continual Unlearning (LACU) framework for diffusion models to enable stable sequential concept removal with improved retention over 10 steps [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Locality-Aware Continual Unlearning for Diffusion Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the Locality-Aware Continual Unlearning (LACU) framework to improve the stability of sequential concept removal in text-to-image diffusion models. This approach addresses the limitations of existing unlearning methods, which typically fail after a few sequential deletions due to coarse mapping targets and lack of protection for semantically related concepts. LACU employs targeted updates and local replay mechanisms to minimize collateral damage to related concepts, enabling stable unlearning over 10 sequential steps while preserving higher retention of related and general concepts compared to previous methods.

The framework uses a score-prediction distance metric to select context-preserving mapping prompts and identify closely related concepts for local replay, effectively shielding vulnerable semantic neighborhoods. Combined with teacher-student distillation and lightweight parameter regularization, LACU ensures that each unlearning step is precise and minimally disruptive, overcoming the degradation issues seen in prior approaches.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2512.02657v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Real-world deployment of text-to-image diffusion models requires continual concept removal as new privacy, copyright, or safety obligations arise over time. Existing unlearning methods, however, are designed for single-step deletion and collapse after only 3-5 sequential applications. We trace this instability to two compounding factors: (i) coarse mapping targets that cause degradation to accumulate unnecessarily across steps, and (ii) the absence of local protection for semantically neighboring concepts, whose shared internal representations make them the first to suffer collateral damage. Because this damage is strongest in the local semantic neighborhood of the forget concept, global replay alone cannot prevent it. Building on this analysis, we propose Locality-Aware Continual Unlearning (LACU), a framework with two complementary mechanisms. Locality-Aware Target Selection chooses, for each forget prompt, the context-preserving mapping prompt that the diffusion model itself treats as most similar to the original prompt, measured by score-prediction distance (how differently the model denoises the same noisy image under two text conditions), ensuring each update is as small and targeted as possible. Locality-Aware Replay uses the same metric to identify the retain concepts closest to the forget concept in the model's own representation and replays them as a local functional regularizer, directly shielding the most vulnerable neighborhood. Combined with teacher-student distillation and lightweight $\ell_2$ parameter regularization, LACU maintains stable unlearning over 10 sequential steps, preserving significantly higher related retention ($RR_{\text{acc}}$) and general retention ($GR_{\text{acc}}$) than recent baselines.

items.title: Researchers establish conditions where predictive inverse dynamics models outperform behavior cloning in sample efficiency and prediction error, validated in 2D navigation and 3D video game environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Does Predictive Inverse Dynamics Outperform Behavior Cloning?
items.summary:
Researchers have identified specific conditions under which predictive inverse dynamics models (PIDMs) outperform behavior cloning (BC) in imitation learning, particularly in terms of sample efficiency and prediction accuracy. PIDMs combine future-state prediction with inverse dynamics modeling, which helps reduce variance but introduces some bias. The study provides a theoretical framework explaining this tradeoff and demonstrates that PIDMs require fewer expert demonstrations than BC to achieve similar or better performance.

The findings were validated through experiments in both 2D navigation tasks and a complex 3D video game environment with high-dimensional visual inputs and stochastic transitions. In these tests, BC needed significantly more samples—up to five times in 2D tasks and over 66% more in the 3D environment—compared to PIDMs. The research highlights how additional data sources can further widen the performance gap between the two methods, offering insights into improving offline imitation learning techniques.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.21718v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Behavior cloning (BC) is a practical offline imitation learning method, but it often fails when expert demonstrations are limited. Recent works have introduced a class of architectures named predictive inverse dynamics models (PIDMs) that combine a future-state predictor with an inverse dynamics model. While PIDMs often outperform BC, the reasons behind their benefits remain unclear. In this paper, we provide a theoretical explanation: PIDMs introduce a tradeoff. Conditioning the IDM on the predicted future state can significantly reduce variance, but the prediction itself introduces additional bias and variance. We establish conditions for PIDMs to achieve higher sample efficiency and lower prediction error than BC, with the gap widening when additional data sources are available. We validate the theoretical insights empirically in 2D navigation tasks, where BC requires up to five times (three times on average) more demonstrations than PIDM to reach comparable performance. Results are also illustrated in a complex 3D environment in a modern video game with high-dimensional visual inputs and stochastic transitions, where BC requires over 66\% more samples than PIDM.

items.title: Researchers derive non-Euclidean gradient noise scales for signSGD and specSGD, enabling adaptive batch sizes that reduce training steps by up to 66% on a 160M parameter Llama model [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Adaptive Batch Sizes Using Non-Euclidean Gradient Noise Scales for Stochastic Sign and Spectral Descent
items.summary:
Researchers have developed non-Euclidean gradient noise scales tailored for the signSGD and specSGD optimization methods, which use generalized norms rather than the traditional Euclidean geometry assumed by standard SGD. This advancement allows for adaptive batch size strategies that significantly improve training efficiency, reducing the number of training steps by up to 66% on a 160 million parameter Llama model while maintaining comparable validation loss to constant batch size baselines.

The team derived these gradient noise scales from the geometry of the dual norms associated with signSGD and specSGD and introduced an efficient variance estimation technique that utilizes local mini-batch gradients across distributed data-parallel systems. Their experiments demonstrate that leveraging these non-Euclidean metrics enables more effective batch size adaptation, addressing limitations of previous heuristic or manually tuned batch scheduling approaches in large-scale machine learning training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.03001v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: To maximize hardware utilization, modern machine learning systems typically employ large constant or manually tuned batch size schedules, relying on heuristics that are brittle and costly to tune. Existing adaptive strategies based on gradient noise scale (GNS) offer a principled alternative. However, their assumption of SGD's Euclidean geometry creates a fundamental mismatch with popular optimizers based on generalized norms, such as signSGD / Signum ($\ell_\infty$) and stochastic spectral descent (specSGD) / Muon ($\mathcal{S}_\infty$). In this work, we derive gradient noise scales for signSGD and specSGD that naturally emerge from the geometry of their respective dual norms. To practically estimate these non-Euclidean metrics, we propose an efficient variance estimation procedure that leverages the local mini-batch gradients on different ranks in distributed data-parallel systems. Our experiments demonstrate that adaptive batch size strategies using non-Euclidean GNS enable us to match the validation loss of constant-batch baselines while reducing training steps by up to 66\% for Signum and Muon on a 160 million parameter Llama model.

items.title: Researchers present LEFT, a unified unsupervised time series anomaly detection framework using learnable fusion of tri-view tokens across time, frequency, and multi-scale domains with cycle consistency constraints [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LEFT: Learnable Fusion of Tri-view Tokens for Unsupervised Time Series Anomaly Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LEFT, a unified unsupervised framework for time series anomaly detection that integrates learnable fusion of tri-view tokens across time, frequency, and multi-scale domains. This approach addresses the challenge of subtle anomalies that may not be detectable in a single view by modeling inconsistencies across complementary representations. LEFT uses adaptive spectral filters to rescale time series data into multiple resolutions and employs a novel cycle consistency constraint to enforce agreement between time and frequency views during training.

The framework learns feature tokens capturing periodicity, local dynamics, and abnormal patterns at varying granularities, enabling effective coordination among the three views with lightweight encoders. By reconstructing fine-grained targets from coarser multi-scale structures, LEFT enhances anomaly detection without relying on annotated data, offering a robust solution for unsupervised time series analysis.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.08638v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As a fundamental data mining task, unsupervised time series anomaly detection (TSAD) aims to build a model for identifying abnormal timestamps without assuming the availability of annotations. A key challenge in unsupervised TSAD is that many anomalies are too subtle to exhibit detectable deviation in any single view (e.g., time domain), and instead manifest as inconsistencies across multiple views like time, frequency, and a mixture of resolutions. However, most cross-view methods rely on feature or score fusion and do not enforce analysis-synthesis consistency, meaning the frequency branch is not required to reconstruct the time signal through an inverse transform, and vice versa. In this paper, we present Learnable Fusion of Tri-view Tokens (LEFT), a unified unsupervised TSAD framework that models anomalies as inconsistencies across complementary representations. LEFT learns feature tokens from three views of the same input time series: frequency domain tokens that embed periodicity information, time domain tokens that capture local dynamics, and multi-scale tokens that learn abnormal patterns at varying time series granularities. By learning a set of adaptive Nyquist-constrained spectral filters, the original time series is rescaled into multiple resolutions and then encoded, allowing these multi-scale tokens to complement the extracted frequency and time domain information. When generating the fused representation, we introduce a novel objective that reconstructs fine-grained targets from coarser multi-scale structure, and put forward an innovative time-frequency cycle consistency constraint to explicitly regularize cross-view agreement. As cross-view agreement is explicitly regularized during training, LEFT can adopt lightweight tri-view encoders while maintaining effective coordination among the three views.

items.title: Researchers introduce principled width-based upscaling and hyperparameter transfer methods for small neural models to accelerate training and reduce tuning costs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: $\mu$pscaling small models: Principled warm starts and hyperparameter transfer
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a principled method for upscaling small neural network models to larger sizes, aiming to accelerate training and reduce the cost of hyperparameter tuning. Their approach builds on existing techniques by introducing width-dependent scaling for weight perturbations and optimizer hyperparameters, ensuring that the upscaled model remains functionally equivalent to the original during training when no perturbation is applied. This method leverages theoretical insights from infinite-width neural network analysis to enable effective hyperparameter transfer from smaller to larger models.

The team demonstrated the effectiveness of their approach on realistic datasets and architectures, showing that it can significantly reduce the tuning effort required when scaling models. By grounding their method in established theory and providing empirical validation, this work offers a practical solution for efficiently training large neural networks initialized from smaller counterparts, which is particularly valuable for accommodating diverse inference budgets.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.10545v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern large-scale neural networks are often trained and released in multiple sizes to accommodate diverse inference budgets. To improve efficiency, recent work has explored model upscaling: initializing larger models from trained smaller ones to accelerate convergence. However, this method can be sensitive to hyperparameters that need to be tuned at the target upscaled model size, which is prohibitively costly to do directly. It remains unclear whether tuning hyperparameters on smaller models and extrapolating via scaling laws is sound in this setting. We address this with principled approaches to width-based upscaling and efficient hyperparameter tuning in this setting. Motivated by $\mu$P and any-dimensional architectures, we introduce a general upscaling method that, like Net2Net, copies and perturbs weights, but uses theoretically grounded, width-dependent scalings for the perturbation noise and optimizer hyperparameters. First, we prove that under zero perturbation, the upscaled model is functionally equivalent to the base model throughout training. Second, we extend the $\mu$P theory to enable infinite-width limit analysis and establish hyperparameter transfer for upscaled models, greatly reducing the tuning cost. We empirically demonstrate that this method is effective on realistic datasets and architectures.

items.title: Researchers propose group-conditional federated conformal prediction for uncertainty quantification across distributed client data with mergeable coresets and validate it on synthetic and real-world datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Efficient Federated Conformal Prediction with Group-Conditional Guarantee
items.summary:
Researchers have developed group-conditional federated conformal prediction (GC-FCP), a method for uncertainty quantification in AI systems that operates across distributed client data. This approach extends conformal prediction to federated settings where calibration data are spread across multiple clients with varying local distributions, often grouped by demographic or semantic attributes. GC-FCP creates mergeable, atom-stratified coresets from local calibration scores, allowing efficient aggregation at a central server while maintaining distribution-free coverage guarantees.

The team validated GC-FCP on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness compared to centralized calibration methods. This technique is particularly relevant for applications in healthcare, finance, and mobile sensing, where data privacy and heterogeneity are critical concerns. The researchers have made their code publicly available to support further exploration and adoption of this federated calibration approach.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.14198v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deploying trustworthy AI systems requires principled uncertainty quantification. Conformal prediction (CP) is a widely used framework for constructing prediction sets with distribution-free coverage guarantees. In many practical settings, including healthcare, finance, and mobile sensing, the calibration data required for CP are distributed across multiple clients, each with its own local data distribution. In this federated setting, data can often be partitioned into, potentially overlapping, groups, which may reflect client-specific strata or cross-cutting attributes such as demographic or semantic categories. We propose group-conditional federated conformal prediction (GC-FCP), a federated extension of conditional conformal calibration for a target mixture over prespecified groups. GC-FCP constructs mergeable, atom-stratified coresets from local calibration scores, enabling compact aggregation at the server when the number of active atoms is moderate. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets validate the performance of GC-FCP compared to centralized calibration baselines. The code of our work can be found at https://github.com/HaifengWen/GC-FCP.

items.summary:
Researchers have developed adaptive contracts for delegating AI text generation tasks that aim to reduce evaluation costs while maintaining cost-effectiveness. These contracts enable selective detailed evaluation based on an initial coarse assessment, addressing the challenge that more elaborate evaluation methods, despite reducing noise, often increase overall costs. The study presents efficient algorithms for computing optimal adaptive contracts under certain conditions and explores randomized adaptive contract models, supported by empirical validation on question-answering and code generation datasets.

The work highlights the trade-off between evaluation noise and cost in pay-for-performance AI contracts and offers solutions that optimize resource use by adapting the evaluation process. The researchers also prove the computational complexity of the problem in general cases and demonstrate the practical benefits of their approach compared to non-adaptive methods through experiments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.17212v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When organizations delegate text generation tasks to AI providers via pay-for-performance contracts, expected payments rise when evaluation is noisy. As evaluation methods become more elaborate, the economic benefits of decreased noise are often overshadowed by increased evaluation costs. In this work, we introduce adaptive contracts for AI delegation, which allow detailed evaluation to be performed selectively after observing an initial coarse signal in order to conserve resources. We make three sets of contributions: First, we provide efficient algorithms for computing optimal adaptive contracts under natural assumptions or when core problem dimensions are small, and prove hardness of approximation in the general unstructured case. We then formulate alternative models of randomized adaptive contracts and discuss their benefits and limitations. Finally, we empirically demonstrate the benefits of adaptivity over non-adaptive baselines using question-answering and code-generation datasets.

items.title: Researchers introduce RRPO, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes RAG rerankers using LLM feedback to improve generation quality without human annotations, outperforming existing baselines on knowledge-intensive benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Optimizing RAG Rerankers with LLM Feedback via Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ReRanking Preference Optimization (RRPO), a reinforcement learning framework designed to improve Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) rerankers by directly aligning them with the quality of large language model (LLM) outputs. Unlike traditional rerankers that rely on static human-annotated relevance labels, RRPO uses LLM feedback to optimize reranking as a sequential decision-making process, eliminating the need for costly human annotations and enhancing the utility of retrieved documents for precise answer generation.

Extensive testing on knowledge-intensive benchmarks shows that RRPO outperforms strong existing rerankers, including RankZephyr. The framework is versatile, generalizing well to different LLM readers such as GPT-4o, integrating effectively with query expansion techniques like Query2Doc, and maintaining robustness even when trained with noisy supervision. This approach addresses a key misalignment in current reranking methods by focusing on the actual usefulness of documents for downstream generation tasks rather than just topical relevance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.02091v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rerankers play a pivotal role in refining retrieval results for Retrieval-Augmented Generation. However, current reranking models are typically optimized on static human annotated relevance labels in isolation, decoupled from the downstream generation process. This isolation leads to a fundamental misalignment: documents identified as topically relevant by information retrieval metrics often fail to provide the actual utility required by the LLM for precise answer generation. To bridge this gap, we introduce ReRanking Preference Optimization (RRPO), a reinforcement learning framework that directly aligns reranking with the LLM's generation quality. By formulating reranking as a sequential decision-making process, RRPO optimizes for context utility using LLM feedback, thereby eliminating the need for expensive human annotations. To ensure training stability, we further introduce a reference-anchored deterministic baseline. Extensive experiments on knowledge-intensive benchmarks demonstrate that RRPO significantly outperforms strong baselines, including the powerful list-wise reranker RankZephyr. Further analysis highlights the versatility of our framework: it generalizes seamlessly to diverse readers (e.g., GPT-4o), integrates orthogonally with query expansion modules like Query2Doc, and remains robust even when trained with noisy supervisors.

items.title: Researchers localize Agent-as-a-Judge prompts to five languages, finding language and backbone model interactions affect evaluation rankings across 4950 runs on 55 DevAI tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Multilingual Prompt Localization for Agent-as-a-Judge: Language and Backbone Sensitivity in Requirement-Level Evaluation
items.summary:
Researchers have localized the Agent-as-a-Judge evaluation prompts into five diverse languages—English, Arabic, Turkish, Chinese, and Hindi—and conducted 4,950 evaluation runs across 55 development tasks using multiple developer-agent frameworks and judge backbones. Their study reveals that the language used by the judge significantly influences the ranking of backbone models, with no single model consistently outperforming others across all languages. For example, GPT-4o scored highest in English, while Gemini led in Arabic and Hindi.

The study also found that localizing judge-side instructions, not just the benchmark content, impacts evaluation outcomes, as demonstrated by a notable drop in satisfaction scores when Hindi instructions were only partially localized. These findings suggest that language should be considered an explicit variable in agentic benchmark evaluations. The researchers have made full requirement-level judgments and runtime data publicly available to support reproducibility and further analysis.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.04532v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evaluation language is typically treated as a fixed English default in agentic code benchmarks, yet we show that changing the judge's language can invert backbone rankings. We localize the Agent-as-a-Judge prompt stack to five typologically diverse languages (English, Arabic, Turkish, Chinese, Hindi) and evaluate 55 DevAI development tasks across three developer-agent frameworks and six judge backbones, totaling 4950 judge runs. The central finding is that backbone and language interact: GPT-4o achieves the highest satisfaction in English (44.72\%), while Gemini leads in Arabic (51.72\%, $p<0.001$ vs.\ GPT-4o) and Hindi (53.22\%). No single backbone dominates across all languages, and inter-backbone agreement on individual requirement judgments is modest (Fleiss' $\kappa \leq 0.231$). A controlled ablation further shows that localizing judge-side instructions, not just benchmark content, can be decisive: Hindi satisfaction drops from 42.8\% to 23.2\% under partial localization. These results indicate that language should be treated as an explicit evaluation variable in agentic benchmarks. Full requirement-level judgments and runtime statistics are released for reproducibility.

items.title: Researchers analyze cultural bias in nine large vision-language models across 4.8 million outputs, identifying socioeconomic and race-related stereotype patterns in moral and political value judgments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cross-Cultural Value Attribution in Large Vision-Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a comprehensive analysis of nine large vision-language models (LVLMs) to investigate cultural biases in their moral, ethical, and political value judgments. Examining 4.8 million model outputs using images depicting the same individuals across different cultural contexts, the study identified consistent patterns of bias related to socioeconomic status and race, particularly involving Middle Eastern persons. These biases include an inversion of the expected relationship between socioeconomic status and authority and race-conditional errors that override cultural cues.

The evaluation combined descriptive methods based on Moral Foundations Theory and lexical analyses with a novel grounding approach comparing model outputs to large-scale human survey data. The findings reveal that image conditioning amplifies certain biases and that these issues persist across various model architectures and sizes, highlighting challenges in ensuring fairness and cultural sensitivity in LVLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.09945v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rapid adoption of large vision-language models (LVLMs) in recent years has been accompanied by growing fairness concerns due to their propensity to reinforce harmful societal stereotypes. While significant attention has been paid to such fairness concerns in the context of social biases, relatively little prior work has examined the presence of stereotypes in LVLMs related to cultural contexts such as religion, nationality, and socioeconomic status. In this work, we aim to narrow this gap by investigating how cultural contexts depicted in images influence the judgments LVLMs make about a person's moral, ethical, and political values. We conduct a multi-dimensional analysis of such value judgments in nine LVLMs using counterfactual image sets, which depict the same person across different cultural contexts. Our evaluation framework pairs descriptive analyses (Moral Foundations Theory categorization, lexical analyses, and value sensitivity) with a novel grounding analysis that compares LVLM cross-context variation against two large-scale human surveys (MFQ-2 and WVS Wave 7). Across 4.8 million LVLM generations, we identify three bias patterns that replicate across architecturally diverse models: an inversion of the socioeconomic-status-to-Authority relationship found in WVS, and two race-conditional failures that override cultural context cues when depicting Middle Eastern persons. Additional ablations show that the socioeconomic-status-to-Authority inversion bias is amplified by image conditioning and persists across different model sizes.
